001.json.summary: After opening prayers to Vishnu's feet, to Vishnu lying on the serpent in the milk ocean, and to Nara, Narayana, Sarasvati and Vyasa, the book begins. Jaimini, a disciple of Vyasa, comes to the great sage Markandeya and praises the Mahabharata: as Vishnu is first among gods and the Brahmin among people, so it is the best of all teachings, covering duty, wealth, desire and freedom. He has four doubts about it: why Vishnu (Janardana), who is beyond all qualities, took a human birth; why Draupadi was the shared wife of the five Pandavas; why Balarama went on pilgrimage to atone for killing a Brahmin; and why Draupadi's five unmarried sons, the great warriors, were killed as if they had no protector. Markandeya says it is his time for rites and not for a long talk, and sends Jaimini to four wise birds, Pingaksha, Vibodha, Suputra and Sumukha, sons of Drona, who live in a cave of the Vindhya mountains and know the Vedas and the scriptures. Jaimini, amazed that birds could have such knowledge, asks how this came about. Markandeya tells a story: in Indra's Nandana garden, Narada found Indra among the apsaras; Indra offered to let whichever dancer Narada liked dance for him, Rambha, Urvashi, Tilottama, Ghritachi, Menaka or another. Narada said the one who thought herself best in beauty and qualities should dance, and when they argued, he said the best was the one who could shake the great sage Durvasas out of his penance. All were afraid except the apsara Vapu, who boasted she would make him a poor charioteer of his senses. She went to his hermitage on the Himalaya and sang sweetly nearby; the sage came, saw her, controlled his mind and, knowing she came to disturb him, cursed her in anger: she would be born as a bird in the family of Garuda for sixteen years, would bear four sons, would find no joy in them, and, killed by a weapon, would return to heaven. Then he left for the heavenly Ganga.

002.json.summary: Markandeya continues the story. From Garuda, son of Arishtanemi, came Sampati, then Suparshva, Kunti and Pralolupa, whose sons were Kanka and Kandhara. On a peak of Kailasa, Kanka met a rakshasa named Vidyudrupa, a follower of Kubera, drinking with his wife; the rakshasa angrily asked why he came near while he was with his wife, and when Kanka said the mountain belonged to all, cut him down with his sword. Kandhara, enraged, did his brother's funeral rites, flew to the rakshasa, found him drunk on a golden couch with his wife Madanika, and challenged him; the rakshasa threw his sword, Kandhara caught it in his beak and broke it, and in the fight that followed tore off his head, arms and legs. The frightened wife took refuge with the bird and offered to be his wife; he took her home. This woman, a daughter of Menaka who could take any form, took a bird form, and Kandhara had by her a daughter named Tarkshi, who was in fact the apsara Vapu, burned by the sage's curse. Mandapala had four wise sons, Jaritari and others, the youngest of whom, Drona, learned in the Vedas, married Tarkshi with Kandhara's consent. When she was seven fortnights pregnant she went to Kurukshetra during the great war between the Kurus and Pandavas and flew into the battle between Bhagadatta and Arjuna; an arrow from Arjuna's bow cut open her belly, and four eggs, white as the moon, fell gently on the ground as if onto cotton, since their lives were not yet over. At the same moment the great bell of Bhagadatta's elephant Supratika, its cord cut by an arrow, fell and covered the eggs. After the war, when Yudhishthira had gone to hear Bhishma's teachings, the sage Shamika came by, heard chirping, lifted the bell and found the motherless chicks. Amazed, he told his disciples that Shukra's words to the fleeing demons had come true: no one dies before the time fixed by the Creator, however he fights or flees, as the demon Shambara survived Indra's thunderbolt but other demons died when their time came. These were no ordinary birds, he said; fate favoured them. He had them taken to the hermitage and kept safe from cats, mice, hawks and mongooses, saying that creatures live or die by their own deeds, yet people must still make effort in all things. He then gathered roots, flowers, fruit and kusha grass and performed the Vedic worship of Vishnu, Rudra, Brahma, Indra, Yama, Agni, Varuna, Kubera, Vayu and the other gods.

003.json.summary: Shamika fed and protected the chicks every day. In a month they flew along the path of the sun's chariot, saw the earth with its cities, oceans and rivers no bigger than a chariot wheel, and returned; by the sage's power their knowledge became clear. They walked around him, bowed and thanked him as their father and teacher for saving them from death, and asked what they should do. Shamika, with his disciples and his son Shringi, asked them to explain how they came to speak and by whose curse they had become birds. The birds said they were the four sons of the sage Sukrisha, brother of Tumburu and son of Vipulasvan, and served their father humbly. Once Indra, wishing to test the sage and to bring about their curse, came as a huge, old, broken-winged bird and begged for food, saying that only human flesh would satisfy him. The sage wondered at such cruelty in old age but said a promise must be kept, called his sons and told them to give their flesh and blood to the bird. Trembling, they refused: a wise person should not destroy his own body for another's; a son pays the debts to ancestors, gods and men but is not meant to give his body; one who lives can do good. In a rage the sage cursed them to be born as animals, then did his own last rites and offered his body to the bird, saying that keeping one's word is the true mark of a Brahmin and brings more merit than sacrifices. Indra said he never eats a living creature and asked him to leave the body by yoga; when the sage was ready, Indra showed his true form, asked pardon, said the test was over, and granted him divine knowledge and freedom from obstacles. The sons then begged their father's pardon, explaining that they feared death and loved life, and described the body as a city with walls of bone and skin and nine gates, ruled by the soul, with intelligence and mind as ministers, attacked by desire, anger, greed and delusion; when attachment enters through the senses, the mind is captured, intelligence is lost and the king perishes; from attachment comes anger, from anger greed, from greed delusion, then loss of memory and of intelligence. The father said his word could not be false, and blamed fate, which had made him do what he never meant; but since they had pleased him, as animals they would gain the highest knowledge and, free of all stains, reach perfection. So, the birds say, they were cursed, born in the battlefield and saved by Shamika, for no one in this world escapes fate. Shamika let them go, and they went to the Vindhya mountains, where these righteous birds still live, devoted to penance, study and meditation.

004.json.summary: Markandeya tells Jaimini to go and question the birds. Jaimini goes to the Vindhya, hears them reciting the Vedas with perfect pronunciation and breath, and marvels that Sarasvati does not leave even those born as animals; everything else leaves a person, but learning does not. He greets them as Vyasa's disciple and comforts them: their father's curse was fate; people rise and fall, give and then beg, kill and are killed; the fruit of knowledge is to be untouched by grief and joy. The birds honour him with water for his feet and say their birth is now fruitful and the fire of their father's anger is cooled by seeing him. Jaimini explains that Markandeya sent him and repeats his four doubts about the Mahabharata. The birds say they know the four Vedas, the law books and their branches, and will answer if they can. They bow to Vishnu, to Brahma and to Shiva, and begin with the first question. Water is called nara, and since it was his first home (ayana) he is called Narayana. This god pervades everything and stands in four forms (the four vyuhas), with and without qualities. The first, beyond all qualities, is seen by the wise as white and wrapped in flames, near and far at once, the final goal of yogis, called Vasudeva, pure, without form or colour. The second, Shesha, holds the earth on its head from below; it is called dark (tamasi) and has taken an animal form. The third acts to protect creatures; it is full of goodness (sattva) and keeps dharma in order, killing demons who break it and protecting gods and good people. The fourth lies on the serpent bed in the waters and, with the quality of passion (rajas), always creates. Whenever dharma declines and adharma rises, the third form takes birth: as the Boar it lifted the earth on one tusk; as the Man-lion it killed Hiranyakashipu and the demons led by Viprachitti; there are the Dwarf and others too many to count, and now the one in Mathura. This form of goodness, called Pradyumna, takes avatars as god, human or animal and takes on their nature by Vasudeva's will. So, though he has nothing to gain, Vishnu took a human birth; the birds say the next answer follows. (The closing line calls this the second chapter.)

005.json.summary: The birds answer Jaimini's second question, why Draupadi was the wife of five men. When Indra killed Vishvarupa, son of Tvashtri, he was overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin and his splendour (tejas) left him and entered Dharma. Tvashtri, enraged at his son's death, tore out a lock of his matted hair and offered it into the fire, and from it rose the huge demon Vritra, blazing and dark, Indra's enemy, who grew every day by the length of an arrow's flight. Afraid, Indra sent the seven sages to make peace, and they made a friendship and an agreement between him and Vritra; but when Indra broke the agreement and killed Vritra, his strength left him and entered Vayu, the wind god. When Indra took the form of Gautama and violated Ahalya, his beauty left him and went to the two Ashvins. Seeing Indra without dharma, splendour, strength and beauty, the demons tried to conquer him and were born as very strong men in the families of kings. In time the Earth, crushed by their weight, went to the gods on Mount Meru and complained that the demons the gods had killed were reborn as kings with huge armies, and asked for relief. So the gods came down to earth with portions of their power. Dharma released the splendour from Indra's body, and from it Kunti bore King Yudhishthira; Vayu released Indra's strength, and Bhima was born; from half of Indra's own power came Arjuna; and the twins born of Madri carried Indra's beauty. So Indra himself was born in five parts, and his wife Krishna (Draupadi) was born from the fire; she was the wife of Indra alone and of no one else, just as masters of yoga can take many bodies. The birds then say they will tell how Balarama went to the Sarasvati.

006.json.summary: The birds answer the third question. Balarama, knowing Krishna's great love for Arjuna, thought hard about what was right: he would not go to Duryodhana without Krishna, nor could he join the Pandavas and kill Duryodhana, who was his son-in-law and pupil. So he decided to bathe at holy places until the war between the Kurus and Pandavas was over, took leave of Krishna, Arjuna and Duryodhana, and went with his army to Dvaraka. Before leaving on pilgrimage the next day, he drank wine and, unsteady on his feet, went with his wife Revati and a group of women into the rich Raivata garden, full of fruit trees and flowering trees of every season (the text lists many: mango, coconut, pomegranate, jackfruit, ashoka, champaka, sal, palm and others), singing birds, and clear lakes with lotuses and water birds. In a bower he found Brahmins learned in the Vedas, of the Kaushika, Bhargava, Bharadvaja, Gautama and other families, sitting on deer skins and kusha grass and listening to a Suta (a bard of the Suta caste) telling sacred stories of the gods and sages. Seeing Balarama with eyes red from drink, they all rose to honour him, except the Suta. Enraged, Balarama killed the Suta, who was seated in the Brahmin's place, and the Brahmins all left the forest. Feeling himself scorned, Balarama thought that he had committed a great sin: the Suta was in the seat of a Brahmin, the Brahmins had left on seeing him, his body smelled like iron, and he felt like a Brahmin-killer. Cursing his anger, his drinking, his pride and his rashness, he resolved to keep a twelve-year vow of atonement while openly declaring his deed, and to turn his pilgrimage into a journey up the Sarasvati against its flow. So he went upstream along the Sarasvati. The birds then turn to the story of the Pandavas' sons.

007.json.summary: The birds answer the fourth question with the story of Harishchandra. In the Treta age there was a royal sage, King Harishchandra, so righteous that in his reign there was no famine, disease or untimely death, and no one was proud of wealth, strength or penance. While hunting in the forest he heard women crying 'Save us!' The cries came from the powers of knowledge (vidyas) that the sage Vishvamitra was mastering by fierce penance; they cried out in fear, and the terrible Lord of Obstacles (Vighnaraja), wishing to spoil Vishvamitra's work, entered the king. Possessed by him, Harishchandra shouted that whoever was doing wrong in his reign would be pierced by his arrows. Vishvamitra became angry, and at once the vidyas vanished. Seeing the sage, the king trembled like a leaf and bowed, saying he was only doing a king's duty: to give, to protect and to fight. Vishvamitra asked to whom he must give, whom protect and whom fight; the king said: give to the best Brahmins and the poor, protect the frightened, fight enemies. Then, said the sage, give me, a Brahmin, the gift I want. Overjoyed, the king offered anything, gold, son, wife, body, life, kingdom. Vishvamitra first asked for the fee of the royal sacrifice (Rajasuya), and then took the whole earth, the kingdom with its armies, stores and treasury, everything except the king's wife, son and body, and even the dharma that follows a person. The king agreed gladly and, told to leave the land, took off his ornaments, put on bark clothes and left with his wife Shaivya and his little son. Vishvamitra stopped him on the road and demanded the sacrifice fee still owed, saying a promise to a Brahmin not kept destroys the giver. The king had nothing left but three bodies and asked for a month. Vishvamitra let him go. The people of the city wept and begged the king to take them with him; moved, he stopped on the road. Vishvamitra, angry, called him a liar who wanted his kingdom back; the king hurried off, pulling his tired wife by the hand, and the sage struck her with a stick; the king only said, 'I am going.' Five of the Vishvedeva gods, full of pity, said Vishvamitra was very sinful for driving this great sacrificer from his throne, and wondered whose Soma they would now drink. Vishvamitra cursed them to become men; when they begged, he said that as men they would have no children, no wives and no jealousy, and would become gods again, free of desire and anger. So these gods were born in parts as the five sons of Draupadi, and because of the sage's curse these great warriors never married. The birds say all four questions are answered.

008.json.summary: Jaimini asks to hear more of Harishchandra, and the birds tell the rest of his story. The king walked with his wife Shaivya and young son to holy Varanasi, the city of Shiva, which belongs to no mortal. At the city gate Vishvamitra was waiting: the month was over and he wanted his fee. The king asked for the half day that remained, and the sage said he would return and curse him if it was not paid. The king did not know where to find the money and thought of selling himself. His wife, weeping, told him to keep his word, since nothing is higher than truth (King Kriti fell from heaven for one lie), and said that since she had borne him a son, he should sell her and pay the Brahmin. The king fainted; she fainted too; the hungry child cried for food. Vishvamitra came back, revived the king with water, praised truth above a thousand horse sacrifices, and said he would curse him at sunset. Urged again by his wife, the king, weeping, offered her for sale in the city, calling himself worse than a demon. An old Brahmin bought her as a servant for his wife, tied the money in the king's bark cloth and dragged her by the hair; the little prince Rohitashva ran after her crying 'Mother', and the Brahmin kicked him; she begged him to buy the boy too, and he did, and led both away while the king lamented. Vishvamitra took the money, called it too little, and gave the king until the end of the day. The king offered himself for sale. Dharma came in the form of a foul, frightening chandala (outcaste) named Praviira, who executes criminals and takes the cloth of the dead, and offered to buy him. The king said he would rather be burned by the curse than serve a chandala; Vishvamitra threatened to curse him; the king begged to be the sage's own slave instead, and Vishvamitra then said that as his slave he sold him to the chandala for a vast sum. The chandala paid, bound the king, beat him and took him to his settlement. There, morning, noon and evening, the king sang of his grief for his wife and son. He was set to work at the cremation ground of Varanasi, to collect the cloth of the dead and a fee for each body, a sixth part for the king, three parts for his master and two for himself. The cremation ground is described in horror: howling jackals, skulls, smoke and stench, ghosts, vetalas, dakinis, vultures and dogs, mourners crying for their dead, half-burned bodies that seem to laugh. Dirty, matted, staff in hand, eating food left for the dead, he lived there twelve months that felt like a hundred years. Asleep from exhaustion, he had a long dream: by the power of fate he was born from an outcaste woman, and as a boy of seven he insulted the relatives of a poor dead Brahmin while demanding the fee; they cursed him to go to hell. Yama's messengers dragged him to hell where he was sawn, cut, burned and fed on pus for what was a hundred years in each day; then he was born as a dog, ass, elephant, monkey, goat, cat, worm, fish, tortoise, boar, parrot, snake, tree and other beings, one each day; then as a king who lost his kingdom at dice, whose wife and son were taken, and who was eaten by a lion; he saw his wife dragged away crying for help; and Yama told him that Vishvamitra's anger could not be turned aside, that the sage would even bring about his son's death, and that he should return to the world of men and finish his suffering. He woke in fear, asked the outcastes whether twelve years had passed (some said no, others yes), prayed to Dharma, Krishna, Brihaspati and Indra for his wife and son, and went back to work, his memory dulled. Then his wife came to the cremation ground carrying their son, who had died of a snake bite, crying aloud. Neither recognised the other at first, so changed were they; the king saw the royal marks on the dead boy and thought of his own son; hearing her cry that fate had spared Harishchandra nothing, loss of kingdom, friends, wife and son, he knew her and the boy, and both fainted. Waking, he lamented over his son, sold like an object by his father; she recognised him by his voice and features and lamented that fate had made a king who walked over the cloths of kings into an outcaste in this horrible place; if this were so, she said, dharma gives no help. He told her how he had become an outcaste and she told how their son died. The king said he would burn himself on his son's pyre, though without his master's leave this would bring rebirth as an outcaste's slave and hell, for no pain is like the loss of a son; he asked her pardon for any harsh word, told her to go back to the Brahmin's house and serve him as a god, and prayed they would meet again in the next world if he had given gifts and pleased his elders. She said she would enter the fire with him. He built the pyre, placed the boy on it, and with folded hands meditated on Narayana, Vasudeva, Krishna in yellow clothes. Then all the gods led by Dharma and Indra came, with Brahma, the Sadhyas, Vishvedevas, Maruts, world guardians, nagas, siddhas, gandharvas, Rudras, the Ashvins and Vishvamitra himself, who now wished for his friendship. Dharma told him not to act rashly, being pleased by his patience, self-control and truth; Indra said he, his wife and son had won the eternal worlds. Indra rained deathless nectar and flowers on the pyre, the gods' drums sounded, and the boy rose up healthy. The king embraced his son, and he and his wife were adorned with divine garlands and clothes. Harishchandra said he could not go to heaven without his master the outcaste's leave; Dharma said it was he himself who had taken that form, knowing the suffering to come. The king then said he would not go to heaven while the people of Kosala grieved for him, since abandoning loyal followers is as great a sin as killing a Brahmin, a teacher, a cow or a woman; let them come with him, or he would go to hell with them; he had ruled and sacrificed by their support, so let all his merit be shared with them, even if it lasted only one day. Indra, Dharma and Vishvamitra agreed. Indra brought countless sky chariots to Ayodhya and invited its people to heaven; Vishvamitra brought Rohitashva and crowned him in Ayodhya, and the king with all his happy people, their families and servants, rose to heaven in chariots and lived in a heavenly city with walls. Seeing his glory, Shukra, teacher of the demons, sang: there never was and never will be a king like Harishchandra; whoever in distress hears his story gains great happiness, and one who wants heaven, a son, a wife or a kingdom gains it; how great is the power of patience and the fruit of giving. The birds say they will next tell the result of the Rajasuya, which caused the destruction of the earth, and the great battle of the Adi and Baka birds that came from it.

009.json.summary: The birds tell what followed Harishchandra's story. After twelve years living in the waters of the Ganga, Vasishtha, the king's family priest, came out and heard everything Vishvamitra had done: how the generous king lost his kingdom, sold his wife and son and served an outcaste. Vasishtha, who loved the king, became angry: even when Vishvamitra killed his hundred sons he had not been so angry as now, hearing that this truthful, calm, blameless king, devoted to gods and Brahmins, was brought to such ruin. He cursed Vishvamitra, a hater of Brahmins, to become a baka (heron-like bird). Vishvamitra cursed him back to become an adi bird. So both great sages became birds and fought furiously; the adi was two thousand yojanas tall and the baka three thousand and ninety. They struck each other with wings and feet; the wind of their wings threw mountains to the ground, the earth shook, the oceans overflowed and the earth tilted towards the underworld; many creatures died, and people fled crying for their children and loved ones. Brahma came with the gods and told them to stop so the worlds could be at peace, but they kept fighting in rage. Seeing the destruction, Brahma removed their bird forms and told Vasishtha and Vishvamitra, now in their own bodies, to give up this dark (tamasic) fight: it was the result of Harishchandra's Rajasuya sacrifice and was destroying the earth; Vishvamitra had not really wronged the king, but had in fact brought him to heaven; they should give up desire and anger, which spoil penance. Ashamed, the two forgave each other and embraced, and Brahma, Vasishtha and Vishvamitra went to their own homes. Those who tell or listen properly to the battle of the adi and the baka and the story of Harishchandra are freed of sin and meet no obstacles.

010.json.summary: Jaimini asks the birds how beings are born and die: how a creature arises and grows, how it lives pressed inside the womb without being digested where even heavy food is digested, how it grows after birth, how it leaves the body at death, and how it experiences the fruit of good and bad deeds. The birds say this is hard for anyone to grasp, and answer by telling how a righteous son named Sumati explained it to his father. A wise Bhargava Brahmin told his son Sumati, who had had his sacred-thread rite but seemed dull (jada), to study the Vedas, serve his teacher and live on alms, then marry, perform sacrifices, have children, go to the forest and finally become a renouncer, and so reach Brahman. The son said nothing at first; urged again and again, he laughed and said he had learned all this and many arts in past lives: he remembered more than ten thousand births, many mothers and fathers, joys and sorrows, time in the womb, illnesses, childhood, youth and old age, births as Brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya and shudra, as animals, insects and birds, as servant and master, rich and poor, killing and being killed, giving and receiving. Wandering on this wheel he has gained the knowledge that leads to freedom, in whose light all the Vedic rites seem without value; so what use are the Vedas to him? He will go to Brahman, beyond pain and pleasure. The amazed father asked how he gained this knowledge and why he had seemed dull, perhaps from a curse. The son said that in his last life he was a Brahmin devoted to the Self and a teacher, but through carelessness and ignorance he died without finishing; from the moment of death his memory did not fail, and he now remembers his births; this memory is the fruit of giving knowledge, and cannot be had by those who only follow the Vedic rites. He will now strive for freedom, and offered to answer his father's doubts. The father asked about the round of birth and death. The son describes death: heat in the body, stirred by strong wind, breaks the vital points, and the udana breath rises and blocks the downward flow. Those who gave water and food feel comfort at that time; those who never lied, did not divide friends, had faith, honoured gods and Brahmins, were generous and modest and did not abandon dharma die easily; those who gave no water or food suffer burning and hunger; givers of firewood overcome cold and givers of sandal overcome heat; liars, false witnesses, those who teach wrongly and those who abuse the Vedas die in confusion. Yama's terrible, foul-smelling messengers come with clubs; the dying person trembles, cries for his family, speaks unclearly and leaves the body. He then enters another body of the same shape, size and age, made by his deeds for suffering, not born of parents. Yama's messengers bind him and drag him south over thorns, stones, fire and pits, burned by the sun and attacked by jackals; givers of umbrellas, shoes, clothes and food travel this road easily. In twelve days he reaches Yama's city. He feels the burning, cutting and rotting of his old body; he receives the sesame water and rice balls (pinda) his relatives offer, is nourished by their oil and massage and their gifts, and suffers less if they sleep on the ground. For twelve days he sees his own house. Then he is dragged to Yama's iron city and sees Yama, dark, red-eyed, with terrible teeth, holding staff and noose, surrounded by Death, Time and hundreds of diseases, and goes to the good or bad state Yama assigns. A false witness or liar goes to the hell Raurava, two thousand yojanas wide, a pit filled with burning coals, where his feet burn away and grow again at every step, taking a day and night for each step until he crosses it; then he passes to other hells, then is born as worms, insects, beasts, trees, cattle and other painful births, then as a hunchback, dwarf or an outcaste such as a chandala or pukkasa, then climbing up through shudra, vaishya and kshatriya to Brahmin and even king of the gods, and sometimes falling again. The doers of good go where Yama sends them, in heavenly chariots with singing gandharvas and dancing apsaras; when they fall from there they are born in the families of kings and great people, enjoy pleasures, and rise or fall again. He says he will next tell how the being enters the womb.

011.json.summary: The son (Sumati) continues to his father. When a man's seed enters a woman's menstrual blood, a being freed from hell or heaven enters it. The two seeds become firm, then a liquid lump (kalala), a bubble, then a piece of flesh (peshi), from which the five main limbs sprout like a shoot from a seed, then fingers, eyes, nose, mouth and ears, then nails, then hair on the skin and on the head, while the covering sheath grows with it, like a coconut in its shell. The child grows head down, hands placed by the knees, thumbs on the knees, eyes behind the knees, nose between them, buttocks on the heels, arms and shins outside. It becomes firm through heat and lives on what the mother eats and drinks; a channel called apyayani is tied to its navel and to the mother's intestines, and through it the food and drink nourish it. Its life there depends on its merit and sin. It remembers its many past lives, is pressed on all sides, grows weary of the world, and resolves that once out of the womb it will act so as never to enter a womb again, remembering hundreds of past sufferings. In the ninth or tenth month it turns head down and is born, squeezed by the birth wind (prajapatya vayu), crying and in pain; it faints, and wakes when touched by the outside air. Then Vishnu's deluding Maya seizes it, and it loses its knowledge; then come childhood, youth, old age, death and birth again, turning on the wheel of the world like a water-wheel bucket (ghati-yantra). Sometimes one goes to heaven, sometimes to hell, sometimes to both after death, sometimes is born here to reap one's deeds, or goes on with a little left over. In hell the great pain is seeing those in heaven rejoice while one is thrown down; in heaven the pain is the constant thought 'I will fall', and seeing those in hell and fearing that fate. There is pain in the womb, in birth, in the weakness of childhood, in youth tied to desire, jealousy and anger, in old age, and most of all in death, in being dragged by Yama's men and thrown into hell, and then again womb, birth, death and hell. So there is no happiness in this world full of hundreds of sorrows; why then, seeking freedom, should he follow the threefold Vedic duties?

012.json.summary: The father praises his son's account and asks him to describe the hells in detail. The son (Sumati) describes them in turn. Maharaurava is twelve thousand yojanas around, with a floor of copper heated by fire below, glowing like the rising moon; Yama's servants throw the sinner in bound hand and foot, and he rolls across it, eaten by crows, herons, wolves, owls, scorpions, mosquitoes and vultures, crying for his father, mother and brother, finding no peace for countless years. Tamas is as large, naturally icy and dark; people run about in the cold, cling to each other, their teeth break from shivering, they suffer hunger and thirst, an icy wind splits their bones, and they eat the marrow and blood that flow out, until their sin is used up. In Nikrintana, potter's wheels turn without stop, and people are placed on them and cut from feet to head by the thread of Time held in the fingers of Yama's servants; they do not die, and the hundreds of pieces join again, and this goes on for thousands of years until the sin is spent. In Apratishtha there are wheels and water-wheels (ghati-yantra): some sinners are whirled on the wheels for thousands of years without rest, others are tied to the water-wheels like pots and turned again and again, vomiting blood, their guts coming out of their mouths and their eyes streaming. Asipatravana is a thousand yojanas of ground covered with blazing fire under a fierce sun; in its middle stands a lovely forest with smooth leaves, whose leaves are swords, guarded by huge, powerful dogs like tigers; thirsty and with burning feet, the beings run to its cool shade, but a wind makes the sword-leaves fall on them, they fall into the fire, and the dogs tear off their limbs while they weep. Taptakumbha, worse still, is a place of jars surrounded by flames and filled with boiling oil and iron powder; sinners are thrown in head first and boiled until their bodies burst and their marrow runs out, pulled out by vultures and thrown back, until head, sinews, flesh, skin and bones melt into the oil, and Yama's men stir them with ladles in the whirling oil.

013.json.summary: The son tells his father of his own experience in hell. In his seventh birth before this one he was born in a vaishya (merchant) family and once kept cows away from a drinking place. For that deed he fell into a terrible hell full of flames and iron-beaked birds, with mud made of the blood of bodies crushed in machines, and loud with the cries of sinners being cut. He spent over a hundred years there, burning and thirsty. Then suddenly a cool, pleasant wind reached him in the midst of the hot sand-pots, and from its touch all the beings there were freed from torment, and he felt the joy that people in heaven feel. Looking up in wonder, they saw nearby a most excellent man, with a terrible servant of Yama, staff in hand and shining like lightning, walking ahead and saying 'Come this way.' Seeing the hell full of hundreds of tortures, the man, full of pity, asked Yama's servant what sin he had committed to be brought to this hell. He was Vipashchit, born in the family of the Janakas in Videha; he had ruled well, performed many sacrifices, protected the earth by dharma, never fled from battle, never turned a guest away, never wronged ancestors, gods, sages or servants, and never desired other men's wives or wealth. Ancestors come to a man on the days of the moon's changes and gods on the lunar days, like cows to a drinking place; if they go away sighing, the householder's merit from sacrifices and good works is lost (the sigh of the ancestors destroys the merit of seven births, that of the gods the merit of three). So he had always been diligent in rites for gods and ancestors; how then had he come to this terrible hell?

014.json.summary: The son says that Yama's servant, though terrible, answered King Vipashchit gently while they listened. All the king said was true, but he had done one small sin: once, when his wife Pivari of Vidarbha was in her fertile period, he let it pass without uniting with her, because he was attached to his other wife, the beautiful Kaikeyi. As fire waits for ghee at the time of offering, so the Creator waits for seed in the fertile period, and one who ignores it from attachment to pleasure falls into hell for failing his debt to the ancestors. That was his only sin, and now he was to go to enjoy his merits. The king agreed to go, but asked what sins brought the torments he saw: iron-beaked crows tearing out eyes and tongues that grow again, people sawn apart, cooked in hot sand and oil, and pecked by iron-beaked birds. The servant first explains that a person experiences his good and bad deeds in turn, and they are used up only by being experienced; sinners go from famine to famine, fear to fear, while the faithful, calm and generous go from joy to joy; good and bad deeds stored over hundreds of thousands of births sprout as joy and pain according to time and place, a small sin giving a thorn in the foot and a great one long disease, weapons, fire and prison; even a small merit gives pleasant smells, sounds and tastes. Then he lists sins and punishments: those who looked at other men's wives with lust or at others' wealth with greed have their eyes torn out by iron-beaked birds for thousands of years; those who taught false doctrines or spoke ill of the Vedas, gods, Brahmins and teachers have their tongues torn out; those who split friends, father and son, teacher and pupil, husband and wife are sawn in two; those who tormented others or took away their comforts lie in hot sand; one who eats at a shraddha he was not invited to is pulled apart by birds; slanderers have their tongues split by razors; those who insulted parents and teachers sink head down in pits of pus, dung and urine; those who ate before gods, guests, servants, ancestors and birds were fed become needle-mouthed giants eating pus; those who served unequal food in one row eat dung; those who touched cows, Brahmins or fire while impure have their hands held in fire-pots; those who touched cows, fire, mother, Brahmins, elder brother, father, sister and elders with their feet stand in burning coals in red-hot iron fetters; those who heard the gods, Brahmins and Vedas abused and enjoyed it have hot iron nails driven into their ears; those who broke water sheds, temples and assembly halls are flayed; those who relieved themselves on paths of cows, Brahmins and the sun have their entrails pulled out by crows; one who gave his daughter to one man and then another is cut up and carried in a river of lye; one who abandoned his family in famine eats his own flesh; those who abandoned dependants, who sold their merit, who stole deposits, and adulterers are crushed, eaten by worms, impaled on an iron silk-cotton tree, or burned in crucibles; a pupil who disrespected his teacher carries a rock on his head; those who fouled water live in a hell of filth; those who did not share food eat each other's flesh; those who abandoned the Vedas or their sacred fires are thrown from mountain peaks; men who lived with remarried widows become worms eaten by ants; those who took gifts from the fallen become insects in stones; one who ate sweets alone while others watched eats burning coals and has his back eaten by wolves; the ungrateful wander blind, deaf, dumb and hungry, and the betrayer of friends passes through every torment with no release known; the stealer of gold, the Brahmin-killer, the drinker of liquor and the violator of his teacher's bed burn for many thousands of years and are then born with leprosy and consumption, again and again to the end of the age; the killer of a cow suffers somewhat less, over three births, and so on for lesser sins. He will next tell what births follow these sins after hell.

015.json.summary: Yama's servant tells King Vipashchit what births follow particular sins after hell. A Brahmin who accepts gifts from a fallen person becomes an ass, and one who performs rites for the fallen a worm; one who wrongs his teacher or desires his wife or wealth becomes a dog; one who insults his parents becomes an ass, and one who abuses them a myna; one who insults his brother's wife becomes a pigeon, and one who harms her a tortoise; one who eats his master's food but does not serve him becomes a monkey; the stealer of deposits becomes a worm, the envious a rakshasa, the betrayer of trust a fish; the stealer of grains becomes a large-mouthed rat; the adulterer becomes a wolf, then a dog, jackal, heron, vulture, snake and kanka bird; one who violates his brother's wife becomes a cuckoo, and one who violates a friend's, teacher's or king's wife a boar; one who obstructs sacrifices, gifts and marriages, or gives a daughter in marriage twice, becomes a worm; one who eats without offering to gods, ancestors and Brahmins becomes a crow; one who insults an elder brother becomes a krauncha bird; the text says a shudra who has relations with a Brahmin woman becomes a worm, and if he has a child by her, a wood-insect, boar, worm, diver bird and chandala; the ungrateful become worms, insects, moths, scorpions, fish, crows, tortoises and then pukkasas; one who kills an unarmed man becomes an ass; the killer of women and children becomes a worm. Stealing particular things brings particular births: food makes one a fly or cat, sesame cake a rat, ghee a mongoose, meat a crow or hawk, salt a water crow, curd a worm, milk a crane, oil an oil-drinking insect, honey a gadfly, cakes an ant, wine a partridge, iron a crow, bronze a harita bird, silver a pigeon, gold a worm, silk a silkworm, fine cloth a parrot, cotton a krauncha, colours a peacock, red cloth a jivajivaka bird, perfumes a muskrat, fruit makes one a eunuch, flowers poor, a vehicle lame, vegetables a harita, water a chataka bird; the stealer of land passes through the hells, then becomes grass, shrubs, creepers and trees, then insects, birds, water creatures, beasts and cattle, then a chandala or pukkasa, lame, blind, deaf, leprous, consumptive and diseased, epileptic, and then a shudra; the same path awaits stealers of cows and gold. Stealing learning, not paying the teacher, and giving one's wife to another bring impotence; offering into an unlit fire brings indigestion and weak digestion. Slander, ingratitude, cruelty, adultery, theft, impurity, mocking the gods, cheating, miserliness and killing are signs of those who have come from hell; kindness, truthfulness, speech for others' good, faith in the Vedas, worship of teachers, gods and sages, keeping good company and friendliness are signs of those come from heaven. As they turned to go, the beings in hell cried out to the king to stay a moment, since the wind touching his body relieved their pain. He asked why, and the servant said: because his body was nourished on food left after feeding ancestors, gods, guests and servants, and because he had performed the horse sacrifice and others properly, his presence softened the machines, weapons, fire and crows of hell. The king said no joy in heaven or in Brahma's world equals the joy of giving relief to suffering beings, and he would stay there like a post. A man who does not help the suffering, even an enemy, has a worthless life; his sacrifices and penance bring no good; one hard-hearted towards children, the sick and the old is a demon, not a man. Dharma and Indra came to take him to heaven; he refused while people cried for help. Indra said they were there by their deeds and he must go by his. The king asked how much merit he had; Dharma said it was countless as drops in the ocean or stars in the sky, and his compassion now had multiplied it a hundred thousand times. The king then asked that by whatever merit he had, the sinners be freed from hell. Indra said that by this he had won a still higher place, and the sinners were freed. Flowers rained on him, and Hari took him to heaven in a chariot; the son says that he and the others released from torment were then born in the births their deeds decided. So, he tells his father, he has described the hells and the births that follow each sin, from knowledge gained in his own past experience.

016.json.summary: The father, having understood how the world turns like a water-wheel, asks his son what he should do. The son tells him, if he trusts his words, to leave household life, live as a forest hermit, then give up his sacred fires and become a wandering renouncer, eating only every other meal, self-controlled and devoted to yoga, untouched by outer objects; he will then gain the yoga that cures the pain of the world and frees him from further union with the elements. The father asks to be taught this yoga, begging his son to cool him, burned by the sun of worldly life, with the water of knowledge of Brahman, to revive him, bitten by the black snake of ignorance, with the nectar of his words, and to free him from the chains of attachment to son, wife, house and land. The son says he will tell the yoga that Dattatreya taught to Alarka, and first tells of Dattatreya's birth. In the city of Pratishthana there lived a Brahmin named Kaushika who, from sins of an earlier life, had leprosy. His wife worshipped him like a god, massaging him, bathing, clothing and feeding him, washing away his phlegm, urine, dung and blood, and speaking sweetly; though he scolded her cruelly in his anger, she still thought him the best of all. Once, though he could not walk, he told her to carry him to a courtesan he had seen living on the royal road, saying he would die if he could not have her. His wife, a devoted wife (pativrata) of good family, tied up her clothes, took extra money for the fee, lifted him onto her shoulders and set out at night under a cloudy sky lit by lightning. On the way the sage Mandavya, an innocent man impaled on a stake as a suspected thief, was in agony; in the dark Kaushika, on his wife's shoulders, touched him with his foot. Mandavya cursed him to die at sunrise when the sun's light touched him. His wife, hearing the curse, declared that the sun would not rise. So the sun did not rise and there was endless night for many days. The gods became afraid: without sunrise there was no Vedic study, no offerings, no measure of days, months, seasons, the sun's half-years or the year, no bathing, giving or fire rites; the gods are fed by sacrifice and in return send rain for the crops, and harm those who eat without offering; without the day all this would end. Brahma told them that power is calmed only by power and penance by penance; the sun did not rise because of the power of a devoted wife, so they should seek the help of Anasuya, the devoted wife of Atri. Anasuya agreed, wishing both to restore day and night and to keep the other woman's husband from dying. She went to the Brahmin woman and spoke of the duty of a wife: by serving her husband alone she herself had gained great fruit; men must pay their five debts, earn wealth by the duty of their caste, give it to the worthy, and with great effort reach the higher worlds; but, the text says, women gain half of all the merit men earn simply by serving their husbands, since women have no separate sacrifice, shraddha or fasting; the husband is a woman's highest refuge. The Brahmin woman agreed that a husband is a woman's god and asked what she could do. Anasuya said the gods wanted day and night restored, for without day all rites and rain would fail and the world would perish; she asked her to let the sun rise. The woman said her husband had been cursed to die at sunrise. Anasuya promised to restore his body and make him new. She agreed; after ten nights Anasuya raised the offering of water and called the sun, which rose red like a lotus over the eastern mountain, and at once the husband died and fell. Anasuya told her not to grieve, and by the truth that she had never seen any man equal to her own husband in looks, character, mind or speech, and by her constant service to him in deed, mind and word, she declared that this Brahmin should live free of disease, young again, for a hundred years with his wife. He rose up young and shining like a god. Flowers rained, divine drums sounded, and the gods offered Anasuya a boon. She asked that Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva be born as her sons, and that she and her husband gain yoga to be free of suffering. The gods agreed and left.

017.json.summary: The son continues. Long after, Atri, the second son of Brahma, saw his wife Anasuya after her monthly bath, beautiful and desirable, and united with her in his mind. The change that arose in him as he meditated was carried by the wind in all directions, white and in Brahma's form, and caught by the ten directions as Soma (the Moon); so Soma was born to Anasuya as the mind-born son of Atri, the support of the life of all beings. Vishnu, pleased, produced from his own body Dattatreya, full of goodness (sattva), who drank Anasuya's milk; he was Vishnu himself born as Atri's second son. Seven days later, when the arrogant Haihaya king came and gave offence, Durvasas was born angry from the womb, a portion of Rudra full of darkness (tamas), wanting to burn the Haihaya at once, furious at the pain of living in the womb. So Anasuya bore three sons from Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, by the gods' boon: Soma from Brahma, Dattatreya from Vishnu and Durvasas from Shiva. Soma, by his cool rays, nourishes plants, herbs and people and lives in heaven; Dattatreya protects creatures by destroying wicked demons and favours the good, being Vishnu's portion; Durvasas burns those who insult him with his look, mind and words. Dattatreya, fixed in yoga, enjoyed the objects of the senses; Durvasas left his parents and wandered the earth keeping the vow called 'the madman's'. Dattatreya, wanting to be free of company, sank into a lake for a long time, but the sages' sons who followed him would not leave its shore even after a hundred divine years. So he came out of the water with a beautiful woman in divine clothes, thinking they would leave him if he was with a woman; when they still did not leave, he drank wine with her; they did not leave him even then. Though he drank wine and lived with music and a woman, the lord of yoga was not stained, just as the wind is not stained by living in an outcaste's house; drinking with his wife, he practised penance, and is meditated on by yogis seeking freedom.

018.json.summary: The son tells how Arjuna, son of Kritavirya (Kartavirya Arjuna), was called by ministers, priests and citizens to be crowned after his father went to heaven, but refused, saying kingship leads to hell: merchants pay a twelfth of their goods, herdsmen and farmers a sixth, as the price of protection; a king who takes the tax and does not protect is like a thief, loses the merit of his sacrifices and good works, and goes to hell, and the theft he fails to stop becomes his sin. So he would rule only if, after penance, he gained such yogic power that he alone could protect the earth. The wise old sage Garga, among the ministers, told him to worship Dattatreya, who lives in a valley of the Sahya mountains, a portion of Vishnu, equal-minded to all, by whose worship Indra regained his throne and killed the demons. Asked how, Garga told the story. The gods led by Indra and the demons led by Jambha fought for a divine year, and the gods were defeated by Viprachitti and other demons. On Brihaspati's advice they went to please Dattatreya, whose behaviour was strange. They found him with Lakshmi, sung to by gandharvas and drinking wine, bowed to him, praised him, brought him food and garlands, and followed him standing and walking. When he asked what they wanted, they said the demons had taken the three worlds and their sacrificial shares. He said: 'I am addicted to wine, impure and not master of my senses; how can you hope for victory through me?' They said he was sinless and untouched, his inner light purified by knowledge. He said that was true, but through contact with this woman he had become impure, since constant enjoyment of women causes fault. They said she was the Mother of the world and cannot be stained, just as the sun's rays touch both Brahmin and outcaste. Laughing, he told them to call the demons to battle and bring them before his sight, so that his glance, like fire, would destroy their strength. The gods challenged the demons, were beaten and fled to Dattatreya's hermitage; the demons followed and saw Dattatreya with his lovely wife Lakshmi at his left side. Overcome by desire for her, they left the gods, lifted her onto a palanquin, put it on their heads and set off for home. Dattatreya laughed and told the gods that Lakshmi had now climbed onto the demons' heads, having passed through seven places. He explained: Lakshmi on a man's feet gives a home, on the thighs clothes and wealth, on the private parts a wife, in the lap children, in the heart his wishes, on the throat ornaments and the embrace of loved ones returning from travel, in the mouth fine speech, authority and poetry; but when she goes to the head she leaves the person for another. So he told them to take their weapons and kill the demons, who had lost their power and merit by seizing another's wife. The demons were destroyed, with Lakshmi pressing on their heads; Lakshmi flew back to Dattatreya, praised by the gods, who bowed to him and returned to heaven free of fear. Garga tells the king to worship Dattatreya in the same way if he wants unequalled power.

019.json.summary: The son (here called Jada, 'the dull one') continues. Hearing Garga, Kartavirya Arjuna went to Dattatreya's hermitage and served him with devotion: massaging his feet, bringing honey, garlands, sandal, scented water, fruit and food, and clearing away his leftovers. Dattatreya told him, as he had told the gods, that he was blameworthy for his wine, his pleasures and the woman at his side, and that he should not trouble him but worship someone able to help. Remembering Garga's words, Arjuna bowed and said: 'Why do you delude me with your own Maya? You are sinless, and this goddess is the source of all beings.' Pleased that the king had spoken his secret, Dattatreya offered him a boon, adding that he will give contentment, sons, wives and wealth to those who worship him, together with Lakshmi, with perfumes, garlands, offerings of meat and wine, sweet food with ghee, songs, honour to Brahmins, and music of the vina, flute and conch, and will destroy those who scorn him. Kartavirya asked for supreme power by which he could protect his people without sin; knowledge of others' thoughts; no rival in battle; a thousand arms; the ability to move unhindered over mountains, sky, water, earth and the underworlds; death only at the hands of a greater man; a guide to the right path if he strayed; worthy guests and endless wealth to give; no loss of property in his kingdom when people remembered him; and constant devotion to Dattatreya. Dattatreya granted all and said he would become a world ruler (chakravartin). Arjuna bowed, called his people and was crowned. Strong with these gifts, the Haihaya king proclaimed that anyone but himself who took up a weapon would be killed as a robber. So in his kingdom no one but he bore arms; he alone guarded villages, cattle, fields, Brahmins, ascetics and caravans, and whoever was in danger from robbers, snakes, fire, weapons or drowning had only to remember him to be saved; nothing was lost while he ruled. He performed many sacrifices with rich fees, practised penance and fought great battles; the sage Angiras, seeing his glory, said no king would ever equal him. On each anniversary of the day he received the boons, he held a festival of worship to Dattatreya, and all his people did the same. Such is the greatness of Dattatreya, a form of Vishnu, whose appearances are told in the Puranas; whoever meditates on his highest form is happy and soon crosses the world; he says he is always easy to reach for his devotees. The son then says he will tell of the birth of Alarka and the yoga Dattatreya taught that royal sage, who was devoted to his father.

020.json.summary: Jada (Sumati) begins the story of Alarka's family. There was a mighty king named Shatrujit, at whose sacrifices Indra was pleased with Soma. His son Ritadhvaja, equal to Brihaspati in wisdom, Indra in valour and the Ashvins in beauty, spent day and night with princes of his age in study, poetry, songs, plays, dice, weapons and practice with elephants, horses and chariots, joined by sons of Brahmins, kings and merchants. Two young naga princes, sons of the serpent king Ashvatara, came up from the underworld disguised as Brahmins and became his close friends, sharing his games, bathing, clothes and perfumes; the prince would not eat, bathe, drink or study without them, and they spent the nights in the underworld sighing until they could return each day. Their father asked why they loved the human world so much, since he saw them so rarely. They said that Ritadhvaja, son of Shatrujit, handsome, honest, brave, sweet-spoken, learned, friendly, modest and full of virtues, had won their hearts, and without him the underworld felt hot to them. The father said a man is blessed whose virtues are praised even in his absence; there are learned men without good conduct and good men without learning, but this prince had both; he asked whether they had done anything for this friend in return, offered any of his own treasures for him, and said a life is worthless that does not repay a friend's kindness. The sons said nothing they could give could match what he had; there was one thing he needed, but they thought only Brahma, Vishnu or Shiva could do it. The father insisted: for people of firm effort nothing in heaven or earth is out of reach; an ant that keeps walking covers thousands of yojanas while Garuda who does not move goes nowhere, and Dhruva, a son of King Uttanapada, reached the fixed place of the pole star. The sons told what the prince had told them of his youth. The Brahmin sage Galava had come to King Shatrujit with a fine horse and complained that a wicked demon kept disturbing his hermitage, taking the forms of lions, elephants and small animals, breaking his meditation and vow of silence; he could burn him with his anger but did not want to waste his hard-won penance. Once, worn out, he had sighed, looking at the demon, and at once this horse fell from the sky and a bodiless voice said: this horse can circle the whole earth without tiring, going with the sun, unhindered in the underworld, sky, water, every direction and over mountains; because it travels the whole circle of the earth (bhu-valaya) it will be called Kuvalaya; mounted on it, Ritadhvaja, son of King Shatrujit, will kill the demon and become famous. So Galava asked the king, who shares in the merit of his kingdom's ascetics, to stop the demon and send his son. The king had the auspicious rites performed, set Ritadhvaja on the horse and sent him with Galava to his hermitage.

021.json.summary: The Naga king asks what the prince did at Galava's hermitage, and his two sons tell him. Ritadhvaja, now called Kuvalayashva, removed all obstacles for the sages. The proud demon, not knowing he was there, came in the form of a boar to attack Galava while he was saying his evening prayers. At the disciples' cry the prince mounted his horse, chased the boar and struck it with a crescent-headed arrow; the wounded beast fled into a great forest of hills and trees, and the swift horse followed for thousands of yojanas until the boar dropped into a deep pit in the earth and the prince and horse fell after it into darkness. He could not find the boar, but found light in the underworld and a city of hundreds of golden palaces like Indra's. It seemed empty, but he saw a woman hurrying along, who would not answer him and went up into a palace. Tying up his horse, he followed and found a beautiful girl on a golden couch. Each thought the other a god; she was overcome and fainted, and he comforted her while her companion fanned her. The companion told him: the girl is Madalasa, daughter of the gandharva king Vishvavasu; the fierce demon Patalaketu, son of Vajraketu, living in the underworld, used dark magic to carry her off from her garden, and means to marry her on the coming thirteenth day, though he is no more fit for her than a shudra for hearing the Veda. The day before, when she wanted to kill herself, Surabhi, mother of cows, told her the demon would not have her; the man from the mortal world who pierced him with arrows would soon be her husband. The companion herself is Kundala, daughter of Vindhyavat and wife of the hero Pushkaramalin, who was killed by Shumbha; she now travels from one holy place to another seeking the next world. Patalaketu, in the form of a boar, had just been wounded by someone protecting sages. Madalasa fainted because she loved the prince at first sight but believed she was destined for whoever wounded the demon, and so would suffer all her life. Kundala asked who he was. He said he was Kuvalayashva, son of King Shatrujit, sent to guard Galava's hermitage, and that he had shot the boar, followed it and fallen into the pit; he was a man, not a god. Overjoyed, Kundala said Surabhi cannot lie, so he must be the one. He said he was under his father's authority; Madalasa thought of Tumburu, the family teacher, who came at once with fuel and kusha grass, lit the fire and performed the marriage rite, then returned to his penance. Kundala, her wish fulfilled, said she would now do penance and bathe at holy places, and before leaving told the prince: a husband must always support and protect his wife, since a wife helps her husband to dharma, wealth and pleasure; when husband and wife follow each other all three are achieved; without a wife a man cannot honour gods, ancestors, servants and guests, his wealth wastes away, and he has no pleasure; equally a wife cannot achieve these without a husband. She embraced her friend and left. As the prince set Madalasa on his horse to leave the underworld, the demons cried out that the jewel Patalaketu had brought from heaven was being stolen, and attacked with clubs, swords, maces, spears and arrows. Laughing, he cut their weapons, filling the underworld with broken arms, then used the missile of Tvashtri, which burned all the demons with Patalaketu, their bones bursting, as the ocean was burned by Kapila's fire. He returned to his father's city and told him all. The father embraced him and said: one who keeps the fame, wealth and strength his father won is a middling man, one who adds to them is the best, and one who loses them is the worst; the son had surpassed him by protecting Brahmins, going to the underworld and destroying the demons; a man known by his father's name is unfortunate, one known by his own is blessed, and one known through his mother's family is the lowest. He told him to prosper and never be parted from the gandharva princess. Ritadhvaja lived happily with Madalasa in his father's city and in gardens and mountains, and every morning she bowed at the feet of his parents.

022.json.summary: The naga sons continue. After a long time King Shatrujit told his son to ride the horse round the earth every morning to protect the Brahmins from the many wicked demons. The prince did so, bowing to his father's feet after each circuit, and spent the rest of each day with Madalasa. One day, on the bank of the Yamuna, he saw a hermitage of Talaketu, Patalaketu's younger brother, a shape-shifting demon disguised as a sage, who remembered the old enmity. Talaketu asked him, as a man true to his word, not to refuse a request: he wished to perform a sacrifice but had nothing for the priests' fee, so the prince should give him the ornament on his neck, and guard the hermitage while he went under the water to praise Varuna with Vedic hymns for the good of all beings. The prince bowed, gave him the necklace and promised to wait and guard the place. Talaketu went under the river, came out elsewhere, and went to the city, where he told Madalasa and others that the hero Kuvalayashva had been fighting a wicked demon near his hermitage to protect ascetics and had been pierced through the chest by a trident by the demon's magic; dying, he had given him this necklace; shudra ascetics had cremated him in the forest, and the demon had taken the horse, neighing and weeping. He left the necklace and went away. The whole household fainted with grief and the king, queens and women wept. Madalasa, seeing her husband's necklace and hearing he was killed, gave up her life at once. There was loud weeping in every house of the city. The king, seeing his daughter-in-law dead, calmed himself and told the people not to weep, since all ties are impermanent: his son died obeying him, protecting Brahmins, and a body that must be lost anyway is well given for Brahmins; his daughter-in-law, born of a good family and devoted to her husband, followed him at once, and, the text says, a woman has no god but her husband, so she is not to be pitied; women who live separated from their husbands are to be pitied, not those who die with them. His son repaid his debt to the Brahmins and to his father's dharma, upheld his mother's purity, his family's honour and his own courage, and gave his life rather than abandon the Brahmins' protection. Kuvalayashva's mother said she had never felt such joy from her own mother or sister as on hearing that her son was killed protecting sages; a mother's labour in childbirth is fruitful when her son either defeats enemies or falls in battle; those who die of disease while relatives weep are born in vain. The king performed the funeral rites for his daughter-in-law and offered water for his son. Talaketu then came out of the Yamuna and sweetly told the prince he could go, since with him standing guard he had finished the Varuna rite he had long wished for. The prince bowed and rode back to his father's city on his horse, swift as Garuda and the wind.

023.json.summary: The naga sons continue. When Ritadhvaja (Kuvalayashva) returned to his city, the people, first sad and then amazed and overjoyed, embraced each other and blessed him with long life. His parents embraced him; astonished, he asked what had happened, and his father told him. Hearing that his beloved Madalasa had died on hearing false news of his death, he was overwhelmed with shame and grief and called himself cruel for living without her; then, steadying himself, he reasoned that dying for her would do her no good and weeping would not become a man; he must fight his enemies and serve his father, on whom his life depended; the only fitting thing was to give up the pleasure of women. He performed the water offerings and rites for her and vowed that if Madalasa could not be his wife, no other woman would be his companion in this life. So, the sons tell their father, he lives without any woman, playing with friends of his age; this is the one thing he needs, and even the gods could hardly do it. Jada says the Naga king Ashvatara, smiling, replied that if people give up an effort thinking it impossible, the loss of effort brings further loss; success depends on both fate and human effort, so he would undertake penance to achieve it. He went to the holy place Plakshavatarana in the Himalaya, fasted, bathed three times a day, and praised the goddess Sarasvati: she holds all that is and is not, the imperishable syllable in which all stands, as fire is in wood; the three measures of Om are the three worlds, Vedas, fires, lights, qualities, times, states and so on; the half-measure beyond them is her highest, changeless form that no tongue can utter. Pleased, Sarasvati, the tongue of Vishnu, offered the brother of Kambala a boon. He asked that she give him and his brother Kambala knowledge of all the musical notes. She granted them the seven notes, the seven gramaragas, seven songs, seven murchanas, forty-nine talas, three gramas, the four kinds of pada, three kinds of tala and laya, and the four kinds of instruments, so that they would be the masters of music in the underworld, the heavens and the earth. The two brothers then sang seven songs to the strings for Shiva on Kailasa morning, noon, evening and night, and after a long time Shiva, pleased, offered a boon. Ashvatara asked that the dead Madalasa, wife of Kuvalayashva, be born as his daughter at the same age, remembering her past, as beautiful as before, a yogini and mother of yoga. Shiva granted it: at the shraddha, Ashvatara should eat the middle rice ball (pinda) himself, pure and focused, and thinking of this wish; she would then arise from his middle hood. He did so, and Madalasa, as she had been, was born from his middle hood as he breathed out; he told no one and kept her hidden in the inner rooms. One day he asked his sons why they had not brought their friend to him. They went to the prince, who said his home and wealth were theirs too and asked them to treat them as their own; they replied that their father wanted to see him; he at once rose, called the naga king 'father' and went with them. Outside the city they entered the river Gomati and pulled him down to the underworld, where he saw them in their true form, shining with the jewels in their hoods and marked with the svastika. Laughing, he praised them. He saw the lovely underworld, full of nagas young and old and naga maidens playing, music of vina, flute and drums, and hundreds of fine houses; in the palace sat Ashvatara in divine garlands and clothes, jewelled earrings and pearls, on a golden throne. The prince bowed at his feet; the naga king embraced him, smelled his head, blessed him and praised his virtues, saying the life of a virtuous man is to be praised while the worthless are dead while alive. He then told his sons that after bathing and taking food and drink they would spend some time in happy conversation with Kuvalayashva, and they all ate and drank together.

024.json.summary: After the meal the naga king Ashvatara pleased the prince with talk and asked him, as a son asks a father, to choose any gift, silver, gold, clothes, vehicles or anything rare. Kuvalayashva said that by his favour his father's house already had gold and all else; while his father lives and rules he has no reason to ask, for those whose father is alive are like the blessed in heaven, sheltered in the shade of his arms, while those who lose their father in childhood are cheated of happiness by fate; touching the naga king's feet with his crown and being embraced by him is gift enough. Pressed again, he said that all wealth, homes, women, food, sons, garlands and pleasures are the fruit of the tree of merit, so his one wish is that the habit of good deeds never leave his heart, since nothing is hard to get for those devoted to merit. Ashvatara agreed but said he must still accept something that is very hard to obtain in the human world. The prince looked at the naga's sons, who told their father that the prince's wife Madalasa, the gandharva king's daughter, had given up her life when a hostile demon deceived her with news of his death, and that he had vowed never to take another wife; he longs to see her. Ashvatara said that a meeting with the dead in the same form is impossible except in a dream or through magic like that of Shambara. The prince, with love and shame, said he would count it a great favour even to see her as an illusion. Ashvatara brought Madalasa from where she was hidden and, to test them, showed her, asking whether this was his wife. The prince, forgetting his shame, ran towards her crying 'Beloved', but Ashvatara stopped him, saying it was an illusion that would vanish at a touch. The prince fainted, crying 'Ah, beloved'; the naga king reflected on how firm his love was. Then Ashvatara revived him and told him everything, how she had been brought back to life; overjoyed, the prince bowed to the naga king, took his wife, mounted his horse, which came when he thought of it, and rode back to his city in splendour.

025.json.summary: Back in his city, Ritadhvaja told his parents how his wife, who had died, had been restored. Madalasa bowed at the feet of her parents-in-law and greeted her family with bows and embraces as before, and the citizens held a great festival. The couple enjoyed themselves for a long time by mountain streams, river banks, forests and gardens, and she, wishing to use up her merit, enjoyed pleasures with him. After a long time King Shatrujit, having ruled well, died, and the people crowned Ritadhvaja, who protected them like his own children. Madalasa bore a first son, whom his father named Vikranta; the servants were pleased, but Madalasa laughed. As the baby lay crying on his back, she sang to him as if lulling him (this is Madalasa's famous lullaby): 'You are pure, my child; you have no name, the name was only made up now; this body of five elements is not you, so why do you cry? It is not you who cry; this sound arises from the prince's body; the qualities and their lack you imagine belong to the elements in the senses. Elements weak from elements grow by food and drink; you have no growth and no decay. When this coat, your body, wears out, do not be confused; this body is a coat tied on you by your good and bad deeds and by pride and the like. You may call some things father, son, mother, beloved, mine and not mine, but honour them only as gatherings of elements. The deluded think pleasures bring happiness, though they bring pain, and take pains for pleasures. A smile is a show of bones, the bright eyes are only eyes, a woman's breasts are thick flesh; is woman, the seat of love, not hell? The earth carries the vehicle, the vehicle carries the body, and in the body sits another person; yet the sense of mine is strongest for one's own body; how foolish this is.'

026.json.summary: Jada continues. As her first son Vikranta grew, Madalasa kept teaching him, through her lullabies, to be free of the sense of 'mine', so that as he grew in strength and mind he grew in self-knowledge and never turned his mind to household life. When a second son was born and his father named him Subahu, Madalasa laughed again and taught him the same way; the third, named Shatrumardana, she also taught, and he did his duties without desire, gaining nothing for the household. When the king was about to name the fourth son, he saw her smiling and asked why she laughed at the names: Vikranta (the striding one), Subahu (strong-armed) and Shatrumardana (crusher of enemies) were fine, heroic names for kshatriyas; if she disliked them, let her name the fourth. She agreed and named him Alarka, saying he would be famous, wise and know dharma. The king laughed and asked what such a meaningless name could mean. Madalasa said all names are only conventions, and his were just as meaningless: the wise say the Self pervades everything, and going from place to place is 'striding', so the all-pervading Self cannot be Vikranta; the Self has no body, so cannot be Subahu; since one Self is in all bodies, who is its enemy or friend, and how can the bodiless be crushed? So if names are made up for daily use, why should Alarka be thought meaningless? The king agreed. When she began to teach Alarka as she had the others, the king objected that she was destroying his line by giving the sons this teaching; he asked her to set this son on the path of action, so that the path of rites would not be cut off and the offerings to the ancestors would not stop; ancestors in heaven, in animal or human births or among spirits, hungry and thirsty, are fed by the rice balls and water of a man who keeps to his duties, and gods, guests, ancestors, ghosts, birds and insects all live on such a man; so she should teach the boy the duties of a kshatriya that bring fruit in this world and the next. Madalasa then sang to Alarka: grow, my son, and please my husband by your deeds, helping friends and destroying enemies; blessed are you who will rule the earth long without rivals, enjoy it, and by dharma gain immortality; feed Brahmins on holy days, fulfil your relatives' wishes, think of others' good, keep your mind from other men's wives, please the gods with sacrifices, Brahmins and dependants with wealth, women with pleasures and enemies with battle; as a child please your relatives, as a boy your teacher, as a young man the women of good families, and in old age the forest dwellers; as king please your friends, protect the good, sacrifice, kill the wicked and enemies in battle, and, my child, die for cows and Brahmins.

027.json.summary: Alarka grew in age and understanding, lulled by his mother's words. After his sacred-thread rite he bowed to Madalasa and asked what he should do for happiness in this world and the next. She taught him the duties of a king. Once crowned, he must first keep his people content without breaking his own dharma; avoid the seven vices that destroy a king at the root; guard himself from enemies by not letting his counsel leak out, for a king whose secrets get out is destroyed eightfold, as a chariot falls apart; learn which ministers are loyal by what the enemy does, and find out enemy spies through his own spies; not trust even friends and relatives blindly, yet trust even an enemy when the work requires; know the state of his realm, its growth and decline, and use the six methods of policy, not follow desire. He must conquer first himself, then his ministers, then his servants, then the citizens, and only then the enemy; one who tries to beat enemies without this is defeated. So he must first conquer desire, anger, greed, pride, arrogance and excitement, remembering how desire destroyed Pandu, anger killed Anuhrada's son, greed killed Aila, pride got Vena killed by Brahmins, arrogance destroyed Anayus's son, and excitement Puranjaya, while Marutta, by conquering them, conquered all. A king should learn from the ways of crows, cuckoos, bees, deer, snakes, peacocks, swans, cocks and iron; act like a worm against his enemy and show the way of ants at the right time; learn from sparks of fire, the silk-cotton seed, the moon and sun, and from the courtesan, lotus, sharabha, the shulika, a pregnant woman's breast and the cowherd's wife. He should take five forms in ruling: like Indra, who pleases the earth with rain for four months, he should please the people with tax relief; like the Sun, which draws water for eight months with its rays, he should take taxes gently; like Yama, he should restrain friend and foe alike when the time comes; like the full moon, he should make all his people glad; like the wind, which moves hidden in all beings, he should move through citizens, ministers and relatives by his spies. A king whose mind is not pulled by greed, desire or wealth, who brings back to their own dharma those who stray, and in whose kingdom the duties of the classes (varnas) and stages of life (ashramas) do not decline, goes to heaven and is happy here and hereafter. Setting people in their own dharma is the king's highest duty; by protecting beings well he fulfils his purpose and gains a share of their dharma.

028.json.summary: Alarka asks his mother about the duties of the classes (varnas) and stages of life (ashramas). Madalasa says: for a Brahmin, giving, study and sacrifice are his dharma, with no fourth except in emergency, and his livelihood is officiating at sacrifices, teaching and accepting pure gifts; for a kshatriya, the dharma is giving, study and sacrifice, and his livelihood is protecting the earth and living by arms; for a vaishya, the same dharma, with trade, cattle rearing and farming as livelihood; for a shudra, the text says, the dharma is giving, sacrifice and service of the twice-born, and his livelihood is crafts, service of the twice-born, and buying and selling. A person reaches perfection by the dharma of his own class and goes to hell for doing what is forbidden. Until the sacred-thread rite a twice-born boy may act, speak and eat as he likes; after it he lives as a celibate student (brahmachari) in his teacher's house, studying, tending the fire, bathing, begging food and offering it to the teacher, eating with his permission, eager in his teacher's work, and studying when called. Having learned one, two or all the Vedas, he pays the fee, and may then enter household life or the forest stage or the fourth stage as he wishes, or remain all his life in his teacher's house, serving the teacher, his son or his pupil without pride. To be a householder he marries, properly, a healthy wife without defect, of equal standing and not of the same sage-lineage; earns wealth by his own work; honours ancestors, gods and guests; supports dependants, servants, children, female relatives, the poor, blind and fallen, and feeds birds and animals; approaches his wife in her season; never neglects the five daily sacrifices; and eats what remains after ancestors, gods, guests and kin, together with his servants.
