When he sees his children's children, he goes to the forest to purify himself, living on forest food, practising austerities, sleeping on the ground, celibate, worshipping ancestors, gods and guests, offering to the fire, bathing three times a day, wearing matted hair and bark, practising yoga and using forest oils. The fourth stage, the renouncer's, means giving up all attachment, celibacy, freedom from anger, sense control, not staying long in one place, starting no undertakings, eating once a day from alms, and seeking and seeing the Self. Common to all classes and stages are truth, purity, non-violence, freedom from envy, patience, kindness, generosity and contentment. One who leaves the dharma of his class and stage should be punished by the king, and a king who ignores such people loses the merit of his sacrifices and good works; so the king must keep all classes in their own dharma, punishing those who stray.

029.json.summary: Alarka asks what a householder must do, what brings bondage if left undone and what brings progress, what helps people and what a good person avoids at home, and how it is done. Madalasa says that by taking up household life a man supports this whole world and wins the worlds he wishes: ancestors, sages, gods, beings, humans, worms, insects, birds, animals and even asuras live on the householder and look to his face, hoping he will give. The threefold Veda is a cow on which the world rests: the Rig is her back, the Yajus her middle, the Saman her face and neck, sacrifices and good works her horns, fine hymns her hair, rites of peace and growth her dung and urine, the varnas her feet; her four teats are the calls svaha, svadha, vashat and hanta: the gods drink from svaha, the ancestors from svadha, the sages from vashat, and humans from hanta. One who cuts off this milk sinks into the dark hells Tamisra and Andhatamisra; one who lets her calves drink at the right time goes to heaven. So a man must feed gods, sages, ancestors, humans and beings daily like his own body. After bathing, he offers water to gods, sages, ancestors and Prajapati, worships the gods with flowers and perfumes, offers to the fire, and places food offerings (bali): for Brahma and the Vishvedevas in the middle of the house, for Dhanvantari in the north-east, Indra in the east, Yama in the south, Varuna in the west, Soma in the north, Dhatri and Vidhatri at the door, Aryaman outside, the house spirits all around, night-roaming beings in the air, and the ancestors facing south; then water for rinsing at each place; then food on the ground for dogs, outcastes (shvapacha) and birds. This is the Vaishvadeva rite, morning and evening. Then he rinses his mouth and watches the door for the eighth part of a muhurta for a guest. A guest is honoured with food, water, perfume and flowers; a friend or fellow villager is not a guest; a guest is a stranger who comes at that time, hungry, tired, asking, without means, and the text calls such a Brahmin the guest; one should not ask his family, Vedic school or learning, but treat him, fair or ugly, as Prajapati himself; he is called atithi because he does not stay. Feeding him frees the householder from the debt to men; one who eats without giving eats sin, and in a later birth eats filth; a guest turned away disappointed leaves his sins and takes the householder's merit. Even water and vegetables, or whatever he eats himself, should be offered to a guest. A daily shraddha with food or water should be done for the ancestors, feeding one or more Brahmins and giving the first portion to a Brahmin; alms should be given to renouncers and students, a mouthful being alms, four mouthfuls the first portion, and four times that the hanta portion. One must not eat without giving as one can; one should feed guests, kin, relatives, petitioners, the disabled, children, the old and the sick, and anyone hungry and poor who wants food; a rich man whose kinsman suffers takes on the sin the sufferer commits. The same is done in the evening, and a guest arriving at sunset is honoured with bed, seat and food. For one who carries the burden of household life, the Creator, gods, ancestors, sages, guests, kin, animals, birds and tiny insects all pour down blessings. She ends with verses sung by Atri: the householder who has the means should honour gods, ancestors, guests, kin, female relatives and teacher, put food on the ground for dogs, outcastes and birds morning and evening, and never eat meat, rice or vegetables prepared at home without first offering a share by rule.

030.json.summary: Madalasa explains that a householder's rites are of three kinds: daily (nitya), the five sacrifices already described; occasional (naimittika), such as rites at a son's birth; and both daily and occasional (nitya-naimittika), such as the shraddha on the days of the moon's changes. First the occasional shraddha for happy events (abhyudaya, nandimukha): at a son's birth, marriage and the like, the Nandimukha ancestors are worshipped, the patron facing north or east offers rice balls mixed with curd and barley, some people leave out the Vishvedeva part, an even number of Brahmins are fed and worshipped clockwise. Then the after-death rites: on the day of death the ekoddishta shraddha (for one person) is done without the gods' part, with one ring of kusha grass, no invocation and no offering into the fire; one rice ball is placed for the departed near the leftovers, with sesame water offered with the sacred thread on the right shoulder and his name spoken; at the end one says 'May it be imperishable for so-and-so' and 'Be pleased', and the Brahmins answer 'We are pleased'. This is done every month for a year. At the end of the year, or whenever it is done, comes the sapindikarana (joining the dead with the ancestors), also without the gods' part, invocation or fire offering, with the thread on the right shoulder and an odd number of Brahmins: four vessels with sesame, perfume and water are prepared, three for the ancestors and one for the departed, and the departed's vessel is poured into the other three while saying the verse beginning 'ye samanah', the rest as before. The ekoddishta is done for women too; but for women there is no sapindikarana when there is no son, and the ekoddishta is done for them every year on the day of death. If there is no son, the sapindas do these rites, then the sahodakas, then the mother's sapindas and sahodakas; a daughter's son does them for a man without sons, and sons of an appointed daughter (putrika) for the mother's father; sons belonging to two families (dvyamushyayana) honour both maternal and paternal grandfathers. If no one is left, the women perform them for their husbands without mantras; if there are none, the king has a member of the same caste perform the cremation and all rites, since the king is the kinsman of all classes. She then turns to the shraddha that is both daily and occasional, whose occasion is the new moon (darsha), the time of the moon's waning, which fixes its time.

031.json.summary: Madalasa continues teaching Alarka about the shraddha. After the sapindikarana, the father's great-grandfather drops out of the rice-ball offering and joins those who receive only the wipings (lepa) of the hand; the father, grandfather and great-grandfather are the three who receive the pinda, the three before them receive the lepa, and with the sacrificer this makes a link of seven generations. Other ancestors, in hell, in animal births or among spirits, are also fed by a proper shraddha: the scattered food feeds those who became pishachas; water from bathing clothes feeds those who became trees; drops from the body feed those who became gods; grains of food left after the pindas are lifted feed those in animal births; scattered food and sweeping water feed children of the family who died before their rites; the water used by Brahmins for rinsing and washing feet feeds others. Even a shraddha made with wrongly earned wealth feeds those born as chandalas and pukkasas. So one should perform shraddha with devotion, even with vegetables, and no one in that family will suffer. Its times: every new moon, the ashtaka days, and by choice when a worthy Brahmin arrives, at eclipses, solstices, equinoxes, the sun's entry into a sign, vyatipata, when suitable materials are available, after bad dreams, and when one's birth star is afflicted by planets. Worthy Brahmins to invite include a learned Vedic scholar, a yogi, a Samaveda singer, those who know special Vedic rites and the six limbs, a daughter's son, priest, son-in-law, sister's son, father-in-law, maternal uncle, one devoted to the five fires or to penance, those devoted to parents, pupils and relatives. To be avoided are a student who broke his vow, the sick, those with missing or extra limbs, son of a remarried woman, the one-eyed, those born of adultery, a betrayer of friends, those with bad nails, impotent, black-toothed, accused by their father, slanderers, sellers of Soma, defilers of girls, physicians, those who abandon teacher or parents, paid teachers, enemies, husbands of women previously married, those who abandon the Veda or fire, and others of wrong conduct. They are invited the day before, and both they and the host must be self-controlled; whoever has sex after giving or eating a shraddha makes the ancestors lie for a month in that seed. The dark fortnight and the afternoon are dearer to the ancestors. The Brahmins are welcomed and seated, an even number for the gods' part and an odd number for the ancestors', or one each, with the mother's father's side treated alike; the gods' side faces east, the ancestors' north. With kusha seats, water offerings, rings of kusha and permission, the gods are invoked with mantras and given barley water, perfume, garlands, incense and lamps; then, with the sacred thread on the right shoulder, the ancestors are invoked with doubled kusha and offered water with sesame. With permission, food without spices or salt is offered into the fire: to Agni who carries offerings to the ancestors, to Soma with the ancestors, and to Yama lord of the dead. The rest is served to the Brahmins with the words 'Enjoy as you please'; they eat silently and the host serves the food they like best, without haste or anger, recites mantras that drive off demons and scatters sesame and mustard seed for protection, since the shraddha is full of dangers. When they say they are satisfied, food is scattered on the ground, water given, and with sesame-mixed food rice balls are placed on kusha near the leftovers for the ancestors, with water poured through the ancestors' part of the hand, and likewise for the maternal ancestors; then rinsing water, a fee, 'Let there be good svadha', the Vishvedevas are dismissed with 'May they be pleased', blessings are asked, and the Brahmins are seen to the door. Then the daily rites and feeding of guests follow, and the host eats with his household. The daughter's son, the kutapa (midday) time and sesame are the three purifiers of a shraddha; anger, travel and haste are to be avoided; silver vessels are praised, since the ancestors milked svadha from the earth in a silver vessel.

032.json.summary: Madalasa tells what pleases or is to be avoided at a shraddha. The ancestors are satisfied for one month by sacrificial food, two by fish, three by deer meat, four by hare, five by bird meat, six by boar, seven by goat, eight by the ena deer, nine by the ruru deer, ten by the gavaya, eleven by mutton, a year by cow's milk or milk-rice; the meat of the vadhrinasa (a long-eared goat), the red goat, kalashaka greens, honey, the khadga (rhinoceros) meat, a daughter's son's offering and anything from one's own family give endless satisfaction, as does a shraddha at Gaya. Good grains are shyamaka millets, wild rice, barley, rice, wheat, sesame, mung, mustard, priyangu and others; to be avoided are some pulses such as rajamasha and masura, garlic, onions, grinjana, radish, karambha, things poor in taste or colour, gourds, salty and saline things, reddish resins, and food got by bribery, from fallen people or from an unjust bride-price. Bad water (smelly, frothy, too little, not enough for a cow, brought at night, from a public drinking place) and the milk of deer, sheep, camels, one-hoofed animals, buffaloes, yaks, a cow within ten days of calving, or milk begged 'for my ancestors', are avoided. The ground must not be full of insects, dry, burnt, noisy or foul-smelling. People who disgrace or harm the family, naked people and sinners spoil the rite by looking at it, as do a eunuch, an outcast, a cock, a village pig and a dog, and demons by their sight; so it should be done screened, with sesame scattered on the ground. Food touched by those impure from a death or birth, the long sick, the fallen or dirty does not nourish the ancestors; the sight of a menstruating woman, a shaven-headed person or drunkard is avoided, and food with hair or insects, seen by dogs, rotten, stale, of brinjal, or fanned by clothes. Whatever is given with great faith in the ancestors' name and family reaches them as the food of whatever birth they now have. Yogis should always be fed at a shraddha, since the ancestors rest on yoga; one yogi eating first saves the host and the other eaters as a boat across water. The ancestors once sang to King Aila: 'When will a son be born in our line who will give us a rice ball on the ground from the leftovers of yogis, or at Gaya, or offer rhinoceros meat, kalashaka and sesame-rich krisara for a month's satisfaction?' A shraddha on the thirteenth day in the star Magha with milk-rice, honey and ghee in the sun's southern course is praised. Satisfied by shraddha, the ancestors please the Vasus, Rudras, Adityas, stars and planets, and give long life, wisdom, wealth, learning, heaven, freedom, happiness and kingdom. She will next tell the lunar days for shraddhas done for particular wishes.

033.json.summary: Madalasa lists the fruits of shraddhas performed for particular wishes. By lunar day: on the first, wealth; second, servants (two-footed beings); third, boons; fourth, destruction of enemies; fifth, prosperity; sixth, honour; seventh, leadership of a group; eighth, great growth; ninth, women; tenth, fulfilment of all desires; eleventh, all the Vedas; twelfth, victory; thirteenth, children, intelligence, cattle, growth, independence, nourishment, long life and lordship. One whose father or ancestors died young or were killed by weapons should perform it on the fourteenth; one who performs it carefully on the new moon gains all desires and endless heaven. By lunar mansion (nakshatra): Krittika gives heaven; Rohini children; Mrigashira vigour; Ardra courage; Punarvasu land; Pushya nourishment; Ashlesha fine sons; Magha leadership among one's people; Purva Phalguni good fortune; Uttara Phalguni generosity and children; Hasta excellence; Chitra beauty and children; Svati success in trade; Vishakha sons; Anuradha world rule; Jyeshtha lordship; Mula good health; Purva Ashadha fame; Uttara Ashadha freedom from sorrow; Shravana good worlds; Dhanishtha great wealth; Abhijit knowledge of the Veda; Shatabhisha success in medicine; Purva Bhadrapada goats and sheep; Uttara Bhadrapada cows; Revati base metals; Ashvini horses; Bharani long life. So one who knows should perform these wish-fulfilling shraddhas under these stars.

034.json.summary: Madalasa says a good householder must honour gods and ancestors with offerings, and feed guests, relatives, beings, servants, animals, birds, ants, mendicants and beggars; one who neglects the daily and occasional rites eats sin. Alarka asks to hear about right conduct (sadachara), which brings happiness here and hereafter. She says that without right conduct there is no happiness and sacrifices, gifts and penance bring no good; a person of bad conduct does not live long, while good conduct removes bad signs. A householder should strive for the three aims: of his wealth he should save a quarter for the next world, use half for his own support and the daily and occasional rites, and invest a quarter to increase his capital; dharma should be done to avoid sin and for the next world, and desire pursued without harming the other aims. Then the rules: wake at the Brahma muhurta and think of dharma and wealth; rinse and face east; perform the morning twilight prayer while stars are visible and the evening one while the sun is visible; avoid idle talk, lies, harsh words, false teachings and bad company; make fire offerings morning and evening; do not look at the rising or setting sun; comb hair, look in the mirror, clean teeth and offer to the gods in the forenoon; do not relieve oneself on village paths, at holy places, in fields, ploughed land or cow pens, or in water; do not look at another's wife naked or at oneself naked; avoid seeing, touching or speaking to a menstruating woman; do not stand on dung, hair, ash, potsherds, husks, coals, bones or rags; eat after honouring ancestors, gods, people and beings, facing east or north, silent, pure, attentive; avoid raw salt and very hot food; do not speak or study while impure, nor touch a cow, Brahmin, fire or one's own head; do not look at the sun, moon or stars by choice; avoid broken seats, beds and vessels; give elders a seat, rise for them, greet them and follow them; do not eat or worship in a single cloth; do not bathe or sleep naked; do not scratch the head with both hands or wash it often without reason; do not study on forbidden days; do not urinate facing a Brahmin, wind, cow or the sun (face north by day, south by night); do not speak of a teacher's faults; do not listen to slander; give way to Brahmins, the king, the suffering, the learned, a pregnant woman, the burdened, the young, the dumb, blind and deaf, the drunk and mad, and others; walk clockwise round temples, sacred trees, crossroads, the learned, teachers and gods; do not wear others' shoes, clothes, garlands, sacred thread or ornaments; on the fourteenth, eighth, full and new moon days avoid oil massage and women; avoid hurting vital points, abuse, slander, deceit, pride and sharpness; do not mock fools, the mad, the addicted, the ugly or those with missing or extra limbs; do not raise a stick against another except to teach a son or pupil; do not cook special dishes for oneself alone; clean the teeth facing east or north and avoid forbidden twigs; do not sleep with the head to the north or west; do not bathe in smelly water or at night, except at eclipses; do not shake hair or clothes, apply perfume unbathed, wear red, bright or black clothes, or reverse garments and ornaments; avoid torn or dirty clothes; avoid food with hair or insects, seen by dogs, licked, stale, meat from the back, meat not offered (vritha-mamsa) and forbidden meat; do not sleep at sunrise or sunset; eat bathed, seated, attentive, not on the bed or ground, not noisily, not in one cloth, and not without giving to onlookers. A man must never go to another's wife, which destroys merit and life like nothing else. Rinse properly before worship and eating, with clean water, facing east or north, avoiding five kinds of earth; sip water three or four times with hands between the knees and touch the openings of the head; after sneezing, spitting or dressing, rinse, or touch a cow's back, look at the sun or touch the right ear. Avoid sleep, study and eating at the twilights, and sex and travel then; worship gods in the forenoon, people at midday, ancestors in the afternoon. A wife should be without defects, not sick, deformed, tawny, talkative or ill-reputed, with a good nose and auspicious marks, and outside the seventh generation on the father's side and the fifth on the mother's; protect one's wife, avoid jealousy, and avoid sleep and sex by day. The text says one should avoid a wife for four nights of her period and also the fifth to avoid a daughter, since sons are born from even nights and daughters from odd. Bathe in clothes after a shave, vomiting, sex or visiting a cremation ground. Do not blame or mock gods, Vedas, Brahmins, the good, teachers, devoted wives, sacrificers or ascetics, nor listen to those who do; dress in white with white flowers; avoid friendship with the arrogant, mad, foolish, rude, thieves, spendthrifts, the greedy, enemies, unchaste women and their husbands, the stronger and the weaker, the suspicious and those who rely only on fate; befriend the good, wise, honest, able and hard-working. Honour with the madhuparka the six worthy guests: friend, initiated sacrificer, king, graduate, father-in-law and priest. After the house worship, make fire offerings to Brahma, Prajapati, the Guhyas, Kashyapa and Anumati, then the house offerings and the Vaishvadeva offerings to Parjanya, the earth, Vayu, the directions, Brahma, the sky, the sun, the Vishvedevas, all beings, Dawn, the lord of beings, and the ancestors in the south with 'svadha namah', and give the first portion of food to a Brahmin. The parts of the hand used in rites are: the Brahma part below the thumb for rinsing, the ancestors' part between forefinger and thumb, the gods' part at the fingertips, and Prajapati's part at the base of the little finger. Do not carry water and fire together, stretch the feet towards teachers or gods, point out a cow suckling her calf, drink water from the joined hands, or blow on fire with the mouth. Do not live where there is no lender, physician, Vedic scholar and flowing river; live where the king is strong and righteous, the land fertile, the citizens law-abiding and without envy, farmers not too self-indulgent and medicines available; not where there are aggressors, old enmities and constant festivals.

035.json.summary: Madalasa tells Alarka what may and may not be eaten, and how things are purified. Stale food is fit to eat if it was kept with oil, and preparations of wheat, barley and milk even without oil; among animals the hare, tortoise, monitor lizard, porcupine and rhinoceros may be eaten, but the village pig and cock must be avoided; meat left from offerings to ancestors and gods, eaten at a shraddha at a Brahmin's wish, sprinkled with water, or taken as medicine, does not defile. Purification: conch, stone, gold, silver, ropes, cloth, vegetables, roots, fruit, split cane, leather, gems, diamonds, coral, pearls and the human body are cleaned with water; iron with water and scrubbing with stone; oily vessels with hot water; winnowing baskets, grain, deer skins, pestle and mortar, and piles of cloth by sprinkling; bark garments with water and earth; grass, wood and herbs by sprinkling; wool and hair with a paste of mustard or sesame and water; cotton with water and ash; wood, ivory, bone and horn by planing; clay pots by firing again. Always clean are alms, an artisan's hand, goods for sale, a woman's mouth, things found on the road of unknown origin, things brought by servants, things praised in words, things long past or passed through many hands, light things, very plentiful things, children, the doings of the old and sick, workshops, kitchens, nursing mothers, and running water without smell or bubbles. Ground is purified by time, burning, sweeping, cows walking on it, plastering, scraping, sprinkling and worship. Food with hair or insects, smelled by a cow or touched by flies is sprinkled with earth, water and ash; copper is cleaned with acid, tin and lead with alkali, bronze with ash and water, liquids by pouring off, things smeared with filth by earth and water until the smell goes, others by removing colour and smell. Water on the ground that satisfies a cow is pure; meat killed by a chandala or beast of prey is pure; cloth on the road is purified by wind. Dust, fire, a horse, a cow, shade, rays, wind, earth, droplets and flies are not defiled by touching impure things; goats and horses are pure at the mouth, not a cow or calf; a mother's flowing milk is pure, and a bird when dropping fruit. Seats, beds, vehicles, boats and grass on the road are purified by the moon, sun and wind. After walking in the street, bathing, sneezing, drinking or feeling unwell, one should rinse and change clothes. From much spoiled food, the top is thrown away and the rest sprinkled. Eating bad food knowingly calls for a three-night fast. One bathes after touching a menstruating woman, a horse, jackal, a woman after childbirth, outcastes, or a corpse-bearer; after touching a human bone with fat, bathe; a dry one, rinse, touch a cow or look at the sun. One should not step over blood, spittle or body scrubbings, linger in gardens at wrong times, or speak to a woman hated by people or without a husband or son; leftovers, urine, faeces and foot-water are thrown outside the house; one should not bathe in another's pond without removing five lumps of earth; bathe in temple tanks, the Ganga, lakes and rivers. After touching or speaking with those who mock gods, ancestors, scripture, sacrifice and mantras, or after seeing a menstruating woman, an outcaste, a fallen person, a corpse, a heretic, a woman after childbirth, a eunuch or a naked person, one purifies oneself by looking at the sun. After touching forbidden food, a woman after childbirth, a eunuch, cat, rat, dog, cock, a fallen person, a chandala or a corpse-bearer, one bathes. A man whose daily rites lapse or whom Brahmins have abandoned is a sinner; the daily rites may stop only during impurity from death or birth. Impurity lasts ten days for a Brahmin, twelve for a kshatriya, a fortnight for a vaishya and a month for a shudra, without giving or fire offerings. Kinsmen burn the body outside, give water on the first, fourth, seventh and ninth days, and gather the ashes and bones on the fourth day, after which touching is allowed. For deaths by weapon, water, hanging, fire, poison, falling or fasting, for a child, one abroad or a renouncer, purification is immediate; for others three days. If another death or birth occurs during impurity, the first period covers it. On a son's birth the father bathes in his clothes. When the period ends, each class touches water, vehicle, weapons, goad or staff and resumes its work, performs the ekoddishta for the dead and gives to worthy Brahmins what is dearest. One should study the three Vedas, earn wealth by dharma, sacrifice, and do only what one's conscience does not reject and need not hide from good people; living so, a householder gains dharma, wealth and desire and good here and hereafter.

036.json.summary: This file holds two adhyayas, the 36th and the 37th. Jada says that Alarka, so taught by his mother, married on reaching youth, had sons, performed sacrifices and always obeyed his father. In old age Ritadhvaja crowned him and prepared to go to the forest with his wife to do penance. Madalasa gave her son a last instruction, to help him give up attachment to pleasure: if ever he faced unbearable sorrow from losing loved ones, from enemies or from losing wealth, as a householder ruling a kingdom (for a householder attached to 'mine' is a home of sorrow), he should take out the message written in tiny letters on a strip inside the gold signet ring she gave him. She gave him the ring with blessings, and Kuvalayashva and Madalasa left the kingdom to him and went to the forest. In the next adhyaya, Alarka ruled justly, punishing the wicked and protecting the good, kept his people in their duties, performed great sacrifices and had strong, righteous sons; he balanced dharma, wealth and pleasure, and many years passed like a single day; he felt no detachment while enjoying pleasures and never felt he had gained enough. His brother Subahu, living in the forest, heard that he was careless and ruled by his senses, and after long thought decided it would be for his good to side with his enemy. So Subahu, the wise one, went to the powerful king of Kashi, as if seeking help to regain his own share of the kingdom. The king of Kashi prepared his army and sent a messenger demanding that the kingdom be given to Subahu. Alarka, knowing his duty, refused to give it on command: if his elder brother came and asked with affection he would give it, but he would not give even a little land out of fear of attack. Subahu did not ask, since begging is not a kshatriya's dharma. The king of Kashi invaded, won over Alarka's neighbours, border chiefs, fort commanders and forest tribes by gifts, division and persuasion, besieged his city and drained his treasury. In deep distress Alarka remembered the ring. After bathing and having Brahmins recite blessings, he took out the message and read his mother's words, thrilled with joy: 'Attachment should be given up completely; if it cannot be, let it be with the good, for the company of the good is the cure. Desire should be given up completely; if it cannot be, let it be desire for freedom, for that is its cure.' Reading it again and again, he decided that the way to good was the wish for freedom, gained through the company of the good, and went in great distress to the sage Dattatreya. He bowed and begged him, the refuge of those who seek refuge, to remove his sorrow. Dattatreya promised to do so that very day and asked him to say truly what his sorrow was and whose. The king reflected on the three kinds of sorrow and on the Self, and, smiling, said to himself: 'I am not earth, water, fire, wind or space; pleasure and pain belong to this body made of them, and if they were mine they would be mine even in another's body. Sorrow and joy are in the mind, and I am not the mind, ego or intellect; I am separate from body and mind. My elder brother wants the kingdom, a heap of five elements; what is that to me, who am other than the body? One who has no hands, flesh, bones or veins has no tie to elephants, horses, chariots or treasure. So I have no enemy, no sorrow, no joy, no city, no treasury, no army. As the one space is seen as many in jars, pots and water vessels, so Subahu, the king of Kashi and I are one, appearing different through different bodies.'

038.json.summary: Alarka bows to Dattatreya and says that, seeing rightly, he has no sorrow; those who see wrongly are always sunk in an ocean of unhappiness. Whatever a person's mind becomes attached to as 'mine' brings him only sorrow: the grief when a cat eats one's own hen is not felt when it eats a sparrow or mouse that one does not own. He is neither sad nor happy, since he is beyond Nature (Prakriti); pleasure and pain belong to the elements acting on elements. Dattatreya agrees: 'mine' is the root of sorrow and 'not mine' the root of peace; by his questioning this knowledge has arisen in Alarka and thrown off the idea of 'mine' like silk-cotton fluff. He describes a great tree of wrong knowledge: it sprouts from 'I', its trunk is 'mine', house and land are its high branches, sons and wife its shoots, wealth and grain its great leaves, merit and sin its flowers, joy and sorrow its fruit; it blocks the path to freedom, is watered by the company of fools, and is full of the bees of craving; those tired by the road of worldly life who rest in its shade, depending on the pleasure of false knowledge, never find lasting good. But those who cut down this tree of 'mine' with the axe of knowledge, sharpened on the stone of good company, go by the path to the cool forest of Brahman, free of dust and thorns, and gain supreme peace. Neither Alarka nor he is the gross body of elements and senses, nor the subtle elements, nor the inner organ; the knower of the field (the Self) is beyond, and the aggregate is made of the qualities; as a gnat and the udumbara fruit, a reed and its sheath, a fish and water are together yet separate, so are the field and the Self. Alarka says that by his grace he now knows the difference between Nature and the power of consciousness, but his mind, held by sense objects, is not steady, and he does not know how to be freed from the bondage of Nature, how not to be born again, how to go beyond the qualities and become one with the eternal Brahman. He asks Dattatreya to teach him yoga, since the company of the good helps people.

039.json.summary: Dattatreya teaches Alarka yoga. Freedom is the separation, through knowledge, of the yogi from ignorance; it is union with Brahman and separation from the qualities of Nature. Freedom comes from yoga, and yoga from right knowledge. Sorrow arises from attachment in those whose minds cling to 'mine', so one seeking freedom must give up attachment; then the idea of 'mine' fades. Being free of 'mine' brings happiness; detachment comes from seeing faults, and detachment and knowledge support each other. The true home is where one lives, true food what keeps one alive; true knowledge is what leads to freedom, all else ignorance. By using up past merit and sin through experience, doing the daily duties without desire, and not storing up new karma, one is not bound to bodies again. First the yogi must conquer himself. He burns faults by breath control (pranayama), sins by concentration (dharana), sense objects by withdrawal (pratyahara) and ungodly qualities by meditation (dhyana); as ores are cleansed by blowing on them, faults of the senses are burned by breath control. Pranayama, the restraint of prana and apana, is of three kinds: light, of twelve measures (a measure being the time of a blink or a short syllable), middle of twenty-four and highest of thirty-six; the first overcomes sweat, the second trembling and the third dejection. As lions, tigers and elephants become gentle when tamed, and a mahout leads a tamed elephant, so the yogi leads his mastered breath, which then harms no one's body. The four stages of pranayama are dhvasti (the fruits of good and bad deeds wear away and the mind is cleared), prapti (lasting restraint of desires for this and the next world), samvit (knowledge of past and future, of distant and hidden things, of the moon, sun, stars and planets) and prasada (calm of mind, the five breaths, the senses and their objects). He should sit in the lotus, half-lotus or svastika posture, with Om in his heart, body even, feet drawn in, mouth closed, thighs firm, heels not touching the genitals, head slightly raised, teeth not touching, gazing at the tip of his nose, covering tamas with rajas and rajas with sattva, and then, fixed in pure sattva, withdraw senses, breaths and mind from their objects, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs. Twelve pranayamas make a dharana. Through this all faults are destroyed and he sees the highest Brahman, the qualities of Nature and his pure Self. Eating moderately and devoted to breath control, he should rise step by step, like climbing a house, only to stages already mastered, since an unmastered stage brings faults, diseases and delusion. Air is to be drawn in slowly, as one drinks water through a pipe, and held at ten points: the navel, heart, chest, throat, mouth, tip of the nose, eyes, between the brows, head and beyond; through these ten he becomes like the imperishable. He should not practise when bloated, hungry, tired or troubled, in great cold or heat, in windy weather, near noise, fire or water, in an old cow pen, at a crossroads, on dry leaves, by a river, in a cremation ground, among snakes, in fearful places, by a well, at shrines or anthills; doing so foolishly brings deafness, dullness, loss of memory, dumbness, blindness and fever. Remedies: for wind, tumours and stomach troubles, eat hot oily gruel and hold it there, or hold the breath against the knot of wind; for trembling, fix the mind on a great steady mountain; for loss of speech, on speech; for deafness, on hearing; for thirst, imagine a mango; in each painful part, concentrate on what helps it, warmth in cold and cooling in heat; for lost memory, place a peg on the head and strike wood with wood; one may also fix the mind on sky and earth, wind and fire; if a non-human being enters the yogi, he should burn it by concentrating on wind and fire. The body must be protected, since it is the means to dharma, wealth, desire and freedom. The yogi should hide his powers, since telling others and pride in them destroy knowledge. The first signs of progress are freedom from greed, health, gentleness, pleasant smell, little urine and faeces, radiance, calm and a gentle voice; people praise him in his absence and creatures do not fear him; one not troubled by cold and heat and fearing no one is close to success. (The heading calls this the 36th chapter, the closing line the 39th.)

040.json.summary: Dattatreya describes the obstacles (upasargas) that arise when the yogi has seen the Self. He begins to desire rites done for gain, human pleasures, women, the fruit of gifts, learning, magic, metals, wealth, heaven, godhood, lordship over the gods, elixirs, flying through the air, sacrifices, entering water or fire, and the fruits of shraddhas, gifts, vows, fasts, good works and worship; the yogi must turn his mind back from these and fix it on Brahman. After these are overcome come five more, of sattva, rajas and tamas: pratibha, when the meaning of the Vedas, poetry, sciences and all arts shines in his mind; shravana, when he hears sounds from thousands of yojanas and knows the meaning of all words; daiva, when he sees in all eight directions like a god, which the wise call madness; bhrama, when his mind wanders without support and he loses all right conduct; and avarta, when his knowledge whirls like a whirlpool and destroys the mind. Even gods whose yoga was ruined by these terrible obstacles keep returning to rebirth. So the yogi should wrap himself in a white blanket made of the mind and meditate on the highest Brahman, eating little and controlling his senses. He should hold seven subtle concentrations in the head, on earth and the rest: concentrating on earth he gains its subtlety, thinks himself to be earth and gives up smell; likewise he gives up taste in water, form in fire, touch in wind, and sound and movement in space; entering the minds of all beings he makes his mind subtle; entering the intellect of all beings he gains supreme subtlety of intellect and gives it up. Whoever knows and gives up these seven subtle things does not return; seeing each and giving up each power, he goes to the highest. Whatever element he becomes attached to, he perishes in it; one who gives up the subtle things, knowing they are bound together, reaches the highest state, while attachment to smell and the like brings him back, even to the state of Brahma. After passing the seven, he may merge into whatever subtle element he wishes, or into the bodies of gods, asuras, gandharvas, nagas or rakshasas, without attachment. He gains the eight powers: anima (becoming smallest), laghima (lightness and speed), mahima (greatness, being honoured by all), prapti (reaching anything), prakamya (all-pervasiveness), ishitva (lordship), vashitva (control) and yatra-kamavasayita (dwelling where he wishes); these signal freedom and supreme peace (nirvana). Then he is not born, does not grow or perish, does not decay or change, is not cut, wet, burned or dried by the elements, and is not carried away by sound and the rest. As a piece of gold whose impurity is burned away by fire becomes one with another piece, as fire put into fire becomes the same fire, as water poured into water becomes one with it, so the yogi whose faults are burned by the fire of yoga becomes one with the supreme Brahman and is never separate again.

041.json.summary: Alarka asks how a yogi should live so as not to fail on the path to Brahman. Dattatreya says honour and insult, which disturb ordinary people, help the yogi when taken the other way: insult is nectar to him and honour the worst poison. He should step where his eyes have checked the ground, drink water strained through cloth, speak words purified by truth and think thoughts purified by reason. He should not go to hospitality, shraddhas, sacrifices, temple festivals or crowds for the sake of gain. He should beg when the cooking fires are out, the smoke gone and everyone has eaten, but not always at the same three houses, and behave so that people despise and slight him, without spoiling the path of the good. He should beg first from householders and from wandering ascetics' homes, this being best; then from modest, faithful, self-controlled, learned householders; and as the lowest way, from those not fallen of other classes. Good foods for a yogi are alms, gruel, buttermilk, milk, barley water, fruit, roots, priyangu, broken grain, oil-cake and barley flour. Before eating he sips water once in silence and offers the first five mouthfuls to the five breaths, prana, apana, samana, udana and vyana, then eats the rest as he likes, sips water again and touches his heart. The five vows of a mendicant are non-stealing, celibacy, renunciation, freedom from greed and, highest, non-violence; the five observances are freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, light food and daily study. He should seek the essential knowledge that achieves the goal, since much learning hinders yoga; one who thirsts to know this and that will not find what is to be known even in a thousand ages. Free of attachment and anger, eating lightly and with senses controlled, he should close the gates of the senses and fix his mind in meditation in empty places, caves and forests. One who controls speech, action and mind is a true tridandi (carrier of the three staffs). For one who sees the whole world as the Self, who is dear and who is not? With pure mind, seeing a clod and gold as equal, he is not born again. Sacrifices are better than Vedic study, repetition of mantras (japa) better than sacrifice, the path of knowledge better than japa, and meditation free of attachment better than knowledge; with that the eternal is reached.

042.json.summary: Dattatreya says a yogi who lives this way cannot be turned back even in hundreds of births, and sees the supreme Self, whose feet, heads and necks are everywhere. To reach it he should repeat the one syllable Om, which is his only study. A, U and M are three measures, of sattva, rajas and tamas; above them is the half-measure, beyond the qualities, known only to yogis, called Gandhari because it rests on the gandhara note, felt at the crown of the head like the touch of an ant's walk. As Om, uttered, goes out through the crown, so the yogi made of Om becomes imperishable in the imperishable. The breath is the bow, the Self the arrow and Brahman the target; it must be hit with care, and he should become one with it like the arrow. Om is the three Vedas, worlds and fires, Vishnu, Brahma and Shiva, and the Rig, Saman and Yajus; the three and a half measures should be known in their true sense, and the yogi absorbed in them dissolves into them. A is the earth (bhur), U the middle region (bhuvah), M with its consonant the heaven (svah); the first measure is the manifest, the second the unmanifest, the third the power of consciousness, and the half-measure the highest state; these are the stages of yoga. By saying Om everything, existent and non-existent, is taken in; the first measure is short, the second long, the third prolonged, and the half beyond speech. This is the imperishable Brahman called Om; whoever truly knows or meditates on it leaves the wheel of rebirth, free of the three bonds, and merges in the supreme Brahman. One whose karma is not yet used up, if he learns the time of his death from omens and remembers Om at the time of departure, becomes a yogi again; so every yogi, whether perfected or not, should know the omens of death so as not to fail at the moment of departure.

043.json.summary: Dattatreya tells Alarka the omens (arishta) by which a yogi can know the time of his death. One who cannot see the Milky Way (path of the gods), the pole star, Venus, the moon's shadow or Arundhati will not live beyond a year; one who sees the sun's disc without rays or fire with a garland of rays, eleven months; one who in a dream vomits or passes gold or silver, ten months; one who sees ghosts, pishachas, cities of gandharvas in the sky or golden trees, nine months; one who suddenly becomes fat or thin and changes his nature, eight months; one whose footprint is broken at the heel or toes in dust or mud, seven months; one on whose head a vulture, pigeon, crow or blue flesh-eating bird sits, six months; one struck by lines of crows or a rain of dust, or who sees his shadow changed, four or five months; one who sees lightning in the south without clouds or a rainbow at night, two or three months; one who sees his body in ghee, oil, a mirror or water without a head, one month; one whose body smells like a goat or a corpse, half a month; one whose heart and feet dry right after bathing, or who stays dry after drinking, ten days. Death is near for one whose broken breath cuts the vital points and who feels no pleasure at the touch of water; for one who dreams of riding a bear or monkey south while singing; whom a woman in red and black, singing and laughing, leads south in a dream; who dreams of a naked, laughing, mighty Jain monk leaping; who dreams he is sunk to the head in a sea of mud (he dies at once); who dreams of hair, coals, ashes, snakes or a dry river (death on the eleventh day); who dreams of being struck with stones by fierce black armed men; towards whom a jackal howls at sunrise; whose heart still aches with hunger right after eating and who grinds his teeth; who cannot smell a lamp, is afraid day and night, and does not see himself in another's eyes; who sees a rainbow at midnight or the planets by day; whose nose bends, ears drop or rise and left eye waters; whose face turns red or tongue dark; who dreams of riding a camel or ass south; who, closing his ears, does not hear the inner sound, and whose eye-light fails; who in a dream falls into a pit whose door closes and cannot get out; whose gaze turns up, unsteady and red, with heat in the mouth and a hollow navel; who in a dream enters fire or water and does not come out; who is struck by evil spirits by night or day (death within seven nights); who sees his clean white clothes as red or black. A change in one's nature is also a sign: one begins to despise and abuse those he always honoured, stops worshipping the gods, scorns elders, teachers, Brahmins, yogis and the wise, and does not honour his parents and sons-in-law. A yogi should watch these omens through the year, fix the time in mind, go to a safe place, give up the fear of death, and practise yoga in the part of the day or night when the omen was seen until that day comes; having conquered that time, staying where his mind is steady, he should master the three qualities in the supreme Self, become one with it, give up even the activity of the mind, and reach the supreme peace beyond the senses, mind and words. Dattatreya then gives examples for the yogi: the moonstone gives water only when touched by moonlight, and the sunstone fire only with sunlight; ants, rats, mongooses, lizards and partridges live in a house as if they own it but simply move elsewhere when it falls, feeling no grief; a tiny mud-carrying insect builds a great heap with its small mouth; a tree full of leaves, flowers and fruit is stripped by animals, birds and men; a mark on a young deer's horn grows with it; a man climbing with a full vessel watches the high path; a man protects with all effort the buried treasure he lives on. The home is where one lives, food what keeps one alive; why say 'mine'? As one uses tools for a task, the yogi should use the intellect and other faculties, which are not his own, to reach the highest. Jada says Alarka bowed and said joyfully: by the gods' grace came this fear of defeat and death; fortunate were the Kashi king's strength, his own weakness, the loss of servants and treasury, and his fear, since they brought him to Dattatreya and to knowledge; misfortune turns to good when good times come; Subahu and the Kashi king were his helpers. He will now give up household life, a forest of trees of suffering. Dattatreya blessed him and told him to live free of 'mine' and 'I' for freedom. Alarka went to the camp of the Kashi king and his brother Subahu and told the king, smiling, to enjoy the kingdom himself or give it to Subahu. The Kashi king asked why he gave it up without a fight, which is not a kshatriya's dharma. Alarka said he once thought so too, but now knew that as the body is made of elements, so the inner faculties and qualities are the same in all beings; consciousness is one, and there is no other; so how can there be friend and enemy, master and servant? Through the pain caused by fear of him he had gained knowledge by Dattatreya's grace; the true victory is to conquer the senses, give up attachment and fix the mind on Brahman; 'I am not your enemy nor you mine, nor is Subahu my wrongdoer; I have seen all this as the Self; look for some other enemy.' Subahu rose in joy, greeted his brother, and spoke to the Kashi king.

044.json.summary: Subahu tells the king of Kashi that he has gained what he came for and will now go. The Kashi king asks why he came and what he gained, since he had asked him to conquer Alarka and take back his ancestral kingdom, and now the army had done so and he could enjoy it. Subahu explains: his brother Alarka, though knowing the truth, was attached to worldly pleasures, while his two elder brothers and he himself were awakened; their mother had poured knowledge into their ears in childhood as she poured milk into their mouths, but not into Alarka's; as good people traveling together grieve when one of them falls behind, so they grieved for him sinking in the delusion of household life, since their bodies are related as brothers. So he had resolved that suffering would bring Alarka to detachment, and took the Kashi king's help to make war. Now detachment had arisen in Alarka from suffering and understanding; his task was done. One who lived in Madalasa's womb and drank her milk should not walk the path of other women's sons. Those who neglect a suffering relative or friend are like people without senses. He wished the king well and asked him to seek knowledge. The Kashi king asked why Subahu would not also help him, since meeting the good is never fruitless. Subahu said: of the four aims of life, dharma, wealth, desire and freedom, the king had the first three but lacked the last; he should not think in terms of 'mine' and 'I', and should reflect in the last part of the night on 'whose am I?', examining the outer and inner world, the unmanifest and the manifest, from the unmanifest down to the gross elements, changeless and unconscious, and who the knower is; knowing this he knows all; taking the not-self as the Self is foolishness, like calling what is not space space. Subahu left; the Kashi king honoured Alarka and went home. Alarka crowned his eldest son and went to the forest, giving up all attachment for his own perfection; in time, free of pairs of opposites and possessions, he gained the unequalled power of yoga and the highest peace (nirvana). Seeing the whole world of gods, asuras and men bound by the ropes of the qualities, pulled by the senses through ideas of son, brother, mine and another's, sunk in the mud of ignorance, and himself freed, he sang: 'Alas, what pain it was that I once ruled a kingdom; only later did I learn that there is no happiness higher than yoga.' Jada tells his father to follow this highest yoga for freedom and reach Brahman, where there is no grief; he himself will go too, since one who has done all he must needs no sacrifice or japa, and with his father's leave he will strive for freedom. The birds tell Jaimini that the wise son took his father's leave and left, giving up all possessions; the father too, in due course, became a forest hermit and then a renouncer, met his son, gave up the bonds of the qualities and gained the highest perfection. So the birds have answered all Jaimini asked.

045.json.summary: Jaimini thanks the birds for explaining the two kinds of Vedic action, worldly (pravritti) and turning away from the world (nivritti), and praises their knowledge, which by their father's grace has removed delusion even in animal birth; meeting such teachers is rare. He asks them to tell how the world of moving and unmoving beings arose and how it dissolves at the end, the lines of gods, sages, ancestors and beings, the periods of the Manus (manvantaras) and the deeds of the dynasties, how many creations and dissolutions there are, how the ages (kalpas) are divided, the shape and size of the earth, its oceans, mountains, rivers and forests, the worlds from earth to heaven and the underworlds, and the movements of the sun, moon, planets and stars. The birds say they will tell it as Markandeya told it to Kraushtuki, a calm Brahmin student. Bowing to Brahma, who creates, keeps the world as Vishnu and ends it as Rudra, Markandeya says: as soon as Brahma was born, this Purana and the Vedas came from his mouths; the great sages made many Purana collections and divided the Vedas in thousands of ways; dharma, knowledge, detachment and power are not gained without his teaching. The seven sages, his mind-born sons, took the Vedas, and the first sages took the Purana; Chyavana learned it from Bhrigu and told it to the twice-born, the sages told it to Daksha, and Daksha told it to Markandeya, who now tells it to Kraushtuki; it destroys the sins of the Kali age. Bowing to Brahma, Hiranyagarbha, he describes creation. Before creation there was Pradhana, the unmanifest, which the sages call subtle, eternal Prakriti, being and non-being, unchanging, unaging, without smell, form, taste, sound or touch, beginningless and endless, the womb of the world, where the three qualities arise and dissolve; after the dissolution it pervaded all. At the time of creation, from the qualities in balance, presided over by the knower of the field, the principle Mahat (the great, intellect) arose, covered by the unmanifest like a seed by its skin, of three kinds: sattvic, rajasic and tamasic. From Mahat came the threefold ego (ahankara): vaikarika, taijasa and bhutadi (tamasic). From bhutadi came the subtle element of sound, and from it space; from space the subtle element of touch and the wind; from wind the subtle element of form and fire (light); from fire the subtle element of taste and water; from water the subtle element of smell and earth; each covers the next. These subtle elements (tanmatras) are called unspecific (avishesha), being neither calm, fierce nor dull. From the sattvic vaikarika ego came at once the ten senses and their gods: the five organs of knowledge (ear, skin, eyes, tongue, nose) and five of action (feet, anus, genitals, hands, speech), with the mind as the eleventh. Space has one quality, sound; wind two, sound and touch; fire three, adding form; water four, adding taste; earth five, adding smell, so earth is the grossest; these gross elements are called specific (vishesha), being calm, fierce or dull. Separate, these seven could not create beings; joined together, presided over by the Person and with the help of the unmanifest, from Mahat down to the gross elements they formed an egg, which grew like a bubble on water. Inside this cosmic egg, floating on the waters, the knower of the field called Brahma grew, the first embodied being, the first creator, through whom the three worlds are pervaded; Mount Meru was its inner membrane, the mountains its outer membrane, and the oceans the fluid in the womb; the whole world with gods, asuras, men, islands, mountains, seas and stars is in the egg. The egg is covered on the outside by water, wind, fire, space and bhutadi, each ten times larger than the last, then by Mahat and the unmanifest; these seven coverings and the eight forms of Prakriti surround it. This Prakriti is eternal, and within it is the Person called Brahma; as a diver rises from the water and shakes the water off, so Brahma comes out of Prakriti. The unmanifest is the field and Brahma the knower of the field. This first creation, of Prakriti, presided over by the knower of the field, arose without deliberate thought, like a flash of lightning.

046.json.summary: Kraushtuki asks what exists when there is no creation, after everything is withdrawn at the end of a dissolution. Markandeya says that when the world dissolves into Prakriti, the wise call it the dissolution of Prakriti (prakrita pratisanchara): the unmanifest rests in itself, all its products withdrawn, and Prakriti and the Person (Purusha) remain alike; tamas and sattva are in balance, neither greater, woven into each other, with rajas in them like oil in sesame or ghee in milk. The day of the Supreme lasts as long as Brahma's life, two parardhas, and the night of dissolution is as long. At the dawn of that day, the Supreme, the beginningless cause of all, enters Prakriti and Purusha and stirs them by his yoga, as the intoxication of youth stirs young women or the spring breeze; when the unmanifest is stirred, the god called Brahma arises in the cosmic egg. He is both the stirrer and the stirred, the lord of Prakriti. Though beyond qualities, he takes on rajas and as Brahma creates; with sattva as Vishnu he protects by dharma; with tamas as Rudra he withdraws the world and sleeps; these three states of the Self-born are Brahma (rajas), Rudra (tamas) and Vishnu (sattva), three gods who are the three qualities, always paired and never apart. Brahma, the four-faced, Hiranyagarbha, was born on the lotus of the earth. His full life is a hundred years by his own measure: ten (or fifteen) blinks make a kashtha, thirty kashthas a kala, thirty kalas a muhurta, thirty muhurtas a human day and night, thirty days a month of two fortnights, six months a half-year, two half-years (south and north) a human year, which is a day and night of the gods (the northern course being their day). Twelve thousand divine years make the four ages (chaturyuga): the Krita age four thousand years with dawn and dusk of four hundred each, the Treta three thousand with three hundred, the Dvapara two thousand with two hundred, and the Kali one thousand with one hundred. A thousand of these make one day of Brahma, in which there are fourteen Manus; with each Manu the gods, seven sages, Indra, the Manu and his royal sons are created and withdrawn. A Manu's period (manvantara) is a little over seventy-one four-age cycles, which the text gives as 306,720,000 human years, or 852,000 divine years. Fourteen times this is Brahma's day, at whose end comes the occasional (naimittika) dissolution: the earth, middle region and heaven perish, Mahar-loka remains, but its people move to Jana-loka because of the heat, and Brahma sleeps on the single ocean through a night as long as his day, then creates again. A hundred such years is his life, called para, and fifty years a parardha. One parardha has passed, ending with the great kalpa called Padma; in the second parardha, now running, the first kalpa is called Varaha.

047.json.summary: Kraushtuki asks how Brahma created beings. Markandeya says that at the end of the Padma kalpa, waking from his night, Brahma, full of sattva, saw the world empty. A verse about Narayana is quoted: water is called nara, and since he lies on it he is Narayana. Waking on the waters and knowing the earth lay within them, he took, as at the start of earlier kalpas, forms like the Fish and Tortoise, and now the Boar form made of Vedas and sacrifice, entered the water, lifted the earth from the underworld and set it on the water, where it floats like a great boat, while the siddhas of Jana-loka meditated on him. He levelled the earth and made the mountains again, which had been shattered by the fire of dissolution and had sunk and stuck wherever the wind piled them; he divided the earth into seven continents and made the four worlds from earth upwards. As he thought of creation, there first arose without thought a creation of darkness: ignorance of five parts, tamas, moha, mahamoha, tamisra and andhatamisra; this was the primary creation (mukhya sarga) of immobile beings, the trees and plants (naga), dark within and without. Seeing it was not fit for his purpose, he meditated again and the creation of beings whose flow is horizontal (tiryak-srotas) arose: animals, full of tamas, ignorant, following wrong paths, thinking themselves wise, proud, of twenty-eight kinds, bright within but covered to each other. Not satisfied, he meditated again and the third, upward-flowing (urdhva-srotas) creation of sattva arose: the gods, full of joy, bright within and without; Brahma was pleased. Seeking a creation fit for his purpose, he then produced the downward-flowing (arvak-srotas) creation: human beings, bright, full of rajas with some tamas, full of sorrow, acting again and again, and able to achieve the goal. The fifth is the creation of favour (anugraha), in four forms: error, success, peace and contentment; the sixth is that of the elemental beings (bhutadi), who are grasping, fond of sharing and without good conduct. The full list of nine creations: the first, of Mahat; the second, of the subtle elements (bhuta sarga); the third, of the senses (vaikarika); these three are the creations of Prakriti; the fourth, primary, of immobile beings; the fifth, of animals; the sixth, of gods; the seventh, of humans; the eighth, the anugraha creation, sattvic and tamasic; these five are the derived (vaikrita) creations; and the ninth, the Kaumara creation, is both prakrita and vaikrita. These are the nine creations of Prajapati.

048.json.summary: Kraushtuki asks for the creation of gods and others in detail. Markandeya says that beings, shaped by past good and bad deeds and not freed at dissolution, were born from Brahma's mind in four kinds, from gods to plants. Wishing to create gods, asuras, ancestors and humans, he focused himself. When tamas rose in him, the asuras were born from his thighs; he dropped that body, and it became night. Taking another body, full of sattva, he was pleased, and the gods were born from his mouth; that body, cast off, became day. From another body of sattva, as he thought of himself as a father, the ancestors (pitris) were born; that body became twilight. From a body of rajas, humans were born; that body became the moonlight before dawn. So night, day, twilight and dawn-light are his four bodies, of the three qualities; therefore gods are strong by day, asuras by night, humans at dawn and ancestors at twilight, and weak at the opposite times. Then in darkness, in a body of rajas and tamas, hungry and thirsty, he created ugly, bearded, hungry beings who tried to eat that body; those who cried 'Let us protect (raksham)!' became rakshasas, and those who cried 'Let us eat (yaksham)!' became yakshas. Seeing them with displeasure, his hair fell from his head and became snakes (sarpa, from crawling; ahi, from being cut off); in anger he made the fierce, tawny flesh-eating bhutas; meditating on speech (go), he produced the gandharvas, so named because they were born drinking speech. After these eight kinds of divine beings, he created birds and animals: goats from his mouth, sheep from his chest, cows from his belly and sides, horses, elephants, asses, hares, deer, camels and mules from his feet, and from his body-hair the herbs, fruits and roots; then he performed a sacrifice with the animals and herbs at the start of the Treta age. The village animals are the cow, goat, man, sheep, horse, mule and ass; the wild are beasts of prey, two-hoofed animals, elephants, monkeys, birds, water animals and reptiles. From his eastern mouth came the Gayatri metre, Rig hymns, the trivrit stoma, the rathantara and the agnishtoma sacrifice; from the southern, the Yajus, trishtubh, the fifteenfold stoma, the brihat saman and the uktha; from the western, the Saman hymns, jagati, the seventeenfold stoma, the vairupa and atiratra; from the northern, the twenty-onefold stoma, the Atharva, the aptoryama, anushtubh and vairaja. He also created lightning, thunderbolts, clouds, rainbows and birds, and all kinds of beings from his limbs, yakshas, pishachas, gandharvas, apsaras, men, kinnaras, rakshasas, birds, beasts and snakes. Each being, created again and again, takes up the same deeds and nature as before, harmful or harmless, gentle or cruel, righteous or not, truthful or false. Brahma gave each its names, forms and duties from the words of the Veda, as the signs of each season return in turn; so these creations happen in every kalpa when Brahma wakes.

049.json.summary: Kraushtuki asks how the human creation and the classes (varnas), with their qualities and duties, came about. Markandeya says Brahma, thinking truly, created a thousand couples from his mouth, full of sattva and brilliance; a thousand from his chest, full of rajas, strong and impatient; a thousand from his thighs, of rajas and tamas, given to effort; and a thousand from his feet, full of tamas, without fortune and of little mind. These couples, delighting in each other, began to unite, and from then on in this kalpa beings are born in couples; but the women had no monthly periods then and did not conceive from union; only at the end of life did they give birth once, to a couple, born by thought. In that first age they lived by rivers, lakes, seas and mountains, with little cold or heat, naturally satisfied, without obstruction, hatred or envy, homeless, acting without desire and always happy; pishachas, snakes, rakshasas, the envious, animals, birds, crocodiles, fish and reptiles, born of adharma, did not yet exist, nor roots, fruits, flowers, seasons or years; the time was always pleasant. In time a wonderful perfection (siddhi) arose, giving them satisfaction without effort, then another, the subtlety of water, with many tastes, granting all wishes; their bodies needed no care and their youth was lasting; children were born to them as couples without intent; all had the same form and lifespan, about four thousand human years, without high or low. Gradually these perfections faded, and wish-fulfilling trees called 'houses' appeared, from which they got everything, at the beginning of the Treta. Then sudden passion arose, the monthly periods began and pregnancies came again and again; the house-trees' branches gave clothes and ornaments in their fruits and a honey without bees in every leaf-cup. Later, greed made them seize the trees as their own, and the trees vanished. Then the pairs of opposites, cold, heat and hunger, arose, and to protect themselves they made dwellings in deserts, hills and caves, used forts of trees, mountains and water, and built artificial forts, measuring by their own fingers. The units of measure are given: the atom (paramanu), the trasarenu, dust, hair-tip, nit, louse and barley grain, each eight times the last; eight barley grains make a finger-width (angula), six a pada, twice that a vitasti, two vitastis a hasta (cubit), four hastas a dhanus or danda, two thousand dhanus a gavyuti and four gavyutis a yojana. They built towns (pura) half a yojana wide, sloping north-east, with walls and moats, and smaller kheta, karvata, dronimukha, kharvata (without walls), branch towns for ministers and vassals, villages (grama) of mostly shudra farmers in the middle of fields, settlements made for a purpose, dramis (villages of strong, often troublesome people favoured by the king), and ghoshas (cowherd camps with carts and herds). In them they built houses modelled on the house-trees, with branches bending up and down, so that houses have 'shalas' like the trees' branches (shakha). When the wish-trees and their honey were all gone, the people, hungry and thirsty, despaired; then at the start of the Treta another perfection appeared: rain fell as they wished, the water running downhill made rivers, and where it met the earth, fourteen kinds of plants, village and wild, grew without ploughing or sowing, and trees and shrubs bore flowers and fruit in season; on these the people lived. But passion and greed arose again, they seized rivers, fields, mountains, trees and herbs for themselves by force, and through this fault the earth swallowed the plants before their eyes. The starving people went to Brahma, who, knowing the earth had swallowed them, made Mount Meru the calf and milked the earth as a cow; from that milk came seeds of crops: seventeen kinds of village grains (rice, barley, wheat, millets, sesame, priyangu, kodo, china, masha, mung, masura, nishpava, kulattha, adhaka, chickpea and others) and fourteen kinds of sacrificial plants, village and wild. When the plants, once grown, did not grow again, Brahma created agriculture, work done by hand, and since then crops are ploughed and ripen. With livelihood established, Brahma set limits and duties for the classes and stages of life, and fixed the worlds they reach: Prajapati's world for Brahmins who perform the rites, Indra's world for kshatriyas who do not flee from battle, the world of the Maruts for vaishyas who keep their duty, and the world of the gandharvas for shudras who do service; the world of the 88,000 celibate sages for students who live with their teacher, the world of the seven sages for forest hermits, Prajapati's world for householders, Brahma's abode for renouncers and immortality for yogis.

050.json.summary: Markandeya continues. As Brahma meditated, mind-born beings arose with their causes and effects, and souls arose from his limbs, all the beings of the three qualities from gods to plants. When these did not multiply, he created mind-born sons like himself: Bhrigu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Angiras, Marichi, Daksha, Atri and Vasishtha, the nine Brahmas of the Puranas; then Rudra, born of his anger, Sankalpa and Dharma. The earlier-born Sanandana and the others, free of desire and envy and knowing the future, would not take part in creating the world; at this Brahma grew very angry, and from his anger arose a being bright as the sun, half man and half woman, who was told 'Divide yourself' and vanished; he separated the female and male, divided the male into eleven and the female into many forms, gentle and fierce, dark and fair. Brahma then made Svayambhuva Manu, born of himself, to protect the people, and Manu took as wife Shatarupa, purified by penance; they had two sons, Priyavrata and Uttanapada, famed for their deeds, and two daughters, Prasuti, given to Daksha, and Akuti, given to Ruchi (the text names her Riddhi); Ruchi and she had a son Yajna and a daughter Dakshina, and from Yajna and Dakshina were born twelve sons, the Yama gods of the Svayambhuva period. Daksha had by Prasuti twenty-four daughters: thirteen, Shraddha, Lakshmi, Dhriti, Tushti, Pushti, Medha, Kriya, Buddhi, Lajja, Vapu, Shanti, Siddhi and Kirti, became wives of Dharma; the other eleven, Khyati, Sati, Sambhuti, Smriti, Priti, Kshama, Santati, Anasuya, Urja, Svaha and Svadha, married Bhrigu, Bhava (Shiva), Marichi, Angiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Vasishtha, Atri, Agni and the Pitris. Dharma's sons were Kama from Shraddha, Darpa from Lakshmi, Niyama from Dhriti, Santosha from Tushti, Lobha from Pushti, Shruta from Medha, Danda, Naya and Vinaya from Kriya, Bodha from Buddhi, Vinaya from Lajja, Vyavasaya from Vapu, Kshema from Shanti, Sukha from Siddhi and Yashas from Kirti; Kama had Harsha. Adharma's wife was Himsa, who bore Anrita (falsehood) and Nikriti; from them came Naraka (hell) and Bhaya (fear), Maya and Vedana (pain); Maya bore Mrityu (death), and Vedana bore Duhkha (sorrow); from Death came disease, old age, grief, craving and anger, all born of sorrow and marks of adharma, without wives or children. Death's other wife Alakshmi (misfortune) bore fourteen sons who carry out Death's orders, living in the ten senses and mind, leading men and women to their objects and to ruin through passion and anger; one lives in ego, another in the intellect. Another, Duhsaha, lives in people's houses: hungry, head-down, naked, in rags, with a crow's voice, a mass of darkness created by Brahma to eat everything. When he wanted to eat the world, Brahma stopped him and, asked where he could live and be fed, gave him as dwelling the houses of men, unrighteous people as his strength, and neglect of the daily rites as his nourishment. Brahma gave him as food: things spoiled, with insects, seen by dogs, from broken vessels, cooled by blowing, leftovers, half-cooked, licked, unconsecrated, eaten on broken seats, eaten facing intermediate directions or at the twilights amid dancing and music, touched or seen by a menstruating woman; offerings and gifts made without faith, by the unbathed, with contempt, without water, with display or in anger; rites by remarried people; the fruit of false scriptures, study without truth, rites of those who have fallen from their duty, and of false ascetics; and an offering called by his name at the end of the Vaishvadeva rite. He will have power over people at times of sex with a pregnant woman, missed twilight rites, household quarrels, unfed servants and animals, houses not sprinkled at twilight, planetary troubles and omens without rites of peace, and over idle fasters, gamblers, womanisers and hypocrites. Brahma told him to avoid houses where people eat purified food and are clean within and without, free of greed and lust; where gods and ancestors are worshipped and female relatives and guests honoured; where there is friendship among children, old people, women and men; where women stay modestly at home; where beds and food suit age and kinship; where people are kind and do good; where elders are not left standing; where trees do not pierce the door; where people live on what remains after feeding gods, ancestors, servants and guests; truthful, patient, non-violent people; women devoted to their husbands; Brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras keeping their own duties; where the son honours teacher, gods and father and the wife her husband; and houses plastered, sprinkled and given flower offerings at twilight, beds touched by sunlight, fire and water kept, with a bull, sandal, vina, mirror, honey, ghee and copper vessels. His homes are where there are thorny trees, nishpava creepers, a remarried wife and anthills; five men, three women and three cows with darkness, firewood and fire; one goat, two asses, three cows, five buffaloes, six horses or seven elephants; tools and vessels thrown about; women sitting on pestle and mortar or the doorstep; talk on rubbish heaps; grain and scriptures stepped over; fire put on pot lids or with a ladle; human bones kept in the house; and among those who eat without giving rice balls and water to kin. He should avoid houses where Padma, Mahapadma, Surabhi, the bull and Airavata are pictured, where unarmed gods (or armed ones only for battle) are worshipped, and where traditional festivals are kept; he may go to those who bathe with winnowing-fan wind, pot water or drops from clothes or nails, but must not touch those who keep local customs, family dharma, japa, fire offering, auspicious rites, worship of the gods, purity and good conduct. Having said this, Brahma vanished, and Duhsaha obeyed.

051.json.summary: Markandeya describes the family of Duhsaha, which fills the world, and how to ward each one off. Duhsaha's wife was Nirmashti, born to the wife of Kali when she saw a chandala during her season. They had sixteen children, eight sons and eight fearful daughters. The sons: Dantakrishti, who sits in the teeth of sleeping children and makes them grind them, to be warded off with white mustard on the bed, bathing with suvarchala herb, reciting good scriptures and wearing camel thorn, rhinoceros bone or linen; Tathokti, who keeps saying 'So be it' and makes people's good and bad words come true, so the wise should speak only auspicious words and, on hearing bad words, name Janardana, Brahma or the family deity; Parivarta, who swaps embryos between wombs and changes a speaker's words, warded off with white mustard and demon-killing mantras; Angadhruk, who foretells good and bad through twitching limbs, countered by striking the limb with kusha; Shakuni, who speaks omens through crows and other birds or dogs, so one should drop a task after a bad omen and hurry on a good one; Gandantarati, who for half a muhurta at the junction (ganda) of stars eats up all undertakings, countered by Brahmins' blessings, praise of the gods, bathing in cow urine and mustard and worship of the star and planets; Garbhaha, who destroys the fruit of women's wombs, warded off by constant cleanliness, written mantras, garlands and a clean home; and Sasyaha, who destroys crops, warded off by wearing old shoes, walking with the right side away, letting a chandala in, offerings outside and naming Soma and water. The daughters: Niyojika, who pushes people to other men's wives and wealth, warded off by holy reading and giving up anger and greed and by thinking 'she is driving me'; Virodhini, who makes quarrels between loving couples, relatives, friends, parents and sons, warded off by offerings, patience and good conduct; Svayamharika, who invisibly steals grain from the threshing floor, milk and ghee from cows, food from the kitchen, leftovers, milk from cows and women, butter from curd, oil from sesame, liquor, dye and thread, warded off by a pair of peacocks, a doll, protective drawings, avoiding impurity and purifying vessels with ash from the sacred fire; Bhramani, who makes a man restless in one place, warded off by white mustard on his seat and bed and by reciting the Bhu Sukta; Rituharika, who stops women's periods, to be cured by bathing at holy places, temples, shrines, mountains and river meetings, by mantras and good medicines; Smritihara, who steals women's memory, cured by staying in secluded places; Bijahara, who steals the seed of men and women, cured by pure food and bathing; and Dveshini, who makes a person hated, cured by fire offerings of sesame with honey, milk and ghee and the Mitravinda rite. These sixteen had thirty-eight children: Dantakrishti's daughters Vijalpa and Kalaha (who causes household quarrels, warded off by offerings of durva grass with honey, ghee and milk and a prayer that the Kushmandas, yatudhanas and other spirit hosts be pleased by Shiva's grace and grant peace in weddings, rites, work, travel and health); Tathokti's son Kalajihva; Parivarta's sons Virupa and Vikrita, who live on treetops, moats, walls and seas and move embryos, so a pregnant woman should not climb trees or hills or cross walls, seas or moats; Angadhruk's son Pishuna, who eats the strength in bones and marrow; Shakuni's five sons, the hawk, crow, pigeon, vulture and owl, taken by Death, Time, Nirriti, Disease and Yama, so a house where they nest or perch on one's head should be left or purified, and even seeing a pigeon in a dream is bad; Gandantarati's six children who live in women's periods on the first four days, the thirteenth, the eleventh, and on shraddha and festival days, which are to be avoided; Garbhaha's son Nighna and daughter Mohini, who eat or confuse the embryo, so that snakes, frogs or tortoises are born, entering a careless pregnant woman who eats meat, sits under trees or at crossroads, cremation grounds or without her upper cloth at night, or weeps at midnight; Sasyaha's son Kshudraka, who destroys crops sown on a bad day by a discontented man, so sowing should be done on a good day after worshipping the moon; Niyojika's four daughters, the Prachodikas, who possess people and show adharma as dharma, loss as gain and bondage as freedom;
