Virodhini's three sons Chodaka (gossip), Grahaka (who catches slander in the ear) and Tamahprachchhadaka (who brings anger); Svayamharika's three sons, who take everything, half, or strength from impure houses; Bhramani's son Kakajangha, who enters those who sing while eating or unite at twilight; Rituharika's three daughters, who take a girl's breasts if her marriage rites are not done properly or on time, the bride's signs if shraddha and mother-worship are skipped, and newborn babies from birth rooms without fire, water, incense, lamps, weapons, pestle, ash and mustard; Smritihara's son Prachanda, whose countless lika descendants and eight fierce chandala-born beings were kept from eating each other by his rule that no lika may live among them; Bijahara's daughters Vatarupa and Arupa, who make men and women barren; and Dveshini's two sons, who spread a man's faults and destroy his friendships. These are all the sinful descendants of Duhsaha, who fill the whole world.

052.json.summary: Markandeya says that was Brahma's dark creation, and now tells the creation of Rudra. At the start of the kalpa, as Brahma meditated on a son like himself, a blue-red boy appeared in his lap, crying loudly and running; asked why he cried, he said 'Give me a name'; Brahma named him Rudra ('the crier') and told him not to cry; he cried seven more times, and Brahma gave him seven more names, Bhava, Sharva, Ishana, Pashupati, Bhima, Ugra and Mahadeva, with eight forms (the sun, water, earth, fire, wind, space, the initiated Brahmin and the moon), eight wives (Suvarchala, Uma, Vikeshi, Svadha, Svaha, the Directions, Diksha and Rohini) and eight sons (Shanaishchara, Shukra, Lohitanga, Manojava, Skanda, Sarga, Santana and Budha). This Rudra married Sati, who gave up her body because of Daksha's anger; she was born again as the daughter of Himavat and Mena, sister of Mainaka, the friend of the ocean, and Bhava married her again. Bhrigu's wife Khyati bore the gods Dhatri and Vidhatri and Shri, wife of Narayana; Dhatri and Vidhatri married Ayati and Niyati, daughters of Meru, and had sons Prana and Mrikandu; Mrikandu was Markandeya's own father, and by Manasvini he had Markandeya, whose son by Dhumravati was Vedashiras; Prana's son was Dyutiman, and they had many deathless descendants. Marichi's wife Sambhuti bore Paurnamasa, father of Virajas and Parvata. Angiras's wife Smriti bore the daughters Sinivali, Kuhu, Raka and Bhanumati. Atri's wife Anasuya bore Soma, Durvasas and the yogi Dattatreya. Pulastya's wife Priti bore Datta (Dattoli), who was Agastya in an earlier birth in the Svayambhuva period. Pulaha's wife Kshama bore Kardama, Arvavira and Sahishnu. Kratu's wife Sannati bore the Valakhilyas, sixty thousand celibate sages. Vasishtha's wife Urja bore seven sons, Rajas, Gatra, Urdhvabahu, Savala, Anagha, Sutapas and Shukra, the seven sages. Agni Abhimani, Brahma's eldest son, had by Svaha three mighty sons, Pavaka, Pavamana and Shuchi, who drinks water, and their forty-five descendants, forty-nine fires in all. The ancestors created by Brahma, the Agnishvattas, Barhishads and those with and without fire, had by Svadha two daughters, Mena and Dharini, both expounders of Brahman, yoginis, full of knowledge and virtue. Whoever remembers with faith these descendants of Daksha's daughters is blessed with children.

053.json.summary: Kraushtuki asks about the Svayambhuva Manu period in full: its length, gods, sages, kings and Indra. Markandeya says a Manu's period is a little over seventy-one four-age cycles, which the text gives in human years as 306,720,000 and in divine years as 852,000. The past Manus are Svayambhuva, Svarochisha, Auttama, Tamasa, Raivata and Chakshusha; Vaivasvata rules now; to come are Savarni (five Savarnis), Raucya and Bhautya. Svayambhuva Manu had ten sons like himself, by whom the earth with seven continents, mountains, seas and mines was settled in the Treta age. Priyavrata had by Prajavati, daughter of Kardama, two daughters, Samrat and Kukshi, and ten sons, of whom seven, Agnidhra, Medhatithi, Vapushman, Jyotishman, Dyutiman, Bhavya and Savana, he crowned as kings of the seven continents: Agnidhra of Jambudvipa, Medhatithi of Plaksha, Vapushman of Shalmali, Jyotishman of Kusha, Dyutiman of Krauncha, Bhavya of Shaka and Savana of Pushkara. Savana's sons Mahavita and Dhataki divided Pushkara between them; the seven sons of Bhavya (Jalada, Kumara, Sukumara, Manivaka, Kushottara, Medhavi and Mahadruma), of Dyutiman (Kushala, Manuga, Ushna, Prakara, Arthakaraka, Muni and Dundubhi), of Jyotishman (whose regions are Udbhida, Vaishnava, Suratha, Lambana, Dhritiman, Prakara and Kapila), of Vapushman (Shveta, Harita, Jimuta, Rohita, Vaidyuta, Manasa and Ketuman) and of Medhatithi (whose regions in Plaksha are Shakabhava, Shishira, Sukhodaya, Ananda, Shiva, Kshemaka and Dhruva) gave their names to the regions (varshas) of their continents. In these five continents from Plaksha to Shaka there is the dharma of classes and stages of life, natural and constant, increased by non-violence. Agnidhra, king of Jambudvipa, had nine sons, Nabhi, Kimpurusha, Harivarsha, Ilavrita, Ramya, Hiranya, Kuru, Bhadrashva and Ketumala, after whom its regions are named; in all except Nabhi's southern land of Hima, people are happy without effort, without old age, death or fear, without dharma and adharma, high or low, without the four ages or seasons. Nabhi's son was Rishabha, and Rishabha's son was the hero Bharata, best of a hundred sons; Rishabha crowned him and went to do penance at Pulaha's hermitage, and the southern land of Hima given to Bharata is called Bharata-varsha after him. Bharata's son was the righteous Sumati, to whom Bharata gave the kingdom before going to the forest. So the descendants of Priyavrata enjoyed the seven continents in the Svayambhuva period.

054.json.summary: Kraushtuki asks about the continents, oceans, mountains, regions and rivers, the size of the elements and of Lokaloka, and the movements of the moon and sun. Markandeya says the whole earth is fifty crore yojanas wide. Its seven continents, Jambu, Plaksha, Shalmali, Kusha, Krauncha, Shaka and Pushkara, each twice the size of the one before, are surrounded in turn by oceans of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, ghee, curd, milk and fresh water, each twice the one before. Jambudvipa is a hundred thousand yojanas across. It has seven boundary mountain ranges: Himavan, Hemakuta, Rishabha (Nishadha), Meru, Nila, Shveta and Shringi; the two in the middle are a hundred thousand yojanas long, and those to the south and north are each ten thousand less; all are two thousand yojanas high and as wide, and six of them run into the sea. The land is low to the south and north and high in the middle, with three regions south and three north and Ilavrita in the middle like a half-moon; Bhadrashva lies east and Ketumala west. In the middle of Ilavrita stands Meru, the golden mountain, 84,000 yojanas high, sixteen thousand deep in the earth, sixteen thousand wide at the base and thirty-two thousand at the top, shaped like a bowl; its sides are white, yellow, black and red on the east, south, west and north, like the Brahmin, vaishya, shudra and kshatriya classes. On top are the eight cities of Indra and the other world guardians in their directions, with Brahma's hall in the middle, fourteen thousand yojanas high. Below it are four support mountains, ten thousand yojanas high, Mandara, Gandhamadana, Vipula and Suparshva, each marked by a great tree: a kadamba, a jambu (rose-apple), an ashvattha and a banyan, eleven hundred yojanas tall. Eight boundary mountains stand around: Jathara and Devakuta in the east, Nishadha and Pariyatra in the west, Kailasa and Himavan in the south, and Shringavan and Jarudhi in the north, running into the ocean. The distance between the ranges is nine thousand yojanas. The fruits of the jambu tree on Gandhamadana, as big as elephants, fall on the peak, and their juice forms the Jambu river, where the gold called jambunada is produced; it circles Meru and returns to the tree's root, and the people there drink it. Vishnu is worshipped as Hayashiras (horse-headed) in Bhadrashva, as the Tortoise in Bharata, as the Boar in Ketumala and as the Fish in the north; in all four the lands are arranged by the stars, and readers of planetary influences live there.

055.json.summary: Markandeya describes the forests and lakes on the four support mountains around Meru: the forest Chaitraratha on the eastern one, Nandana on the southern, Vaibhraja on the western and Savitra on the northern; and the lakes Arunoda in the east, Manasa in the south, Shitoda in the west and Mahabhadra in the north. He lists the great mountains on each side of Meru: to the east Shitarta, Chakramunja, Kulira, Sukankavan, Manishaila, Vrishavan, Mahanila, Bhavachala, Subindu, Mandara, Venu, Tamasa, Nishadha and Devashaila; to the south Trikuta, Shikharadri, Kalinga, Patangaka, Ruchaka, Sanuman, Tamraka, Vishakhavan, Shvetodara, Samula, Vasudhara, Ratnavan, Ekashringa, Rajashala, Pipathaka, Panchashaila, Kailasa and Himavan; to the west Suraksha, Shishiraksha, Vaidurya, Kapila, Pinjara, Mahabhadra, Surasa, Pingala, Madhu, Anjana, Kukkuta, Krishna, Pandara, Sahasrashikhara, Pariyatra and Shringavan; to the north Shankhakuta, Vrishabha, Hamsanabha, Kapilendra, Sanuman, Nila, Svarnashringi, Shatashringi, Pushpaka, Meghaparvata, Virajaksha, Varahadri, Mayura and Jarudhi. The lovely valleys of these mountains, with forests, clear water and lakes, are where people of great merit are born; they are earthly heavens, even better than heaven, where no new merit or sin is earned, only past merit enjoyed, even by gods. On these mountains are the fine homes of vidyadharas, yakshas, kinnaras, nagas, rakshasas, gods and gandharvas, with gardens, lakes and pleasant winds in every season, and no one there is ever unhappy. So the earth is a four-petalled lotus, with Bhadrashva, Bharata and the other lands as its petals. Bharata, the land to the south, is the land of action (karma-bhumi): only there are merit and sin earned; it is the chief land on which all rests, and from there a person goes to heaven or freedom, human birth or hell, or animal birth.

056.json.summary: Markandeya tells of the descent of the Ganga. From the foot of Narayana flows the goddess Ganga, who goes by three paths; she enters the moon, the source of nectar and support of the waters, and, purified by contact with the sun's rays, falls on top of Meru and divides into four, falling without support from Meru's peaks onto the four support mountains. The eastern stream, called Sita, floods the Chaitraratha forest and Arunoda lake, then flows over Shitanta and other mountains through Bhadrashva to the sea. The southern stream, Alakananda, goes to Gandhamadana, the Nandana forest and Manasa lake, then over the southern mountains to the Himalaya, where Shiva held her and did not let her go until Bhagiratha pleased him with fasts and praise; released, she entered the southern ocean in seven streams, three flowing east and one following Bhagiratha's chariot south. The western stream, Suchakshu, goes to Vipula, the Vaibhraja forest and Shitoda lake, then over Suchakshu and Trishikha mountains and through Ketumala into the salt ocean. The northern stream, Soma (Bhadrasoma), goes to Suparshva, the Savitra forest and Mahabhadra lake, then over Shankhakuta, Vrishabha and other mountains and through Uttara Kuru to the ocean. In Kimpurusha and the other lands the people are happy, free from fear and from high or low; each of the nine lands has seven chief mountains and rivers flowing from them. In the eight lands other than Bharata, water springs from the ground, while in Bharata it comes from the clouds; in those eight lands perfection (siddhi) comes in six ways: from wish-giving trees, by nature, from the place, from the subtlety of water, from the mind through meditation, and from dharma through worship; there are no ages, no mental or bodily illness, and no new merit or sin is begun.

057.json.summary: Kraushtuki notes that only in Bharata does action bring merit or sin and lead to heaven and freedom, and asks for a full description of it. Markandeya says Bharata has nine parts separated by the sea and not reachable from one another: Indradvipa, Kasherumat, Tamravarna, Gabhastiman, Nagadvipa, Saumya, Gandharva, Varuna and this ninth, surrounded by the sea, a thousand yojanas from south to north. At its eastern end live the Kiratas and at its western end the Yavanas; in the middle live Brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras, purified by sacrifice, study, trade and their other work, by which they gain heaven or freedom, merit or sin. Its seven chief mountain ranges are Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Shuktiman, Riksha, Vindhya and Pariyatra, with thousands of smaller hills such as Kolahala, Vaibhraja, Mandara, Dardura, Mainaka, Raivata, Arbuda, Rishyamuka, Gomanta, Shriparvata and Chakora; among them live peoples, both mlechchhas and Aryas. The great rivers are listed by their mountain of origin: from the Himalaya the Ganga, Sarasvati, Sindhu, Chandrabhaga, Yamuna, Shatadru, Vitasta, Iravati, Gomati, Dhutapapa, Bahuda, Drishadvati, Vipasha, Gandaki, Kaushiki and others; from Pariyatra the Vedasmriti, Vetravati, Charmanvati, Shipra, Avanti and others; from Riksha the Shona, Narmada, Mandakini, Dasharna, Chitrakuta, Tamasa and others; from the Vindhya the Tapi, Payoshni, Nirvindhya, Vaitarani and others; from Sahya the Godavari, Bhimarathi, Krishna, Venya, Tungabhadra, Kaveri and others; from Malaya the Kritamala and Tamraparni; from Mahendra the Rishikulya and others; and from Shuktiman the Kumari and others; all are holy, flow to the sea, are mothers of the world and destroy sin, and there are thousands of lesser ones. He then lists the peoples by region: the Middle Country (Matsyas, Kurus, Kuntalas, Kashi, Koshala and others); the beautiful region north of the Sahya on the Godavari, with Bhargava's town Govardhana; the northern peoples (Bahlikas, Abhiras, Gandharas, Sindhu-Sauviras, Madras, Kaikeyas, Kambojas, Daradas, Chinas, Tusharas, Kashmiris and many more); the eastern peoples (Pragjyotishas, Videhas, Tamraliptas, Mallas, Magadhas and others); the southern peoples (Pundras, Maharashtras, Kalingas, Abhiras, Shabaras, Pulindas, Vidarbhas, Dandakas, Ashmakas, Kuntalas, Andhras and others); the western peoples (Shurparakas, Bharukachchhas, Kashmiris, Surashtras, Avantis, Arbudas and others); those living on the Vindhya (Karushas, Keralas, Utkalas, Dasharnas, Koshalas, Vaidishas, Nishadhas and others); and mountain peoples (Niharas, Hamsamargas, Kurus, Khasas, Trigartas, Kiratas and others). Only here is the order of the four ages kept. Bharata is shaped like a bow, with the sea to the south, west and east and the Himalaya to the north like its string. It is the seed of all: from here, by good and bad deeds, one reaches the state of Brahma, Indra, the gods and Maruts, or birth as animals, apsaras, reptiles or plants; it is the only land of action, and even the gods wish to fall from heaven and be born as humans here, since a human can do what gods and asuras cannot.

058.json.summary: Kraushtuki asks how Vishnu is placed in Bharata in the form of the Tortoise (Kurma), and how good and bad fortune for people is shown through him. Markandeya says the Tortoise lies facing east over the nine parts of Bharata, and the lunar mansions (nakshatras) and lands are spread over his body in nine groups. In the middle (the water) are the Sarasvatas, Matsyas, Shurasenas, Mathura, Dharmaranya, Pariyatra, Kurus, Udumbaras, Videhas, Panchalas and others, under Krittika, Rohini and Mrigashira. At his mouth are Vrishadhvaja, Anjana, the Magadhas, Mithila, Pragjyotisha, Lauhitya, Udayagiri, Tamralipta, Koshala and others, under Ardra, Punarvasu and Pushya. At the south-east foot are Kalinga, Vanga, Koshala, Chedi, Vidarbha, Kishkindha, Nishadha, Dasharna, the Shabaras and others, under Ashlesha, Magha and Purva Phalguni. At the southern side are Lanka, Mahendra, Malaya, Bhrigukachchha, Konkana, the Abhiras, Avanti, Maharashtra, Karnata, Chitrakuta, Chola, Kaveri, Rishyamuka, Nasikya, Simhala, Kanchi, Telinga, Tamraparni and others, under Uttara Phalguni, Hasta and Chitra. At the south-west foot are the Kambojas, Pahlavas, Sindhu-Sauviras, Anarta, Kiratas, Paradas, Pandyas, Saurashtra, Daradas, Dravidas and others, under Svati, Vishakha and Anuradha. At the tail are the Haihayas, Konkanas, Panchanada and others, under Jyeshtha, Mula and Purva Ashadha. On the left (north-west) side are the Mandavyas and others, under Uttara Ashadha, Shravana and Dhanishtha. At the northern side are Kailasa, Himavan, the Kaikeyas, Yamunas, Trigartas, Takshashila, Ambala, Malavas, Madras, Hunas, Gandharas, Yaudheyas and others, under Shatabhisha and the two Bhadrapadas. At the north-east foot are the Kinnara kingdom, Kashmir, Abhisara, Daradas, Khasas, Yavanas, Pauravas, Gandharvas and others, under Revati, Ashvini and Bharani. When these stars are afflicted, these lands suffer, and they prosper when the planets are well placed; danger comes to a land from the planet that rules its star. Good and bad come to people from their land, region, king, own stars and planets; the virtuous suffer only through their wealth, cattle, servants, friends, children or wife, those of little merit in themselves, the very sinful everywhere, and the sinless never. So the wise should know their land's star and their own planetary troubles and perform rites of peace and the 'lokavadas' (customs that fall to earth from the troubles of gods and demons, which should not be neglected), together with non-violence, fasting, bowing at shrines, japa, fire offerings, gifts, bathing, avoiding anger, friendliness to all, avoiding false and harsh speech, and worship of the planets; then all troubles from planets and stars are calmed. All the gods stand in the Tortoise, each with its star, with Agni, the earth and the moon in the middle; the twelve zodiac signs are also spread over his body (Aries to Gemini in the middle and mouth, Cancer and Leo at the south-east foot, and so on around to Pisces and Aries at the north-east foot). So from troubles of planets and stars one can tell troubles of lands, and should bathe and give gifts and offerings. This is Vishnu's foot, with Brahma in the middle, Narayana the inconceivable cause of the world.

059.json.summary: Markandeya says that in Bharata there are the four ages, Krita, Treta, Dvapara and Kali, and the four classes, and people live four hundred, three hundred, two hundred and one hundred years in the four ages in turn. East of the great mountain Devakuta lies Bhadrashva, with five chief mountains, Shvetaparna, Nila, Shaivala, Kauranja and Parnashalagra, many small hills, thousands of lands, and wide cool rivers such as Sita, Shankhavati, Bhadra and Chakravarta; its people shine like conch and pure gold, are holy, live a thousand years, are all equal, and have by nature eight virtues such as patience; there Vishnu is worshipped as Hayashiras, four-armed, with three eyes. West lies Ketumala, with seven chief mountains, Vishala, Kambala, Krishna, Jayanta, Hariparvata, Vishoka and Vardhamana, and thousands of hills where many peoples live, some huge and some only a finger tall, who drink from great rivers such as Vankshu, Shyama, Kambala, Amogha and Kamini; their lifespan is the same, and Hari is there in the form of the Boar, with the stars arranged on his body. North lies Uttara Kuru, where trees always bear sweet fruit and flowers and give clothes and ornaments in their fruits and grant all wishes; the ground is made of gems and the wind always fragrant; people born there have fallen from the world of the gods, are born in couples at the same time and love each other like chakravaka birds, and live fourteen and a half thousand years; its two chief mountains are Chandrakanta and Suryakanta, with the holy river Bhadrasoma in the middle, thousands of other rivers, some flowing with milk and ghee, lakes of curd and fruits tasting like nectar; there Vishnu is worshipped as the Fish, facing east, divided into nine with three stars to each part; in its sea are the islands Chandradvipa and Bhadradvipa. He will next describe Kimpurusha and the other lands.

060.json.summary: Markandeya describes the remaining lands of Jambudvipa. In Kimpurusha people live ten thousand years, free of illness and sorrow; there is a great grove of plaksha trees like the Nandana garden, and the men drink its fruit juice and keep their youth, while the women smell of lotuses. In Harivarsha people are born shining like silver, fallen from the world of the gods and godlike in form; they drink the juice of sugarcane, never grow old, and live as long, free of disease. In Ilavrita, the middle land of Meru, the sun does not burn and people do not age; the rays of the sun, moon, stars and planets do not shine there, outshone by Meru's own light; people are born bright and fragrant as lotuses, with lotus-petal eyes, eat the juice of jambu fruit and live thirteen thousand years; the land is shaped like a bowl around Meru. In Ramyaka there is a tall green-leaved banyan tree, and people live ten thousand years on the juice of its fruit, devoted to pleasure, pure, free of old age and bad smell. North of it is Hiranmaya, with the river Hiranvati shining with lotuses, where people are born very strong, brilliant, huge, courageous, rich and handsome.

061.json.summary: Kraushtuki, having heard about the earth, oceans, planets, stars, worlds and underworlds and the Svayambhuva period, asks about the other Manu periods, their gods, sages and kings. Markandeya begins the Svarochisha period. In the city of Arunaspada on the bank of the Varuna river lived a Brahmin more handsome than the Ashvins, gentle, of good conduct, learned in the Vedas, who loved guests and sheltered those who came at night; he longed to see the beautiful lands of the earth. One day a guest came who knew the power of herbs and mantras; when asked, he described lands, cities, forests, rivers, mountains and holy places, and said that by the power of mantras and herbs he could travel a thousand yojanas in half a day. The Brahmin begged for this power, and the guest gave him an ointment for his feet and charmed the direction he named. With it the Brahmin went to see the Himalaya, thinking he would go a thousand yojanas in half a day and return in the other half. He reached the mountain without tiring and walked about, but the melting snow washed the ointment off his feet. Now slow, he wandered, delighted, among the lovely slopes where siddhas, gandharvas, kinnaras and apsaras played, with waterfalls, dancing peacocks, cuckoos and fragrant breezes, and could not have enough of it. Deciding to return home and come again the next day, he found he could not move fast, and worried: his ointment was gone, the mountain was hard to cross and he was far from home; he would miss his fire rites and daily duties; he hoped to meet some ascetic who would show him the way. The beautiful apsara Varuthini, daughter of Mauli, saw him and fell in love at once, thinking she had never seen anyone so handsome among gods, demons, siddhas, gandharvas or nagas, and that she would be the most fortunate woman in the three worlds if he loved her. She showed herself; he greeted her politely, told her who he was and how he had lost his ointment, and asked who she was. She said she was Varuthini, who always wandered on this mountain, overcome with love for him at first sight, and at his command. He asked only for a way to get home before sunset, since a Brahmin's daily and occasional rites suffer when he is away, and travel is not praised for Brahmins. She begged him not to speak of leaving her: this place was better than heaven; he could enjoy garlands, clothes, ornaments, food, music of kinnaras and pleasures and never grow old there; and she embraced him. He told her not to touch him and to go to someone like herself: the offerings made morning and evening give eternal worlds, and the three worlds rest on offerings. She asked whether she was not dear to him; she would die without him; she asked him to stay a short while and enjoy rare pleasures, and said that saving her life would earn him merit and pleasures in another birth, while refusing her would bring her death and sin to him. He said his teachers had told him never to desire another man's wife, so he would not desire her, whether she wept or wasted away. Then, after touching water and purifying himself, he bowed and prayed quietly to his household fire (garhapatya): 'You are the source of all rites, from you come the other fires; fed by you, the gods give rain and crops on which the world lives; by the truth that the world arises from you, by the truth that I have never neglected my Vedic duties at their times, and that my mind has never desired another's wealth or wife, may I see my home today while the sun is still up.' (The speaker labels in verses 66 to 67 of this text seem confused, and one verse number is missing.)

062.json.summary: As the Brahmin spoke, his household fire (garhapatya) entered his body, and he shone in a ring of light, lighting up the place like the fire god in person; seeing him so, the divine woman Varuthini loved him even more. Filled with the fire's power, he set off as fast as before, while she watched him go, sighing, and in a moment he was home and performed all his rites. Varuthini, her heart fixed on him, spent the rest of the day and night sighing and weeping, blaming her own bad luck; she took no pleasure in play, food, forests or caves, envied a pair of chakravaka birds, and cursed her youth, saying the fire of love would surely consume her if he did not come back. A gandharva named Kali, who had once loved her and been rejected, saw her state and wondered why she was so sad, whether she had been cursed or insulted; by meditation he learned the truth and thought that his old good fortune had now made her within his reach: she loved a man, so if he took that man's form she would surely enjoy his company. So by his own power he took the Brahmin's form and went to where she sat. Seeing him, she came to him with joy and begged him to be kind: if he left her she would die, and he would suffer great sin and loss of his rites; by saving her he would surely gain merit; she must have some life left, since he had come back. Kali, as the Brahmin, said that his rites would suffer if he stayed, but he would unite with her only on one condition: that she keep her eyes closed during their union in the forest and not look at him. She agreed to do whatever he wished.

063.json.summary: Kali, in the Brahmin's form, enjoyed himself with Varuthini on the mountain slopes, in flowering forests, by lakes, in caves and on river banks; and during their union she, with her eyes closed, kept thinking of the Brahmin's form as it had shone when filled with the fire. In time she conceived a child from the gandharva's seed and her thought of the Brahmin's form; Kali comforted her and left, still in the Brahmin's form, with her loving consent. The child was born bright as fire, lighting all directions with his own rays like the sun, so he was called Svarochis ('shining by his own light'). He grew in qualities as the moon grows in digits, and learned the science of arms, the Vedas and other knowledge. As a young man, walking on Mount Mandara, he saw a frightened girl who cried 'Save me!'; he told her not to fear and asked what was wrong. She said she was Manorama, daughter of the vidyadhara Indivara and of Marudhanvan's daughter; with her friends Vibhavari, daughter of the vidyadhara Mandara, and Kalavati, daughter of the sage Para, she had gone to Kailasa and laughed at a sage thin and weak from penance; he cursed her to be soon seized by a rakshasa; her friends scolded him, saying his Brahminhood was worthless without patience, since a Brahmin's mark is patience and his penance is controlling anger; so he cursed one with leprosy and the other with consumption, and it happened at once. Now a huge rakshasa had been following her for three days, roaring nearby. She knew the secret 'heart' of all weapons (astra-hridaya), given by Shiva to Svayambhuva Manu, by him to the siddha Vasishtha, by him to her mother's father Chitrayudha, and by him to her father as a wedding gift; she had learned it as a child from her father, and gave it to Svarochis so he could kill the demon. He touched water and received it with its secrets and the way to withdraw it. Then the terrible rakshasa came roaring, saying he would eat her; Svarochis, thinking 'let the great sage's word come true', let the demon seize her, then in anger fixed the fierce Chanda weapon in his gaze and stared at the demon, who let her go and begged him to withdraw it, saying he had been freed from a terrible curse. The rakshasa explained: he was Indivara, her father, son of Nalanabha, king of the vidyadharas; he had begged the sage Brahmamitra, who knew the eightfold Ayurveda, to teach it to him, and when refused, had learned it while invisible as the sage taught his pupils; after eight months he laughed for joy, the sage recognised him and cursed him to become a rakshasa in seven nights, but softened, said he would regain his form when, having lost his memory, he tried to eat his own child and was burned by the fire of a weapon. Now freed, he gave Svarochis his daughter and the whole eightfold Ayurveda, and took his own shining form again. Manorama said she loved Svarochis too, but could not enjoy happiness while her friends suffered for her sake. Svarochis promised to cure them with Ayurveda. Her father gave her to him in marriage on the mountain and returned to his city; Svarochis went with her to the garden where the two girls lay sick and cured them with healing herbs and juices, and the two, freed of disease, lit up the mountain with their beauty.

064.json.summary: Markandeya continues telling Kraushtuki the story of Svarochis. The girl whom Svarochis has just freed from her illness speaks to him with joy: she is Vibhavari, daughter of Mandara the vidyadhara; she offers herself to him in return for his help and promises him a skill (vidya) by which he will understand the cries of all living beings. Svarochis, who knows dharma, agrees. Then the second girl speaks. Her father was Para, a great Brahmin sage who lived as a celibate from youth and had mastered the Vedas and their branches. Once in spring, when the cuckoos were calling, the famous apsaras Punjikastana came near him; he was overcome by desire, and from their union she was born on this great mountain. Her mother left her alone as a baby on the ground in the empty forest full of snakes and wild beasts, and she grew day by day, nourished by the growing phases (kalas) of the moon; so her father, a great gandharva who took her in, named her Kalavati. When a demon, an enemy of the gods, asked for her and her father refused, the demon killed him while he slept. In deep despair she was about to kill herself, but Sati, the truthful wife of Shiva and daughter of Daksha, stopped her: she said Kalavati would have a great husband named Svarochis, his son would be a Manu, and all the treasures (nidhis) would obey her and give her whatever wealth she wanted through the skill called Padmini, honoured by the treasure Mahapadma, which Sati gave her. Since Sati never speaks falsely, Kalavati says, he must be Svarochis, and she gives him this skill and herself, since he has saved her life. With Vibhavari's loving approval he accepts Kalavati too, and the godlike Svarochis takes the hands of both girls in marriage while divine drums sound and apsaras dance.

065.json.summary: Markandeya tells Kraushtuki that Svarochis, bright as a god, lived happily with his wives on that great mountain with its lovely forests and waterfalls. The treasures (nidhis), which obeyed the skill called Padmini, brought him every kind of enjoyment: jewels, sweet drinks, garlands, clothes, ornaments, fragrant ointments, shining golden seats, golden jugs and vessels, and beds with divine covers, and his wives were as happy there as in heaven. A female swan (kalahamsi), seeing them, said to a female chakravaka bird in the water that this young man was blessed and very fortunate, since he enjoyed all he wished with wives he loved; in the world handsome husbands often have plain wives and the reverse, and a marriage of mutual love is very rare. The chakravaki was not impressed. She said he was not blessed, because he felt no shame in being close to other women; his heart cannot be with all of them, since love settles on one place only, so he cannot truly love his wives, nor they him; they are only a pastime to him, like servants. If they loved him, they would die when he embraces another while they think of him; he was bought like a servant at the price of the skill they gave him, and love does not stay equally with many. She said she and her own husband were truly blessed, since each of their hearts had long rested on the other alone. Svarochis, who understood the speech of all creatures, heard this, felt ashamed and thought it was true. After a hundred years of pleasure on the mountain, he saw in front of him a sleek, strong deer moving with his herd, surrounded by beautiful female deer that came sniffing at him. The deer told them to go away and leave their shame elsewhere: he was not Svarochis, nor of his kind; there are many shameless males like that, go to them. A single female followed by many males is laughed at, and so is one male eyed with desire by many females; such a man loses his religious duties day by day, always attached to one wife while wanting another. Let them seek some other such man who has turned his back on the next world; he himself is not like Svarochis.

066.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Hearing the deer reject the does in this way, Svarochis felt he had fallen; moved by the words of the chakravaki and the deer, he thought of leaving his wives. But when he was with them again his desire grew, he put aside his feeling of disgust, and he lived with them for six hundred years more, still enjoying pleasures without going against dharma and doing the religious rites. Three sons were born to him: Vijaya by Manorama, the daughter of Indivara; Merunanda by Vibhavari; and the mighty Prabhava by Kalavati. Through the power of the Padmini skill he built three cities for them: Vijaya in Kamarupa in the east for Vijaya, Nandavati in the north for Merunanda, with high walls and ramparts, and Tala in the southern region for Prabhava. One day, hunting in the forest, he drew his bow at a boar far away, but a female deer came and begged him again and again to shoot her instead, since his arrow would free her from her sorrow. He saw she was not sick and asked why she wanted to die. She said her heart was set on a man whose heart was attached to other women, and without him death was the only cure: she wanted him alone. He said she was a deer and he a man, so how could they be joined? She asked him to embrace her if his heart turned toward her. When he embraced her she at once took a divine form, and, shy and full of love, told him she was the goddess of this forest, and the gods had asked her to bear from him a son, a Manu, who would protect the earth. He then fathered on her a son with every good mark, shining like himself. At the birth divine drums sounded, gandharva kings sang, apsaras danced, clouds and sages sprinkled spray, and the gods rained flowers. Seeing his brightness, which lit up the directions, the father named him Dyutiman ('the shining one'), and because he was Svarochis' son he was also called Svarochisha. Later Svarochis, walking by a mountain waterfall, saw a male swan with his mate, who kept asking him for love. The swan said it was time to stop, since they had played long and old age was near. She answered that there is no wrong time for enjoyment, since the whole world is made for it: self-controlled Brahmins sacrifice, give gifts and do pure deeds wanting pleasures in this world and the next, and pleasure is the fruit people want. The swan said that those whose minds cling to pleasure and to relatives never gain the highest understanding; beings attached to sons, friends and wives sink like old wild elephants stuck in the mud of a lake. Look at Svarochis, he said, attached to desire from childhood, sunk in the mud of affection, first for his wives and now for sons and grandsons; how will he ever be lifted out? He himself was not like Svarochis, ruled by women; he had discernment and had now turned away from pleasures. Hearing the bird, Svarochis was troubled, took his wives to another forest for penance, and after hard austerities with them went, free of all sin, to the pure worlds.

067.json.summary: Markandeya tells Kraushtuki that the Lord then made Dyutiman, called Svarochisha, a Prajapati and the Manu, and describes his period (manvantara): its gods, sages, sons and kings. In the Svarochisha period the gods were the Paravatas and the Tushitas, and the Indra was the famous Vipashchit. The seven sages were Urja, Stamba, Prana, Datta, Ali (as printed), Rishabha, Nishchara and Arvavira (the list as printed names eight). Chaitra, Kimpurusha and others were the seven very powerful sons of the great Manu, who ruled the earth. As long as his period lasted, the whole earth was enjoyed by his widespread family; this was the second Manu period. A person of faith who hears the story of Svarochis and the birth of Svarochisha is freed from sins.

068.json.summary: Kraushtuki says Markandeya has told him in full the story of Svarochis and the birth of Svarochisha, and now asks about the skill called Padmini, which provides all enjoyments, and the eight treasures (nidhis) that depend on it: their nature and the wealth tied to each. Markandeya says the goddess of the Padmini skill is Lakshmi, and the treasures rest on it. They are Padma, Mahapadma, Makara, Kacchapa, Mukunda, Nandaka (Nanda), Nila and the eighth, Shankha. Where there is real prosperity they appear, and through them success comes; by the grace of the gods and by serving good people, a person's wealth is always watched over by them. Padma is a treasure of sattva (goodness): the man it rests on, and his sons and grandsons always, are generous; he gathers gold, silver, copper and other metals and trades in them, performs sacrifices and gives fees, fulfils all wishes in order, and builds halls and temples. Mahapadma is also of sattva: such a man gathers rubies and other gems, pearls and coral and trades in them, gives to those devoted to yoga and builds homes for them, and becomes like them himself; his sons and grandsons are the same, and it stays for seven generations. Makara is a treasure of tamas (darkness): the man it looks on, though well behaved, becomes mostly tamasic; he collects arrows, swords, spears, bows, shields and armour, is very friendly with kings, gives to warlike kings and their favourites, and takes pleasure only in trading weapons; it stays with one man only, not his sons, and he may die at the hands of robbers for his wealth or in battle. Kacchapa ('tortoise') is also tamasic: such a man does all his dealings with pure goods, trusts no one, and like a tortoise drawing in its limbs he holds on to his jewels with an anxious mind, neither giving nor enjoying them for fear of losing them, and buries them in the ground; it too stays with one man. Mukunda is of rajas (passion): such a man collects vinas, flutes, drums and other instruments, gives money to singers and dancers, bards, heralds, flatterers and actors, enjoys pleasures with them day and night, and loves loose women and people of that kind; it stays with one man. Nanda is a great treasure of rajas and tamas: such a man becomes very stubborn; he gathers and trades all metals, jewels and good grains, supports his own people and guests, cannot bear even a small insult, is very pleased when praised and gives freely, grows gentle toward whatever he wants, and has many fine wives with children; it stays for seven generations, grows by an eighth part, gives long life to all of them, and makes him support relatives and those who come from far; but he is not honoured in the next world, feels no affection for those he lives with, grows cool to old friends and makes new ones. Nila, holding sattva and rajas, makes a man gather cloth, cotton, grain, fruit and flowers, pearls, coral, conch shells and pearl oysters, wood and other things born of water, and trade in them only; he makes tanks, ponds and gardens, dams rivers, plants trees, and enjoys ointments and flowers; it lasts three generations. Shankha, of rajas and tamas, stays with one man only: he eats the food and wears the clothes he gets alone, while his servants eat poor food and wear poor clothes, and he gives nothing to friends, wife, brothers, sons or daughters-in-law, always caring only for himself. These treasures are the gods of wealth for men; a mixed glance from them gives mixed results, while a single one gives its own nature; and the Padmini, Lakshmi herself, rules over them all.

069.json.summary: This chapter, part of the story of the Uttama Manu period, survives here only from its verse 53; the opening is missing and the first line is garbled. A sage who knows the past, present and future is speaking to King Uttama. He says that after thinking it over he understood the matter, and that is why he did not offer the king the guest water (arghya) in the proper way: the king is indeed worthy of it by his birth in the family of Svayambhuva, yet the sage does not consider him fit for it. The king asks what he has done, knowingly or unknowingly, to lose this honour, since he has come after a long time. The sage asks whether he has forgotten that he abandoned his wife in the forest, and with her gave up his whole dharma. A man who fails in his rites for a fortnight becomes untouchable, and the king has failed in his daily rites for a year. A wife should be agreeable to her husband whatever his character, and a husband must support his wife even if she is ill-behaved. The Brahmin whose wife was carried off also had a difficult wife, yet, wanting dharma, he came and urged the king to act. The king sets others back on their duty when they slip; who will set him back on his own? Ashamed, the king agrees and asks who took the Brahmin's wife and where she is. The sage says a rakshasa named Balaka, son of Adri, carried her off, and the king will see her today in the forest of Utpalavataka; he should go quickly and reunite the Brahmin with his wife, so that the Brahmin does not, like the king, become a place of sin day after day.

070.json.summary: Markandeya continues. King Uttama bows to the sage, mounts his chariot and goes to the Utpalavata forest, where he sees the Brahmin's wife, looking just as her husband described, eating bilva fruits. He asks how she came to this forest. She says she is the daughter of Atiratra, a Brahmin who lives in the forest, and the wife of Vishala's son Susharman; the evil rakshasa Balaka carried her off while she slept at the edge of the house, parting her from her mother and brothers; she curses him to be burned to ashes. He brought her into this deep forest and left her, and she does not know why, since he neither enjoys her nor eats her. The king says her husband sent him and asks where the rakshasa is; she says he stays at the edge of this same forest. Following the path she shows, the king finds the rakshasa with his followers, who at once falls with his head to the ground at the king's feet, says he lives in the king's land, offers him the guest water and a seat, and asks for orders. The king asks why he took the Brahmin's wife: she is not beautiful, so it cannot have been for a wife, and if it was for food, why has he not eaten her? The rakshasa says they are not man-eaters like other rakshasas; they eat the fruit of good deeds, and they eat the inner nature of men and women: when they eat people's patience, the people become angry, and when they eat a bad nature, the people become good. They have rakshasa women as lovely as apsaras, so why would they want human women? The king asks why, then, he took her from the Brahmin's house. The rakshasa says the Brahmin knows mantras and, as a priest at every sacrifice, drives them away by reciting the rakshasa-killing mantras, so they go hungry; so they caused him this defect, since a man without his wife is not fit to perform sacrifices. On hearing the word 'defect', the king becomes very sad, for the sage had said he was unworthy of the guest water, and the rakshasa was speaking of the same defect, being without a wife. The rakshasa again bows and asks for orders. The king says that since the rakshasa eats people's nature, he should now eat the bad temper of this Brahmin woman so that she becomes well behaved, and take her to her husband's house; that will be all the hospitality he needs. By his power the rakshasa enters her and eats her very fierce ill temper. Freed of it, she says she was parted from her husband because of the fruit of her own past deeds, and the rakshasa was only the means; neither he nor her husband is at fault, only she herself, for in another life she must have parted someone. The rakshasa promises to take her home and asks for any other task; the king asks him to come whenever he remembers him in time of need. The rakshasa agrees and takes the woman, now pure of her bad temper, to her husband's house.

071.json.summary: Markandeya continues. After sending the woman home, King Uttama sighs and wonders what good he can do now: the sage said he was unfit for the guest water, and the rakshasa spoke of the Brahmin's 'defect'; he himself has abandoned his wife. He decides to ask the sage, who sees by knowledge, drives to him, bows and tells him all that happened. The sage says he already knew all this and why the king has come, and he tells him: a wife is the strong cause of a man's dharma, wealth and pleasure, above all of dharma, and one who abandons her abandons dharma. A man without a wife, whether Brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya or shudra, is not fit for his own duties; just as women must not leave their husbands, men must not leave their wives. The king says it was the ripening of his past deeds: she was never kind to him though he was kind to her, so he left her; he had borne everything she did with a burning heart, afraid of being separated from her; now, left in the forest, he does not know where she is, or whether lions, tigers or night-wanderers have eaten her. The sage says she has not been eaten and her conduct is unstained; she is now in the underworld (Rasatala). The famous Naga king Kapotaka saw her wandering in the forest after the king left her, fell in love with her beauty and took her to the underworld. But his daughter Nanda, seeing that the lovely woman would become a rival to her mother, the Naga king's wife Manorama, took her to her own house and hid her in the inner rooms. When her father asked for her and Nanda would not give her up, he cursed his daughter to become mute. So the queen remains there, brought by the snake king but protected by his daughter. The king, overjoyed, asks why his wife does not love him though everyone else in the world loves him greatly, and though she is dearer to him than life. The sage explains that at the time of the marriage the king was looked on by the Sun, Mars, Saturn, Venus and Jupiter, while at that moment his wife was looked on by the Moon and Mercury; these two groups are opposed to each other, so there is strong discord between them. He tells the king to go, rule the earth by his own dharma, and perform all religious rites with his wife at his side. Uttama bows, mounts his chariot and returns to his city.

072.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Back in his city, King Uttama sees the Brahmin with his wife, now well behaved, and happy. The Brahmin says he has achieved his aim, since the king, who knows dharma, protected his dharma by bringing back his wife. The king says the Brahmin is fortunate in keeping his duty, while the king is in trouble with no wife at home. The Brahmin says that if wild beasts have eaten her, he should simply marry another; in anger he has failed to protect dharma. The king says she is alive and her conduct unstained, so how can he do that? The Brahmin asks why, then, he chooses the sin of living without a wife. The king says that even if brought back she is always against him, bringing sorrow, not joy, and asks the Brahmin to make her obedient to him. The Brahmin says he will perform for the king the helpful rite called Mitravinda, done by those who want friendship, which creates love between husband and wife who do not love each other; the king should then bring her, and she will love him greatly. The king brings all the materials, and the Brahmin performs the rite seven times over. Knowing that love for her husband has been planted in her, he tells the king to bring her and enjoy life and perform sacrifices with her. The king, surprised, remembers the mighty, truthful rakshasa, who comes at once, hears the matter, goes to the underworld and brings the queen. Seeing her husband she says again and again with joy, 'Be gracious to me.' He embraces her and says he is pleased already. She asks one favour: for her sake the Naga king cursed his daughter, her friend, to become mute; if he can, he should undo this. The king asks the Brahmin what rite will cure the muteness, and the Brahmin performs a rite to Sarasvati (sarasvati-ishti), reciting the Sarasvati hymns with a focused mind. When Nanda's speech returns, Garga tells her in the underworld that her friend's husband has done her this very hard service. Learning this, Nanda hurries to the city, embraces the queen, praises the king with blessings and, seated, gives him a boon in return: he will have a very mighty son whose rule (chakra) will be unchecked on earth, who will know the truth of all sciences of wealth, be devoted to dharma and be the lord of a Manu period, a Manu. She embraces her friend and returns to the underworld. The king lives happily with his wife for a long time, ruling his people, and a son is born to them, lovely as the full moon. All the people rejoice, divine drums sound and flowers rain down. The assembled sages, seeing his beauty and future character, name him Auttama, since he was born in the highest (uttama) family, at the highest time and with the finest limbs. This son of Uttama became the Manu Auttama. Whoever always hears the whole story of Uttama and the birth of Auttama never falls into hatred, and one who hears or reads it is never parted from beloved wife, sons or relatives. Markandeya then offers to describe his period, its Indra, gods and sages.

073.json.summary: Markandeya tells Kraushtuki about the third Manu period, that of the Prajapati Auttama: its gods, Indra, sages and kings. There were five groups of gods, each true to its name: the Svadhamans; the group called Satya; the Shivas, auspicious by nature and known to destroy sin; the Pratardanas; and the Vashavartins. These five groups shared in the sacrifices, and each had twelve members. Their Indra, the teacher of the three worlds, was named Sushanti, having performed a hundred sacrifices; to this day people on earth sing a verse adorned with the syllables of his name to remove troubles, saying that Sushanti, the lovely king of the gods, together with the Shivas, Satyas and others and the Vashavartins, gives peace (shanti). The Manu's sons were Aja, Parashuchi and Divya, of great strength and courage, famous and like gods, and kings born of their line ruled the earth for as long as this Manu's period lasted, which is a little over seventy-one cycles of the four ages (Krita, Treta and the rest) described earlier. The seven sages of this period were the seven sons of a great sage who was foremost in penance (the text reads 'varishtha', 'the best'). This was the third Manu period. Markandeya then announces the fourth, that of Tamasa, a Manu born from a non-human womb, whose fame lit up the world, and says that the deeds, births and power of all the Manus are beyond the senses.

074.json.summary: Markandeya tells Kraushtuki of the birth of Tamasa, the fourth Manu. There was a famous, mighty king named Svarashtra, wise, the performer of many sacrifices and unbeaten in battle. The Sun, worshipped by his minister, gave him a very long life, and he had a hundred fine wives; but his wives did not live as long, and in time they died, as did his servants and ministers. Without his wives and the servants born with him, he grew troubled in mind and lost strength day and night. When he was weak and left by his servants, his neighbour (or rival) named Vimarda drove him from his kingdom. In despair he went to the forest and did penance on the bank of the Vitasta river: in summer amid five fires, in the rains under the open sky, in winter lying in water, fasting and keeping his vows. Then in the rainy season came a great flood, with clouds raining day after day; the directions could not be told apart and all seemed smeared with darkness. The swollen river swept him away from the bank; carried far by the water, he came upon a female deer (rohi) in the water and caught hold of her tail. Pulled along by her in the dark, he reached a bank, crossed a wide, deep stretch of mud and came to another lovely forest. The touch of the deer, as she dragged the thin king clinging to her tail, gave him great joy, and he became filled with desire. Seeing him eager and stroking her back, the deer spoke: why did he touch her back with a trembling hand? His heart had not gone to a wrong place, and she was not forbidden to him, but this Lola was blocking their union. Curious, the king asked who she was, how a deer could speak like a human, and who this Lola was. She said she had once been his beloved Utpalavati, the chief of his hundred queens, daughter of Dridhadhanvan. Asked what deed had brought her, a faithful and dutiful wife, to this birth, she explained: as a girl in her father's house she went to the forest with friends and saw a male deer with a doe; she struck the doe, which ran away in fright. The male deer angrily scolded her for ruining his time for begetting young, and she, afraid at hearing him speak like a man, asked who he was. He was Sutapas, son of the sage Nirvritichakshus, who had become a deer out of desire for the doe; since she had parted them he would curse her, unless she gave herself to him. She refused, saying she was no doe and he could find another. In anger he said that since she had said 'I am not a doe', she would become a doe. She begged him again and again, saying she was a young girl who did not know how to speak, and that a woman chooses a husband herself only when her father is not alive. He said his word never fails: after death, in this same forest, she would become a doe; while a deer she would carry in her womb the mighty Lola, son of the sage Siddhavirya; when he entered her womb she would remember her past life and speak human speech; when he was born she would be freed from the deer state, honoured by her husband, and reach worlds evil-doers cannot reach; and Lola would kill his father's enemies, conquer the whole earth and become a Manu. So, she said, she had died and become an animal, and from the king's touch this child had been conceived in her; Lola in the womb was the obstacle. The king rejoiced that his son would conquer his enemies and become a Manu. The doe gave birth to a son with all good marks; all beings, and the king above all, rejoiced, and she, freed from the curse, reached the highest worlds. The assembled sages, foreseeing his future greatness, named him Tamasa, because he was born while his mother was in a dark (tamasi) birth and the world was covered in darkness (tamas). Raised by his father in the forest, when he grew up he asked who his father was, how he was his son and who his mother was. His father told him everything, from the loss of the kingdom on. Tamasa worshipped the Sun and received all the divine weapons with the means of withdrawing them, defeated his father's enemies, brought them before his father, released them with his permission and kept to his own duty. His father, having seen his son's face with joy, left his body and reached the worlds earned by his penance and sacrifices. Tamasa conquered the whole earth and became the Manu Tamasa. In his period the gods were the Satyas, Sudhis, Surupas and Haris, groups of twenty-seven; their lord, the Indra, was Shikhi, mighty and marked by a hundred sacrifices. The seven sages were Jyotirdharma, Prithu, Kavya, Chaitra, Agni, Valaka and Pivara. The sons of Tamasa, very strong kings, were Nara, Kshanti, Shanta, Danta, Janu, Jangha and others. Whoever reads or hears of the Tamasa period is not troubled by darkness (tamas).

075.json.summary: Markandeya tells of the fifth Manu, the famous Raivata. There was a great sage named Ritavak. He had no son, and then a son was born to him at the end of the Revati constellation (nakshatra). He performed for him in due form the birth rites, the sacred thread and the other rites, but the boy grew up ill-behaved. From the time of his birth the sage suffered long illness, and the boy's mother was afflicted with leprosy and other diseases. While the father wondered why, the wicked son took the wife of another sage's son. Ritavak in grief said that being childless is better for men than having a bad son: a bad son always pains the hearts of father and mother, makes his ancestors in heaven fall, does not help friends or satisfy the ancestors, brings his friends to misery and his enemies joy, and makes his parents old before their time; blessed are those whose sons are honoured by all, kind to others, calm and devoted to good deeds. Burning in mind, he asked the sage Garga: he had studied the Vedas under vows, married properly, done all the Vedic and household rites with his wife, and fathered this son for the sake of a son, by the proper rite and not for pleasure, fearing the hell called Put; was the son bad through his own fault or the father's? Garga said the son was born at the end of Revati, an evil time, which brought him sorrow; it was the fault neither of the father, nor of the mother, nor of the family; the end of Revati was the cause. Ritavak then cursed: since his only son's bad character came from the end of Revati, let Revati fall at once. At his curse the Revati star fell before the eyes of the astonished world onto Mount Kumuda, suddenly filling it with forests, caves and waterfalls, and from this the mountain became famous as Raivataka, the loveliest on earth. The light of that star became a lotus lake, and from it a girl of great beauty was born. The sage Pramucha, seeing her born from the light of Revati, named her Revati and raised her near his hermitage on that mountain. When she grew up, he wondered who her husband should be, and for a long time found no fit match. So he went into the fire-hall to ask Agni, who said her husband would be a king named Durgama, very strong, sweet of speech and fond of dharma. Soon after, while hunting, King Durgama came to the hermitage: a descendant of Priyavrata, son of Vikramashila and of Kalindi. Not seeing the sage, he called the slender girl 'beloved' (priya) and asked where the holy sage had gone, as he wished to bow to him. Hearing him call her 'beloved', the sage hurried out of the fire-hall, saw the king bowing with royal marks, and told his disciple Gautama to bring the guest water quickly, since the king had come after a long time and, above all, as his son-in-law was worthy of it. The king wondered about the word 'son-in-law' but kept silent and accepted it. The sage welcomed him and asked after his treasury, army, friends, servants, ministers and himself, and his wife; he would not ask after his other wives, since this wife was here. The king, puzzled, asked who his wife here was. The sage said it was Revati, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds. The king said he knew his wives at home, Subhadra daughter of Shanta, the daughter of Kaveri, Sujata of Surashtra, Kadamba daughter of Varutha, Vipatha and Nandini, but did not know any Revati. The sage reminded him that he had just called this lovely woman 'beloved'. The king said he had spoken so, but without wrong intent, and asked him not to be angry. The sage said his intent was indeed not wrong: Agni had moved him to speak, for when the sage asked who her husband would be, Agni named him; so he should accept the girl the sage was giving him. The king fell silent, and the sage prepared the wedding. The girl humbly asked her father, if he loved her, to hold the wedding under the Revati star. He said Revati was no longer in the moon's path; other stars suited a wedding. She said without it the time seemed fruitless to her. He explained that the ascetic Ritavak had cursed and thrown down Revati, and he had promised her to the king; if she refused, they were in trouble. She asked whether Ritavak's penance was greater than her father's; was she the daughter of a Brahmin in name only? He said she was the daughter not of such a man but of an ascetic able to create other gods. Then, she said, why not put the star back in the sky and hold the wedding under it? He agreed, and by the power of his penance set Revati back in the moon's path as before, performed the wedding with mantras, and asked the king what wedding gift he wanted, promising even something hard to get. The king, born in the line of Svayambhuva Manu, asked for a son who would rule a Manu period. The sage granted it: his son would be a Manu, enjoy the whole earth and know dharma. The king took Revati to his city, and from her was born the Manu Raivata, endowed with all virtues, unbeaten by men, knowing all the sciences, the Vedas and statecraft. In his period the gods were the Sumedhas, Bhupatis, Vaikunthas and Amitabhas, fourteen in each group, and their lord, the Indra, was Vibhu, marked by a hundred sacrifices. The seven sages were Hiranyaloma, Vedashri, Urdhvabahu, Vedabahu, Sudhama, the great sage Parjanya and Vasishtha, master of the Vedas and Vedanta. The Manu's sons were the mighty Balabandhu, Suyashtavya, Satyaka and others. The Manus up to Raivata all descend from Svayambhuva, except Svarochisha. Whoever always hears or reads this excellent story is freed from all sins and reaches the world he desires.

076.json.summary: Markandeya, having told five Manu periods, now tells of the sixth, that of Chakshusha. In another life he was born from the eye (chakshus) of the Supreme Being (Parameshthin), and so he was called Chakshusha in this birth too. When he was born, his mother held him in her lap, fondled him and hugged him again and again. The baby, who remembered his past lives, laughed, and his mother, alarmed and angry, asked why he laughed: had he gained understanding too early, or did he see something good? The child said: did she not see the cat in front of her wanting to eat him, and the second one, invisible, the child-stealer (jataharini)? His mother, out of love for her son, with hair standing on end and eyes full of tears, fondled and hugged him; that was why he laughed. The cat and the child-stealer were eager for their own gain and loved him for it; she too seemed to act for her own gain: they wanted to devour him, while she hoped to enjoy the fruit of him over time. She did not know who he was, he had done nothing for her, and their bond was only five or seven days old, yet she loved him with tears and called him 'dear' and 'good one' without guile. The mother said she did not hug him to get help from him but out of love; if he did not like it, she was left by him; she gave up any gain she might have from him. She put him down and left the birth-room. The child-stealer then took the abandoned baby, dull in his outer body and senses but pure within, and put him on the bed of the newly delivered wife of King Vikranta, taking her son; that child she put in another house, taking its son, and the third she ate; so day by day she swapped two and ate the third. King Vikranta, thinking him his own son, had the rites of a kshatriya done for him and joyfully named him Ananda. When he had received the sacred thread, his teacher told him first to go and greet his mother. Laughing, the boy asked which mother to honour, the one who bore him or the one who raised him. The teacher said this was his mother, Haimini, chief queen of Vikranta and daughter of Rutha (as printed). Ananda said she was the mother of Chaitra, who lived in the village of Vishala and was being raised as son of the great Brahmin Bodha. The puzzled teacher asked where he was from. Ananda said he was born in the house of a kshatriya king, from his wife Giribhadra; the child-stealer took him, left him with Haimini, took her son to the house of the Brahmin Bodha and ate Bodha's son; Haimini's son was there given the rites of a Brahmin, while Ananda was given his rites here; which mother should he greet? The teacher said this was a very deep problem and his mind was confused. Ananda said there was no reason for confusion in a world so arranged: who is anyone's son or relative? Relationships begin at birth and earlier ones are ended by death; even the bond formed in this life ends when the body dies. In the round of births, who is not a relative, and who is one for ever? He himself had two fathers and two mothers in this one life; what wonder, then, in other bodies? He would do penance, and the king's real son Chaitra should be brought from Vishala. The king, his wife and relatives, amazed, gave up their sense of possession and let him go to the forest; the king brought Chaitra, made him fit to rule, and honoured the Brahmin who had raised him as a son. Ananda, still a boy, did penance in the great forest to wear away his karma, which blocks liberation. Brahma came and asked why he did such hard penance; he said he wanted to purify himself and destroy the karma that binds him. Brahma said one who still has karma to fulfil is not fit for liberation; he still had a role of sattva to play: he was to be the sixth Manu; he should go and do that work, and when it was done he would gain liberation; enough of penance. Ananda agreed and stopped; Brahma called him Chakshusha, and by his former name he became the famous Manu Chakshusha. He married Vidarbha, daughter of King Ugra, and had famous, brave sons by her. In his period the gods were five groups of eight: the Apyas, the Prasutas, the Bhavyas, the Yuthagas, and the Lekhas, who drank nectar. Their lord, the Indra who had performed a hundred sacrifices, was Manojava. The seven sages were Sumedha, Viraja, Havishman, Unnata, Madhu, Atinama and Sahishnu. The Manu's mighty sons, kings of the earth, were led by Uru, Puru and Shatadyumna. Markandeya then says the present Manu is Vaivasvata, whose seventh period he will describe next. A wise person who tells or hears of the Chakshusha period gains sons, health, happiness and wealth.

077.json.summary: Markandeya tells the story of the birth of Vaivasvata Manu. Sanjna, daughter of Vishvakarma, was the wife of the Sun (Martanda, Vivasvat), and by her he fathered the Manu, famous and learned in many fields, called Vaivasvata as Vivasvat's son. Whenever the Sun looked at her, Sanjna closed her eyes, so he angrily told her that since she always restrained her eyes when she saw him, she would give birth to Yama, the restrainer of beings. Frightened, she let her eyes dart about, and he said that since her gaze was unsteady, she would bear an unsteady daughter, a river. So, by her husband's curse, Yama and the great river Yamuna were born to her. Sanjna could bear the Sun's heat only with pain; unable to bear it, she wondered where she could go to find peace without angering him, and decided to take shelter with her father. She made a shadow-body of herself (Chhaya) and told it to live in the Sun's house as she had, to treat the children and the Sun well, and never to reveal her going even if asked, but always to say she was Sanjna. Chhaya-Sanjna agreed, saying she would do so until she was seized by the hair or threatened with a curse, and then she would tell what had happened. Sanjna went to her father Tvashtri (Vishvakarma), who honoured her, and stayed there for some time. Soon her father, praising her lovingly, said that many days with her seemed like half a moment, but dharma was being lost: a woman living long with her relatives brings no good name; her relatives wish her to stay in her husband's house; she was married to the Sun, lord of the three worlds, and should not stay long at her father's; she should go back and come again to visit. She agreed, honoured her father, but went instead to the Northern Kurus, and, not wanting the Sun's heat and afraid of his brightness, did penance there in the form of a mare. The Sun, thinking the second woman was Sanjna, fathered on her two sons and a lovely daughter. Chhaya-Sanjna loved her own children greatly but did not treat Sanjna's daughter and two sons the same way, favouring her own day by day in care and comforts. Manu bore this, but Yama did not, and in anger he raised his foot to kick her, though, being patient, he did not bring it down on her body. Chhaya-Sanjna, with trembling lips and hands, cursed him: since he threatened his father's wife with his foot, breaking all limits, that foot would fall to the ground today. Frightened, Yama went to his father, bowed and said this was a great wonder never seen before: a mother giving up love and cursing her son; as Manu had told him, she could not be their mother, for a mother is never bad even to bad sons. The Sun called Chhaya-Sanjna and asked where Sanjna had gone. She said she was Sanjna, daughter of Tvashtri, his wife, and these were his children by her. When she would not tell despite many questions, the Sun in anger was about to curse her, and then she told him what had happened. Knowing the truth, he went to Tvashtri's house, where Vishvakarma honoured him with great devotion and, asked about Sanjna, said she had come there, sent, as she said, by him. Through meditation the Sun saw her doing penance as a mare in the Northern Kurus, and understood the purpose of her penance: that her husband should have a gentle, pleasant form. So he asked Vishvakarma, her father, to cut down his brightness. Vishvakarma put the Sun on his lathe for a year (the text speaks of the year-long turning) and trimmed his brightness, while the gods praised him. The chapter ends here, and the story continues in the next.

078.json.summary: Markandeya continues the story of the Sun and Sanjna. As Vishvakarma trimmed the Sun's brightness, the gods and divine sages gathered and praised the Sun, worthy of praise by all three worlds. Their hymn bows to him as the form of the Rig, Sama and Yajur Vedas, the one home of knowledge, the remover of darkness, pure light, spotless, the highest, the Supreme Self, whose form pervades the whole world. In the middle of the hymn come two verses saying this fine hymn should be heard with faith, as a disciple with a focused mind who has paid his teacher, and not by empty-minded people, so that it bears fruit. The praise goes on: bow to the cause of all, the goal of those who know; to him whose form is the Sun and light, Bhaskara, maker of day, cause of night, maker of twilight and moonlight. He is all this world; as he turns, the whole universe of moving and unmoving things turns, held by him; all that his rays touch becomes pure, and water and other things are purified by the touch of his rays; fire offerings, gifts and other religious acts bring no benefit until the world is joined with his rays. All the Rig verses, Yajus formulas and Sama chants come from his body, so he is made of the three Vedas; he is the form of Brahman, higher and lower, with and without form, subtle and gross, made of time from the blink and the kashtha on, the destroyer. They ask him to be gracious, take a form of his choice and calm his brightness. So praised, the Sun, the endless mass of light, gave up his brightness. His Rig-portion became the earth, his Yajus-portion the sky, and his Sama-portion heaven. From the fifteen parts of his brightness cut away, Tvashtri (Vishvakarma) made Shiva's trident, Vishnu's discus, the terrible spikes (shanku) of the Vasus, Agni's spear, Kubera's palanquin, and the fierce weapons of the other enemies of the asuras and of the yakshas and vidyadharas. The Sun now carries only the sixteenth part, his brightness having been cut into fifteen parts. Then, taking the form of a horse, the Sun went to the Northern Kurus and saw Sanjna in the form of a mare. Seeing him come and fearing he was another male, she turned to face him to guard her back; their noses met, and from the mare's mouth were born two sons, Nasatya and Dasra (the Ashvins). At the end of the seed came Revanta, armed with sword, shield and armour, riding a horse, with arrows and quiver. Then the Sun showed his matchless true form; she rejoiced to see it, took her own form, and he brought his loving wife Sanjna back to his home. Her first son became Vaivasvata Manu; the second, Yama, because of the curse, became Dharmadrishti ('one who sees by dharma'). The father himself set a limit to the curse: worms would take flesh from his foot and fall to the ground. Because Yama saw by dharma and treated friend and foe alike, the Sun made him the ruler of the dead (the office of Yama). Yamuna became the river flowing through the Kalinda hills; the Ashvins were made the physicians of the gods; and Revanta was made lord of the guhyakas. Of Chhaya-Sanjna's children, the elder son was like the elder Manu and received the name Savarnika; he will be a Manu when Bali is Indra. The father made Shanaishchara (Saturn) one of the planets. Their third child, the daughter Tapati, bore Kuru, a lord of men, to King Samvarana. Markandeya says he will now describe the seventh period, that of Vaivasvata Manu, with its sons and kings, sages, gods and Indra. (The closing line of this chapter places it, oddly, in the Savarnika Manu period, under the title 'the birth of Vaivasvata'.)

079.json.summary: Markandeya describes the seventh Manu period, that of Vaivasvata, which is the present one. Its gods are the Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sadhyas, Vishvedevas, Maruts, Bhrigus and Angirases, eight groups. The Adityas, Vasus and Rudras are sons of Kashyapa; the Sadhyas, Maruts and Vishvedevas are three groups of sons of Dharma; the Bhrigu gods are sons of Bhrigu, and the Angiras gods sons of Angiras. This creation, coming from Marichi's line, is the ruling one now. The Indra is the great Urjasvi, who shares in the sacrifice. All the Indras, past, future and present, have the same marks: all have a thousand eyes, hold the thunderbolt, destroy cities, are generous (Maghavan), strong as bulls, horned, move like elephants, have performed a hundred sacrifices, outshine all beings in brightness, and gain the qualities of lordship through pure causes such as dharma. They are lords of the three worlds, past, future and present: the earth is Bhurloka, the middle region (antariksha) is the sky, and the divine region is heaven, together called the three worlds. The seven sages of this period are Atri, Vasishtha, the great sage Kashyapa, Gautama, Bharadvaja, Vishvamitra the Kaushika, and Jamadagni, son of the great Richika. The nine sons of Vaivasvata Manu are Ikshvaku, Nabhaga, Dhrishta, Sharyati, the famous Narishyanta, Nabhaga-Arishta (as printed), Karusha, Prishadhra and the world-famous Vasuman. A person who hears or reads of this Vaivasvata period is at once freed from all sins and gains great merit. (As in the previous chapter, the closing line puts this chapter in the Savarnika Manu period.)

080.json.summary: Kraushtuki says Markandeya has told him of the seven Manus from Svayambhuva on, with the gods, kings and sages of their periods, and asks about the other seven Manus still to come in this kalpa, with their gods and others. Markandeya says the Savarni already mentioned, the son of Chhaya-Sanjna who is like the elder Manu, will be the eighth Manu. His seven sages are Rama, Vyasa, Galava, Diptiman, Kripa, Rishyashringa and Drona. The gods will be in three groups, the Sutapas, the Amitabhas and the Mukhyas, each of twenty. The Sutapa group of twenty includes Tapas, Tapta, Shakra, Dyuti, Jyoti, Prabhakara, Prabhasa, Dayita, Dharma, Tejorashmi, Chirakratu and others; another group of twenty includes Prabhu, Vibhu, Vibhasa and others; and a third group includes Dama, Danta, Rita, Soma, Vitta and others, twenty in all (the text's wording about which name belongs to which group is not fully clear). These chief gods, rulers of the Manu period, are all sons of Kashyapa, son of Marichi, and will exist in the period of Savarna Manu. Their Indra will be Bali, son of Virochana, the daitya who even now stays in the underworld, bound by an agreement. The sons of Savarna Manu, who will be kings, are Viraja, Arvavira, Nirmoha, Satyavak, Kriti, Vishnu and others.

081.json.summary: Markandeya begins to tell how Savarni, son of the Sun, became the eighth Manu through the power of the Great Illusion (Mahamaya). Long ago, in the age of Svarochisha Manu, there was a king named Suratha of the Chaitra line who ruled the whole earth and cared for his people like his own children. Enemy kings, the Kolavidhvamsis, defeated him in battle, and back in his own city his strong and wicked ministers took his treasury and army. On the excuse of hunting he rode alone into a deep forest and came to the peaceful hermitage of the sage Medhas, where even wild beasts were calm. Living there, he kept worrying about his lost city, his favourite elephant, his servants now serving other kings, and his treasury being wasted. Near the hermitage he met a merchant (vaishya) named Samadhi, born in a rich family, who had been driven out by his greedy wife and sons, who took his wealth; yet he still worried whether they were well and could not make his mind hard against them. The two went to the sage, and the king asked why both of them, though they knew better, still felt attachment to those who had hurt them. The sage said all creatures have knowledge of objects, even birds and beasts; birds feed their young though hungry themselves, and people want sons hoping for return; yet all are thrown into the whirlpool of 'mine' by Mahamaya, the yoga-sleep of Vishnu, who forcibly pulls even the minds of the wise into delusion. She creates the world; when pleased she grants freedom; she is both the highest knowledge that frees and the cause of bondage. Asked who she is, the sage says she is eternal, the world is her form, but she is said to be 'born' whenever she appears to help the gods. At the end of an age, when Vishnu slept on the serpent Shesha in the single ocean, two demons born from the wax of his ears, Madhu and Kaitabha, rose to kill Brahma, who sat on the lotus from Vishnu's navel. Brahma praised the Yoga-sleep: she is Svaha and Svadha, the syllables and the half syllable beyond speech, Savitri, the creator, keeper and destroyer of the world, the great knowledge, great illusion, great memory, Prakriti of the three qualities, the dark Night of destruction, Shri, modesty, peace and patience, armed with sword, trident, club, discus, conch and bow, more beautiful than all beautiful things; since she made even Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma take bodies, no one can praise her fully.
