He asked her to confuse the two demons and wake Vishnu. She came out of Vishnu's eyes, mouth, nose, arms, heart and chest and stood before Brahma; Vishnu woke and fought the two with his arms for five thousand years. Deluded by Mahamaya, the proud demons offered him a boon; he asked that they be killed by him. Seeing the whole world covered with water, they asked to be killed where the earth was not flooded, and Vishnu cut off their heads with his discus on his thigh. So she appeared when praised by Brahma, and the sage says he will tell more of her power.

082.json.summary: The sage (Medhas) tells how, long ago, the gods and the demons fought for a full hundred years, with Mahisha leading the demons and Indra the gods. The demons won, and Mahishasura became Indra himself. The defeated gods, led by Brahma, went to Shiva and Vishnu and told them how Mahisha had taken over the duties of the Sun, Indra, Agni, Vayu, the Moon, Yama, Varuna and the others, and had driven the gods out of heaven to wander the earth like mortals; they asked for a way to kill him. Hearing this, Vishnu and Shiva frowned in anger, and a great light (tejas) came out of the faces of Vishnu, Brahma and Shiva and the bodies of Indra and the other gods. It joined into one blazing mass like a mountain and became a woman whose light filled the three worlds. Shiva's light became her face, Yama's her hair, Vishnu's her arms, the Moon's her breasts, Indra's her waist, Varuna's her legs and thighs, Earth's her hips, Brahma's her feet, the Sun's her toes, the Vasus' her fingers, Kubera's her nose, Prajapati's her teeth, Agni's her three eyes, the two twilights' her brows and Vayu's her ears. The gods gave her their weapons: Shiva a trident, Vishnu a discus, Varuna a conch, Agni a spear, Vayu a bow and quivers, Indra a thunderbolt and a bell from his elephant Airavata, Yama a staff, Varuna a noose, Brahma a rosary and water pot, the Sun his rays, Time a sword and shield, the Milk Ocean a necklace, clothes and ornaments, Vishvakarma an axe and armour, the ocean lotus garlands, the Himalaya a lion to ride and jewels, Kubera a cup full of wine, and Shesha a serpent necklace. Honoured with these, she roared and laughed again and again; the worlds shook, the seas trembled and the mountains moved, while the gods cried 'Victory' and the sages praised her. The demons armed themselves, and Mahishasura ran towards the sound and saw the goddess filling the three worlds, her feet pressing the earth, her crown touching the sky, her thousand arms covering all directions. The battle began. Mahisha's general Chikshura, Chamara, Udagra, Mahahanu, Asiloma, Bashkala, Ugradarshana, Bidalaksha, Kala and others fought her with vast numbers of chariots, elephants and horses, and Mahisha himself with countless thousands. She cut their weapons easily and rained her own on them; her lion moved through the army like fire through a forest; from her breath came hundreds of thousands of attendants (ganas) who fought and played drums and conches. With trident, club, spear, sword, bell and noose she cut, crushed and pierced the demons; headless bodies rose and kept fighting or danced to the music, rivers of blood flowed, and in a moment Ambika destroyed the great army as fire burns a heap of grass and wood, while the gods rained flowers from the sky.

083.json.summary: The sage tells King Suratha how Mahishasura himself was killed. Seeing his army being destroyed, the general Chikshura attacked Ambika with a rain of arrows; she cut them easily, killed his horses and charioteer, broke his bow and banner and wounded him. He ran at her with sword and shield, struck the lion on the head and the goddess on her left arm, but his sword shattered; his blazing trident, thrown at Bhadrakali, she broke into a hundred pieces with her own trident and killed him. Chamara came on an elephant; his spear fell powerless at her shout of 'hum', she cut his trident with arrows, and the lion leapt onto the elephant, wrestled with him and tore off his head. Udagra was killed with stones and trees, Karala with teeth and fists; she crushed Uddhata with her club, killed Bashkala with a dart, Tamra and Andhaka with arrows, Ugrasya, Ugravirya and Mahahanu with her trident, Bidala with her sword, Durdhara and Durmukha with arrows, Kala with the staff of death, and Ugradarshana and Asiloma with her sword. As his army was wiped out, Mahishasura took his buffalo form and scattered her attendants with his muzzle, hooves, tail, horns, roar and breath, then rushed to kill her lion. In his rage the earth cracked under his hooves, his tail made the ocean flood, his horns tore the clouds and mountains fell from the sky at his breath. Chandika threw her noose and bound him; he left the buffalo form and became a lion; as she cut its head he became a man with a sword; she shot him down and he became a great elephant that dragged her lion with its trunk; she cut off the trunk, and he became a buffalo again and shook the three worlds. Angry, the Mother of the world drank the finest drink again and again and laughed with red eyes, while he roared and hurled mountains with his horns, which she smashed with arrows. She said: 'Roar, roar for a moment, fool, while I drink this honey; when I have killed you here the gods will soon roar.' She leapt onto him, pressed his neck with her foot and struck him with her trident; half-emerged from his own mouth and held by her power, he still fought, and she cut off his head with her great sword and threw him down. So Mahisha, with his army and friends, was destroyed; all beings cried 'Victory', the demon army fled crying, the gods rejoiced and praised her with the great sages, the gandharvas sang and the apsaras danced.

084.json.summary: After Mahishasura is killed, Indra and the gods, bowing low with joy, praise the goddess (this hymn is often called the Shakrādi Stuti). She spreads through the world by her own power and is the united power of all the gods; even Vishnu, Brahma and Shiva cannot describe her strength. She is fortune (Shri) in the homes of the good and misfortune in the homes of the wicked, intelligence in the wise, faith in the good and modesty in the well born. Though made of the three qualities, she is the cause of all worlds, unknown even to Vishnu and Shiva, the first and highest Nature (Prakriti). She is Svaha, by which the gods are fed in sacrifices, and Svadha, by which the ancestors are fed; she is the highest knowledge practised by sages seeking freedom, the three Vedas, the means of living (varta), wisdom (Medha), Durga the boat across the hard ocean of worldly life, Shri who lives in Vishnu's heart, and Gauri who lives with Shiva. The gods marvel that Mahisha, seeing her lovely moon-like face, still struck it, and that seeing her face angry he did not die at once. Those she favours are honoured, wealthy, famous and righteous; when remembered she removes fear and gives good thoughts; she removes poverty, pain and fear. She kills the wicked so the world may be happy and so that they, dying in battle, go to heaven instead of hell; that is why she uses weapons instead of burning them with a look; even with enemies her mercy is shown. They ask her to protect them with her trident, sword, bell and the twang of her bow, in the east, west, south and north, with her gentle and her fearful forms and all the weapons in her hands. Worshipped with flowers from the Nandana garden, perfumes and incense, the goddess, pleased, offers the gods a boon. They say all is done since their enemy is dead, but ask that whenever they remember her she will remove their great troubles, and that she will be pleased with any mortal who praises her with these hymns and increase his wealth, family and fortune. Saying 'So be it', Bhadrakali vanished. The sage says he has told how she arose from the bodies of the gods, and will now tell how she arose again from the body of Gauri to kill the wicked demons Shumbha and Nishumbha and to protect the worlds.

085.json.summary: The sage tells how, long ago, the proud and mighty demons Shumbha and Nishumbha took the three worlds and the sacrificial shares from Indra, and took over the offices of the Sun, Moon, Kubera, Yama, Varuna, Vayu and Agni, driving the gods out. Remembering the goddess's promise to destroy their troubles whenever they called on her, the gods went to the Himalaya and praised Vishnu's Maya. Their hymn bows again and again to the goddess, the great goddess, Shiva's consort, Nature, the gentle one, the fierce one, Gauri, the support of the world, Durga who takes one across difficulties, the very gentle and the very fierce; then, in its famous refrain, it bows 'to her, to her, to her, again and again' as the goddess who is present in all beings as Vishnu's Maya, as consciousness, intelligence, sleep, hunger, shadow, power, thirst, patience, birth, modesty, peace, faith, beauty, fortune, steadiness, livelihood, memory, compassion, right conduct, contentment, nourishment, mother and error, who rules the senses and pervades all beings, and who fills the whole world as pure consciousness. They ask her to bring them good and destroy their troubles. While they were praising, Parvati came to bathe in the Ganga and asked whom they were praising; from the sheath of her body came the auspicious goddess, who said the hymn was for her, sung by the gods driven out by Shumbha and defeated by Nishumbha. Because she came out of Parvati's body-sheath (kosha) she is called Kaushiki, and Parvati, left dark, became Kalika, living in the Himalaya. Chanda and Munda, servants of Shumbha and Nishumbha, saw Ambika in her most beautiful form and told Shumbha that a woman lighting up the Himalaya, a jewel among women, was there; since he already owned all the jewels of the three worlds (Indra's elephant Airavata, the Parijata tree, the horse Uchchaihshravas, Brahma's swan chariot, Kubera's treasure, Varuna's umbrella and noose, Death's spear, clothes purified by Agni and more), why should he not take her too? Shumbha sent the messenger Sugriva, who told her sweetly that Shumbha, lord of the three worlds, who enjoys all the best things, invited her to marry him or his brother Nishumbha and gain great wealth. Smiling, the goddess said this was true, but she had once foolishly made a vow: only one who beats her in battle, removes her pride and equals her in strength will be her husband; so let Shumbha or Nishumbha come, defeat her and take her hand. The messenger called her proud: how could a single woman face those whom Indra and all the gods could not, and warned that she would be dragged by the hair. She answered that they are indeed strong, but her vow was made without thought and cannot be broken; let him report her words to the demon king and let him do what is right.

086.json.summary: The angry messenger told the demon king everything the goddess had said. Shumbha in a rage ordered the demon chief Dhumralochana to take his army and bring her by force, dragging her by the hair, and to kill anyone, god, yaksha or gandharva, who tried to protect her. Dhumralochana went quickly with sixty thousand demons, saw the goddess on the snowy mountain and shouted that she must come to Shumbha and Nishumbha willingly or he would drag her there by the hair. The goddess said that if he, a strong warrior sent by the demon king with an army, takes her by force, what can she do to him? He rushed at her, and Ambika burned him to ashes with just the sound 'hum'. She then showered the angry demon army with sharp arrows, spears and axes, and her lion, shaking its mane and roaring fearfully, fell on the army, killing demons with blows of its paws, with its mouth and by trampling them, tearing open their bellies with its claws, cutting off heads and arms, and drinking blood; in a moment the whole army was destroyed. Hearing that Dhumralochana and his army had been killed by the goddess and her lion, Shumbha, his lip trembling with anger, ordered the great demons Chanda and Munda to go with a large army and bring her quickly, by the hair or bound; and if there was any doubt in the fight, to kill her and her lion with all their weapons, then come back.

087.json.summary: Ordered by Shumbha, the demons led by Chanda and Munda marched with a full army of four divisions and saw the goddess smiling, seated on her lion on a great golden peak of the Himalaya. When they tried to seize her, some with drawn bows and swords, Ambika grew very angry and her face turned black as ink. From her frowning forehead came Kali, with a terrible face, holding a sword and noose and a strange skull-topped staff (khatvanga), wearing a garland of human heads and a tiger skin, dreadful with dried flesh, with a huge mouth, lolling tongue, sunken red eyes and a roar that filled all directions. She fell on the demon army and ate it: with one hand she threw elephants into her mouth with their riders and bells, and chewed up warriors with their horses and chariots with their drivers; she seized some by the hair or neck, trampled others and crushed others with her chest; she caught their weapons in her mouth and ground them with her teeth. In a moment the army was destroyed. Chanda covered her with terrible arrows and Munda hurled thousands of discuses, which entering her mouth looked like many suns entering a cloud. Kali laughed fearfully, mounted her great lion, ran at Chanda, seized him by the hair and cut off his head with her sword; Munda rushed at her and she struck him down too, and the rest of the army fled in fear. Kali took the heads of Chanda and Munda to Chandika and said with loud laughter: 'I have brought you these two great beasts as an offering in the sacrifice of battle; Shumbha and Nishumbha you will kill yourself.' Chandika said that since she had brought Chanda and Munda, she will be famous in the world as Chamunda.

088.json.summary: After Chanda and Munda were killed and much of his army destroyed, Shumbha in a rage ordered all his forces out: the eighty-six Udayudha chiefs, the eighty-four Kambus, fifty clans of Kotiviryas, a hundred clans of Dhaumras, and the Kalakas, Daurhridas, Mauryas and Kalakeyas; he himself marched out with many thousands. Chandika filled earth and sky with the twang of her bow, the lion roared, Ambika rang her bell, and Kali, opening her mouth wide, roared louder still; the angry demons surrounded them on all sides. Then, for the destruction of the demons and the good of the gods, the powers (shaktis) of Brahma, Shiva, Skanda, Vishnu and Indra came out of their bodies in the same form, ornaments and mounts as their gods: Brahmani on a swan chariot with rosary and water pot, Maheshvari on a bull with trident, snake bracelets and the crescent moon, Kaumari on a peacock with a spear, Vaishnavi on Garuda with conch, discus, club, bow and sword, Varahi in the boar form, Narasimhi in the man-lion form scattering the stars with her mane, and Aindri on the king of elephants with the thunderbolt and a thousand eyes. Shiva, surrounded by them, told Chandika to kill the demons quickly. From the goddess's body came the fierce power of Chandika, howling like a hundred jackals, who sent Shiva himself as her messenger to tell Shumbha and Nishumbha: let Indra have the three worlds and the gods their offerings, and go to the underworld if you want to live; if you want battle, come and let my jackals feed on your flesh. Because she sent Shiva as messenger she is known as Shivaduti. The angry demons attacked Katyayani with arrows and spears; she cut them with her arrows, while Kali tore enemies with her trident and staff, Brahmani robbed them of strength by sprinkling water from her pot, Maheshvari, Vaishnavi, Kaumari and Aindri killed them with trident, discus, spear and thunderbolt, Varahi with snout, tusks and discus, Narasimhi with her claws, and Shivaduti with her laughter, eating those who fell. As the demons fled, the great demon Raktabija came to fight: from every drop of his blood that fell on the ground rose a demon as large as he was. When Aindri struck him with her thunderbolt, warriors like him rose from his blood; when Vaishnavi's discus, Kaumari's spear, Varahi's sword and Maheshvari's trident struck him, thousands more filled the world, and the gods were terrified. Chandika told Kali (Chamunda) to open her mouth wide, catch the blood and eat the demons born from it, so that Raktabija would run out of blood. The goddess struck him with her trident while Kali drank his blood; his club did not even hurt Chandika; Chamunda ate the demons that sprang up in her mouth, and the goddess killed the bloodless Raktabija with trident, discus, arrows and swords. The gods were overjoyed and the band of Mothers danced, drunk with blood.

089.json.summary: King Suratha asks what Shumbha and the very angry Nishumbha did after Raktabija was killed. The sage says both were furious; Nishumbha rushed at the goddess with the best of the demon army, and Shumbha came too with his forces. Shumbha and Nishumbha fought her, raining arrows like two clouds; Chandika cut their arrows and wounded them. Nishumbha struck her lion on the head with sword and shield (the text repeats this verse twice); when she cut his sword and shield, he threw a spear, which she split with her discus; his trident she crushed with her fist, his club her trident burned to ashes, and as he came with an axe she brought him down with arrows. Seeing his brother fall, Shumbha came in his chariot with eight huge arms holding weapons, filling the sky. The goddess blew her conch, twanged her bow and rang her bell, which destroyed the strength of the demons; the lion roared, Kali leapt up and struck the earth with her hands, and Shivaduti laughed fearfully, so that the demons trembled. When Ambika said 'Stop, wicked one', the gods in the sky cried 'Victory'. Shumbha's flaming spear she struck down with a great fiery missile; their arrows cut each other by hundreds and thousands; then she struck Shumbha with her trident and he fell unconscious. Nishumbha recovered, shot at the goddess, Kali and the lion, made ten thousand arms and covered Chandika with discuses; Durga cut them all. He ran at her with a club, which she cut with her sword, then with a trident; she pierced his heart with her trident, and out of his heart came another mighty man crying 'Stop!'; laughing, she cut off his head and he fell. The lion ate demons, crushing their necks with its teeth, as did Kali and Shivaduti; others were killed by Kaumari's spear, driven off by Brahmani's water purified with mantras, pierced by Maheshvari's trident, crushed by Varahi's snout, cut to pieces by Vaishnavi's discus and struck by Aindri's thunderbolt; some died, some fled the battle, and others were eaten by Kali, Shivaduti and the lion.

090.json.summary: Seeing his brother Nishumbha, dear to him as life, killed and his army being destroyed, Shumbha angrily told Durga not to be proud, since she fought relying on the strength of others. The goddess said: 'I alone exist in this world; who else is there besides me? See, wicked one, these powers of mine are entering into me.' Brahmani and all the other goddesses then merged into her body, and Ambika alone remained; she said that she had stood there in many forms through her power, but had now withdrawn them and stood alone, and told him to stand firm. A terrible fight followed between the goddess and Shumbha, watched by gods and demons, with arrows, weapons and divine missiles; she broke his missiles easily with sounds like 'hum'. When he covered her with hundreds of arrows, she cut his bow; she cut the spear in his hand with her discus; as he ran at her with a sword and a shield shining with a hundred moons, she cut both, killed his horses and charioteer and broke his chariot; she cut his iron club with arrows. He still rushed at her with his fist raised and struck her on the chest; she slapped him on the chest and he fell, but rose again, seized her and leapt up into the sky, where she fought him without any support. They wrestled in the sky for a long time, amazing the siddhas and sages; then Ambika lifted him, whirled him round and threw him to the ground. He jumped up and ran at her with his fist raised to kill her, and the goddess pierced his chest with her trident and threw him down. He fell dead, shaking the whole earth with its oceans, islands and mountains. When the wicked one was dead the whole world became calm and well, the sky became clear, the clouds of bad omen and the meteors stopped, the rivers flowed in their courses, the gods were filled with joy, the gandharvas sang sweetly, others played music and the apsaras danced, pure winds blew, the sun shone brightly, and the sacred fires burned calmly. (The last verse is incomplete in this text.)

091.json.summary: When the great demon king was killed, the gods led by Agni and Indra, their faces bright with joy, praised Katyayani (this hymn is known as the Narayani Stuti). They ask the goddess, who removes the pain of those who come to her, to be pleased and protect the world: she alone is its support as the earth and nourishes it as water; she is Vishnu's power of endless strength, the seed of the world and the highest Maya, who deludes all and, when pleased, gives freedom; all forms of knowledge and all women in the world are parts of her. Each verse then ends 'O Narayani, salutation to you': to her who lives as intelligence in every heart and gives heaven and freedom, who brings change through the divisions of time, the most auspicious of all auspicious things, the power of creation, keeping and destruction, the refuge of the helpless; and to her forms as Brahmani on the swan chariot sprinkling holy kusha water, Maheshvari with trident, moon and snake on a great bull, Kaumari with peacock, cock and spear, Vaishnavi with conch, discus, club and bow, Varahi lifting the earth on her tusk, Narasimhi, Aindri with crown and thunderbolt who took Vritra's life, Shivaduti with her great roar, and Chamunda with terrible teeth and a garland of heads; and to her as Lakshmi, modesty, great knowledge, faith, nourishment, Svadha, the great night, the great illusion, wisdom and Sarasvati, with hands, feet, eyes, heads and ears on every side. They pray to Durga to protect them from fear, and that her gentle three-eyed face, her flaming trident, her bell which destroys the demons' strength, and her sword smeared with demon blood protect them. When pleased she removes all disease, when angry she destroys all hopes; those who take refuge in her meet no disaster and become a refuge for others. Who but she could have destroyed the demons by making herself into many forms? She guards the world among demons, poisonous snakes, enemies, robbers, forest fires and the open sea. They ask her to protect them always, as she did now, and to remove the sins of the world and the great troubles caused by evil omens. The goddess offers a boon, and the gods ask that she always remove the troubles of the three worlds and destroy their enemies. She then foretells her future appearances: in the twenty-eighth age of the Vaivasvata period, when two other demons named Shumbha and Nishumbha are born, she will be born from Yashoda in the house of Nandagopa, live on the Vindhya mountain and kill them; in a very fierce form she will kill the Vaiprachitta demons and her teeth will become red as pomegranate flowers, so she will be called Raktadantika; after a hundred-year drought she will be born, not from a womb, and look on the sages with a hundred eyes, and be called Shatakshi; she will feed the world with life-giving vegetables grown from her own body until the rain comes and be called Shakambhari, and there she will kill the demon Durgama and be called Durga; taking a terrible form on the Himalaya she will eat demons to protect the sages and be called Bhima; and when the demon Aruna troubles the three worlds she will take the form of countless bees and kill him, and be called Bhramari. Whenever trouble arises from demons, she will come down and destroy the enemies.

092.json.summary: The goddess tells the gods the rewards of reciting her story. Whoever praises her daily with these hymns with a focused mind, she will free from all trouble. Those who recite with devotion the killing of Madhu and Kaitabha, of Mahishasura and of Shumbha and Nishumbha, on the eighth, ninth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight, will have no sin or disaster from sin, no poverty, no separation from loved ones, and no fear from enemies, robbers, kings, weapons, fire or floods. So this story of her greatness should be read and heard with devotion; it calms all troubles from epidemics and the three kinds of evil omen. She will never leave the temple where it is properly recited daily; it should be recited at offerings, worship, fire rites and festivals, and she will accept with love worship and fire offerings made with or without knowledge. At the great yearly worship in autumn, one who hears it with devotion will by her grace be free of all trouble and gain wealth and grain. Hearing it, a man becomes fearless, enemies perish, good fortune comes and the family prospers. It should be heard in all rites for peace, after bad dreams and in severe troubles from the planets; troubles and planetary afflictions are calmed and bad dreams become good. It calms children seized by child-seizing spirits (bala-graha), brings friendship where people have fallen out, weakens all wicked people and destroys demons, ghosts and goblins just by being read. Hearing it once pleases her as much as a year of worship with animal offerings, flowers, water offerings, incense, perfumes, lamps, feeding Brahmins, gold and other gifts. Hearing the story of her births removes sins, gives health and protects from evil beings; hearing of her battles removes fear of enemies; the hymns of the gods, of the Brahmin sages and of Brahma give a good end. A person caught in a forest fire, surrounded by robbers in a lonely place, seized by enemies, chased by lions, tigers or wild elephants, sentenced to death or imprisoned by an angry king, tossed by wind on a ship at sea, under falling weapons in battle, or in any terrible trouble or pain, is freed by remembering her story, and lions, robbers and enemies run away. The sage says the fierce goddess Chandika then vanished before the gods' eyes; the gods, free of fear, took back their offices and their shares of sacrifice, and the surviving demons went to the underworld. Though eternal, she appears again and again to protect the world; she deludes the world and gives birth to it; when asked she gives knowledge and when pleased, prosperity. She fills the universe as Mahakali at the time of destruction; she is the great plague in time, and also creation and the keeping of beings; in good times she is Lakshmi bringing growth to the home, and in bad times misfortune (Alakshmi) bringing ruin. Praised and worshipped with flowers, incense and perfumes, she gives wealth, sons, a mind set on dharma and a good end.

093.json.summary: The sage ends the story of the goddess's greatness for King Suratha: such is the power of the goddess who upholds this world; by Vishnu's Maya the king, the merchant and other wise people are deluded, have been deluded and will be deluded. He tells the king to take refuge in this highest goddess, who when worshipped gives enjoyment, heaven and final freedom. Markandeya says that, hearing this, King Suratha, tired of his strong attachment and of the loss of his kingdom, bowed to the sage and went at once to do penance, and so did the merchant. To see the Mother, they stayed on a river bank, where the merchant chanted the highest hymn to the goddess (Devi Sukta). They made a clay image of the goddess on the river bank and worshipped it with flowers, incense, fire offerings and water offerings; fasting, with controlled and fixed minds, they also gave her offerings sprinkled with blood from their own bodies. After three years of such worship, Chandika, the upholder of the world, appeared before them pleased and offered whatever they wished. The king chose a kingdom that would not be lost in another life, and in this life his own kingdom back, won by force after destroying his enemies' power. The merchant, whose mind had turned away from the world, chose the knowledge that removes the attachment of 'mine' and 'I'. The goddess told the king that in a few days he would regain his kingdom by killing his enemies and it would stay secure; and that after death he would be born again from the Sun god (this verse is incomplete in the text). To the merchant she gave the knowledge he wanted, for his final success. Having given both their wishes, and praised by them with devotion, she vanished. So, having received the goddess's boon, Suratha, the best of kshatriyas, will be born from the Sun and become the Manu Savarni.

094.json.summary: Markandeya continues the story of Ruchi and the ancestors (pitris). (The file opens with the closing line of the previous chapter, 'the chapter called the praise of the ancestors, the ninety-third'.) As Ruchi was praising them, a towering mass of light suddenly appeared, filling the sky. Seeing this great light covering the world, Ruchi knelt on the ground and sang another hymn. He bows always to the ancestors, with form and without form, of blazing light, meditative and with divine sight; to those who are the leaders of Indra and the other gods, of Daksha and Marichi, of the seven sages and others, who grant wishes; to the ancestors of Manu and the great sages, of the sun and moon, those in the oceans, of the stars and planets, of wind, fire and sky, of heaven and earth; to those honoured by the divine sages and all worlds, who always give unfailing gifts; to Prajapati, Kashyapa, Soma, Varuna and the lords of yoga; to the seven groups (ganas) of ancestors in the seven worlds; to self-born Brahma whose eye is yoga; to the ancestor groups who rest on Soma and bear forms of yoga, and to Soma, the father of the worlds; to the other ancestors who have the form of fire, since this whole universe is made of Agni and Soma; to those in light, whose forms are moon, sun and fire, who are the form of the world and of Brahman. With a controlled mind he bows to all these yogi ancestors again and again and asks them, the eaters of svadha, to be gracious. So praised, the ancestors came out of the light, lighting up the ten directions, adorned with the flowers, perfumes and ointments he had offered, and stood before him. He bowed to them with devotion and said 'Bow to you' to each one separately. Pleased, they told him to choose a boon. With bowed head he said Brahma had now ordered him to create, so he wanted a blessed, divine wife able to bear children. They granted that he would at once have a very lovely wife, and by her a son, a great Manu, wise, lord of a Manu period, known by his father's name as Raucya in the three worlds; that Manu would have many mighty sons who would rule the earth; and Ruchi himself, after becoming a Prajapati, creating the four kinds of beings and finishing his task, would reach perfection (siddhi). They add that whoever praises them with devotion by this hymn will receive from them enjoyments, the highest self-knowledge, bodily health, wealth, sons and grandsons and whatever else he wants; so people wanting merit and lasting satisfaction for the ancestors should praise them with it. If at a shraddha (rite for the dead) it is recited with devotion by someone standing before the eating Brahmins, the ancestors, pleased by hearing it, will be present, and the shraddha becomes unfailing, even if it is done without a Veda-learned Brahmin, is spoiled, is done with wealth wrongly gained or in a wrong way, with unfit or spoiled offerings, at the wrong time or place, without the rules, without faith or out of show. Where it is read at a shraddha, their satisfaction lasts twelve years; in the cool season (hemanta) twelve years, in the late winter (shishira) twice that, in spring sixteen years, in summer sixteen, in the rains unfailing satisfaction even if the rite was incomplete, and in autumn fifteen years. In a house where it is kept written down, they will be present whenever a shraddha is done. So Ruchi should have it heard before the Brahmins as they eat at a shraddha, for it nourishes the ancestors. Having said this, the ancestors went to heaven.

095.json.summary: Markandeya tells Kraushtuki that, after the ancestors left, a lovely, slender apsaras named Pramlocha rose from the middle of the river nearby. Bowing modestly, she spoke sweetly to the great Ruchi: she had a very beautiful daughter, born to her from Pushkara, the great son of Varuna; she offered this girl to him as his wife, and by her he would have a son, a wise Manu. Ruchi agreed, and she brought out of the water the lovely girl named Malini. On the bank of the river Ruchi called the great sages and took her hand in marriage by the proper rite. By her he had a son of great strength and wisdom, known on earth by his father's name as Raucya. The gods, seven sages, sons and kings of his Manu period have already been told. When this Manu period is heard, people surely gain growth in dharma, health, wealth, grain and sons; and one who hears the hymn to the ancestors and the groups of ancestors gains all desires by their grace.

096.json.summary: Markandeya now begins the birth of the Manu Bhautya, with the gods, sages, sons and kings of his period. Bhuti, a disciple of Angiras, was a sage who was very quick to anger, gave fierce curses for small faults, and spoke harshly. Out of fear of him, the wind did not blow hard at his hermitage, the sun did not burn too much, the rain-god did not make much mud, the full moon did not make it too cold; the seasons gave up their order and the trees of the hermitage gave flowers and fruit at all times at his command, and waters flowed as he wished, even those in his water pot. He could not bear much hardship and was very irritable. Having no son, he turned his mind to penance, fasting and exposed to cold, wind and fire to gain a son; but the moon, the sun and the wind did not trouble him much, and, troubled by the pairs of opposites, he gave up the penance without gaining his wish. His brother Suvarcha invited him to a sacrifice. Before going, he told his disciple Shanti, a calm, self-controlled, humble and well-behaved sage, always busy in serving his teacher, that while he was away Shanti must watch over the sacred fire in the hermitage with great care so that it never went out. Shanti agreed, and the teacher went to his younger brother's sacrifice. While Shanti was bringing fuel, flowers and fruit from the forest for his teacher and doing other service, Bhuti's fire went out. Seeing it, Shanti was very upset and afraid, and thought: what should he do? If his teacher saw the fire-place without fire, he would put him in terrible trouble; if he put another fire in its place, his teacher, who sees everything directly, would burn him to ashes; he grieved less for himself than for the sin of making his teacher angry and causing a curse; a teacher whom even the gods fear would surely not spare him. After much thought he took refuge with Agni (Jatavedas) and, kneeling, with folded hands and a focused mind, sang a hymn to the seven-flamed god. The hymn bows to Agni, the means of all beings, who has one, two and five fire-places and is sixfold in the Rajasuya; who gives all the gods their living; who is the mouth of all the gods, so that through the offerings he receives all gods are pleased and live by him. The offering poured into him becomes cloud, then water, from which all plants grow, on which all creatures live and with which men perform sacrifices that nourish gods, daityas and rakshasas; so he is the source of all and made of all; all beings, from gods to trees, birds and reptiles, are fed and grow by him, arise from him and dissolve in him. He creates the waters and consumes them again, and cooked by him they nourish beings. He is brightness in the gods, beauty in the siddhas, poison in snakes, wind in birds, anger in humans, delusion in birds and beasts, firmness in trees, hardness in earth, fluidity in water, speed in the wind, and pervasion in the sky; he moves within all beings, protecting them. Poets call him one and threefold, and imagining him eightfold made him the carrier of the sacrifice; the great sages say he created the universe and without him it would at once perish. Brahmins who worship him reach the goal their duty brings, with offerings to gods and ancestors and the calls svadha and svaha. He is the purifier and digester of all that is eaten and drunk, the ripener of crops, the cloud, the wind, the seed, past, present and future, the light in all beings, the sun, day, night and both twilights, Hiranyaretas, Hiranyagarbha, and time in all its units, from the muhurta down to the truti and lava. Then come seven prayers, each ending 'with it protect us from sins and from great fear in this world', to his seven tongues: Kali, which ends time; Karali, the cause of the great dissolution; Manojava, marked by lightness; Sulohita, which fulfils the wishes of beings; Sudhumravarna, which gives disease to creatures; Sphulingini, from which all bodies come; and the tongue of the creator of the world (Vishvasrij), which gives creatures comfort. He asks the tawny-eyed, red-necked god with a black path to save him from all faults and lift him from the round of births, calls him by many names, and in the final verses, in longer metres, praises him as the highest truth dwelling in the heart-lotus of all beings, the submarine fire (vadava) drinking the ocean's waters, worshipped by great sages in sacrifices, drinker of Soma, sung in all branches of the Veda, and the one through whose offerings Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva, Indra, Aryaman, Varuna, the sun, moon and all gods and asuras gain their wishes; all that is defiled becomes pure at the touch of his flames, and bathing with his ash is the highest bath. He ends by asking Agni, named Shuchi, bright as lightning, to be gracious and to protect him with his kind form and seven flames, as a father protects his son.

097.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Praised in this way, Agni appeared before Shanti, his body wrapped in garlands of flame, and, pleased with the hymn, told him in a voice deep as thunder to ask a boon. Shanti said he had already gained his aim in seeing Agni in bodily form, but asked: his teacher had gone to his brother's sacrifice; when he returns, may he see his fire-place, abandoned through Shanti's fault, occupied by Agni as before. And if Agni would grant more: may his sonless teacher have an excellent son; may his teacher feel friendship for that son and be gentle in mind toward all beings; and may Agni grant boons to whoever praises him with this hymn. Agni, pleased by the hymn and by his devotion to his teacher, said that since Shanti had asked both boons for his teacher and not for himself, he was very pleased with him. All he asked would happen: his teacher would have friendship toward all beings and a son, named Bhautya, very strong, brave and wise, who would rule a Manu period. Whoever praises him with this hymn with a focused mind will gain all he wishes and merit. Read for dharma at sacrifices, at the parva days, at holy places, in worship and fire offerings, it nourishes him greatly; heard once, it destroys the sins of a day and night; heard, it at once removes the faults of fire offerings done at the wrong time or by unfit people; heard on full-moon, new-moon and other parva days, it destroys sin. Then Agni vanished at once, like a lamp flame going out. Shanti, delighted, with hair standing on end, entered his teacher's hermitage and saw the fire blazing in the fire-place as before. Just then his teacher returned from his younger brother's sacrifice. Shanti bowed at his feet, and the teacher, seated and honoured, said: 'Child, I feel great love for you and for other beings; I do not know why; if you know, tell me quickly.' Shanti told him everything, from the fire going out onwards. Hearing it, the teacher embraced him with tearful eyes and gave him the Vedas with all their branches and sub-branches. Bhuti's son was born, the Manu named Bhautya. In his period the gods will be five groups: the Chakshushas, Kanishthas, Pavitras, Bhrajiras and Dharavrikas; their Indra will be Shuchi, very strong and with all the qualities of an Indra; the seven sages will be Agnidhra, Agnibahu, Shuchi, Mukta, Madhava, Shukra and Ajita; and the Manu's sons will be Guru, Gabhira, Bradhna, Bharata, Anugraha, Shrimani, Pratira, Vishnu, Sankrandana, Tejasvi and Subala. This, Markandeya says, is the fourteenth Manu period. He then lists the fruits of hearing each period: the first brings dharma; Svarochisha, all desires; Auttama, wealth; Tamasa, knowledge; Raivata, intelligence and a beautiful wife; Chakshusha, health; Vaivasvata, strength; Surya-Savarnika, virtuous sons and grandsons; Brahma-Savarni, greatness; Dharma-Savarnika, a good mind; Rudra-Savarnika, victory; Daksha-Savarnika, being the best among one's kin and full of virtues; Raucya, the power to destroy enemy armies; and Bhautya, the grace of the gods, the sacred fire (agnihotra) and virtuous sons. One who hears all the periods in order, with their gods, sages, Indras, Manus, sons, kings and family lines, is freed from all sins; the gods, sages, Indras and kings of those periods are pleased and give him a good mind, by which he does good deeds and reaches a good state as long as the fourteen Indras last; and for one who hears the periods in order, all seasons become safe and all planets kind.

098.json.summary: Kraushtuki says Markandeya has fully explained the Manu periods, and now asks to hear the whole line of kings from Brahma on. Markandeya says he will tell the origin and deeds of all the kings, starting from Prajapati, the root of the world. This line is adorned by hundreds of kings who performed many sacrifices, won battles and knew dharma, such as Manu, Ikshvaku, Anaranya and Bhagiratha; hearing of their births and deeds frees a person from all sins; from it thousands of royal lines branch out like the hanging roots of a banyan tree. Brahma, wishing to create various beings, created Daksha from his right thumb and Daksha's wife from his left thumb. Daksha's lovely daughter was Aditi, and on her Kashyapa fathered the god Martanda (the Sun). He is Brahma's own form, the giver of boons to all worlds, the beginning, middle and end in creation, preservation and destruction, from whom and in whom all this exists, whose form is this world of gods, asuras and humans, the self of all beings, the eternal Supreme Self; he, the shining one, was born from Aditi after she worshipped him. Kraushtuki asks about the nature of Vivasvat (the Sun), why the first god became the son of Kashyapa, how Aditi and Kashyapa worshipped him, what he said when worshipped, and the power of his incarnation. Markandeya says the forms of the formless shining Sun are these: clear supreme knowledge (vidya), eternal light, aloneness (kaivalya), knowledge, manifestation, freedom of will, awareness, understanding, comprehension, memory and discernment. He then tells how the Sun appeared. When all was without light, dark and covered on every side, there arose a single great egg, the imperishable supreme cause. Brahma, the great-grandfather, born from the lotus, the creator and lord of the worlds, who was inside it, broke it open. From his mouth came the great sound Om; then Bhuh, then Bhuvah, then Svah. These three utterances (vyahritis) are the form of Vivasvat; Om is the Sun's subtle, highest form. From it come Mahah, the gross, then Janah, grosser still, then Tapah and Satya: so his embodied forms stand in seven. These forms exist and do not exist, as they come and go between being and not being. That beginning and end which is the highest, subtle, formless and supreme, called Om, is the supreme Brahman, his true body.

099.json.summary: Markandeya continues telling Kraushtuki how the Sun appeared. When the egg split, from the first (eastern) mouth of Brahma, whose birth is unmanifest, came the Rig verses, red like the japa flower, made of light, loose and separate, carrying the nature of rajas. From the southern mouth came the Yajus formulas, unchecked, of many colours and also unjoined. From the western mouth of Brahma came the Saman chants with their metres. From the northern mouth came the whole Atharva Veda, dark like a mass of bees or collyrium, with fierce forms, used both for harmful magic (abhichara) and for peace rites, mostly of joy, sattva and tamas, both gentle and harsh. The text says the Rig verses have rajas, the Yajus sattva, the Samans tamas, and the Atharva tamas and sattva. Blazing with matchless light, these at first stood apart. Then the first light, called Om, by its nature surrounded that light; the light of the Rig, Yajus and Saman became one in that supreme light, and the three kinds of rites, for peace (shantika), for prosperity (paushtika) and for harm (abhicharika), merged into the three Vedas. At once, darkness destroyed, the whole universe became clear and visible, across, above and below. Then that supreme light of the Vedic metres, formed into a disc and united with the highest light, took the name Aditya, because it existed at the beginning (adau); it is the imperishable cause of this universe. The three Vedas (trayi), called Rig, Yajus and Saman, blaze at morning, noon and afternoon: the Rig verses in the forenoon, the Yajus at midday, the Samans in the afternoon. Peace rites are set in the Rig in the forenoon, prosperity rites in the Yajus, and harmful rites in the Saman in the evening; rites for the ancestors in the afternoon are done with the Saman (the verse on midday and afternoon is not fully clear). In creation Brahma is made of the Rig, in preservation Vishnu is made of the Yajus, and at the end Rudra is made of the Saman, so its sound is impure. So the shining Lord is the self of the Vedas, rests in the Vedas, is made of Vedic knowledge, and is called the Supreme Person. Eternal, he is the cause of creation, preservation and destruction, and by taking on rajas, sattva and the other qualities he takes the names Brahma, Vishnu and the rest. He is always to be praised by the gods; he is the form of the Vedas yet formless, the first, the form of all mortals, the light that supports the universe, whose nature cannot be known, reached through Vedanta, the supreme lord above all.

100.json.summary: Markandeya continues. As the Sun's light burned above and below, Brahma, born from the lotus, wishing to create, worried: the creation he made would be destroyed by the great heat of the Sun, the cause of creation, preservation and destruction; living beings would lose their breath and the waters would dry up, and without water there could be no creation. So Brahma, grandfather of the worlds, became absorbed in the Sun and sang a hymn to him. He bows to the one of whom all this is made and who is made of all, whose form is the universe, the supreme light on which yogis meditate; who is made of the Rig, the store of the Yajus and the source of the Saman, of unthinkable power, made of the three Vedas, the half-syllable (of Om) in gross form, the supreme form fit to go beyond the qualities; the cause of all, the highest to be known, the first, the supreme light whose form cannot be known, and gross as the self of the gods. Brahma says that when he creates, it is the Sun's first power, urged by him, that creates the world in the form of water, earth, wind and fire, with its gods, objects and all that begins with Om; it is not by Brahma's own will, and the same is true of preservation and dissolution. The Sun is fire; by drying the water he creates the earth and he cooks the worlds; he is the all-pervading sky; in five forms he protects this universe. Those who know the Supreme Self worship him with sacrifices as Vishnu, made of all offerings, and self-controlled ascetics who seek liberation meditate on him as the lord of all. Bowing to him as the form of the gods, of sacrifice and of the supreme Brahman, on whom yogis meditate, Brahma asks him to draw in his light, since Brahma is ready to create. So praised by Brahma the creator, the Sun drew in his light and kept only a little. Then Brahma created the world as in earlier kalpas: gods, asuras and others, humans, animals and others, trees and creepers, and also the hells.

101.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Having created the world, Brahma divided it as before into classes (varnas) and stages of life, seas, mountains and continents, and from the Vedas he made the forms and dwellings of gods, daityas, snakes and others. Brahma's son was the famous Marichi, whose son was Kashyapa. Kashyapa had thirteen wives, daughters of Daksha, and many children: Aditi bore the gods, lords of the three worlds; Diti the daityas; Danu the fierce, mighty danavas; Vinata Garuda and Aruna; Khasa the yakshas and rakshasas; Kadru the nagas; Muni the gandharvas; Krodha the kulyas (as printed); Arishta the apsaras; Ira the elephants such as Airavata; Tamra daughters led by Shyeni, from whom came birds such as hawks, bhasa birds and parrots; Ila the trees; and Pradha the water creatures. The world is filled with the offspring of these sons and daughters. Among Kashyapa's sons the chief were the gods, and the groups were of sattva, rajas and tamas. Brahma made the gods sharers in the sacrifice and lords of the three worlds. But their rivals, the daityas, danavas and rakshasas, attacked them together, and there was a terrible war; for a thousand divine years the gods were defeated, and the strong daityas and danavas won. Seeing her sons driven out, the three worlds taken and their shares of the sacrifice cut off, Aditi, deeply grieved, made great efforts to worship the Sun (Savitri). With a focused mind, eating little and keeping strict rules, she praised the mass of light in the sky. She bows to his supreme, subtle, golden body, the light of all lights and the support of all lights; to his fierce form that takes up the waters for the good of the worlds; to his very fierce form that over eight months gathers the moon-made essence (rasa); to his form as cloud that releases all that essence as rain; to his form that ripens all the plants born from the rain; to his cool form that gives snow and cold to feed the crops of that season; to his gentle spring form, neither too hot nor too cold; to the form that nourishes all the gods and ancestors and ripens the crops; to his Soma-form, the single nectar that gives life to plants and is drunk by the gods and ancestors; to his universal form joined with Agni and Soma, nourishing and burning; to his form that burns as the union of the Rig, Yajus and Saman, the universe called the three Vedas; and to his higher form called Om, not gross, endless and pure (this verse is marked in the text as spoken by Markandeya, though it continues the hymn). The goddess praised the Sun this way day and night, without food. After a long time the Sun became visible to her in the sky. She saw a great peak of light and said: 'Be gracious; I cannot see you. As before I saw you in the sky, hard to look at, burning, now I see the same mass of light here on earth; be kind, let me see your form; you who pity your devotees, I am your devotee: protect my sons.' She ends with verses in a longer metre: as the creator he makes the universe, he protects it, and at the end it all dissolves into him; there is no other refuge in any world. He is Brahma, Hari, the Unborn, Indra, Kubera, the lord of the ancestors (Yama), the lord of waters, the wind, Soma, Agni, the lord of the sky, the mountain and the ocean; what praise can fit him, the home of all forms? Brahmins devoted to their duties worship him daily with many words, and yogis meditating on him reach the highest state. He burns, cooks, protects and turns to ashes the universe; he reveals it with his rays and delights it with rain-filled clouds; as the lotus-born he creates, as Achyuta he protects, and as Rudra at the end of the age he destroys, he alone.

102.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Then from that light the Sun appeared, glowing like heated copper. As Aditi bowed at the sight of him, he told her to choose whatever boon she wished from him. Bowing her head, with her knees pressed to the ground, she said: the strong daityas and danavas have taken the three worlds and the shares of the sacrifice from her sons; for their sake let him be gracious, take birth with part of himself as their brother and destroy their enemies, so that her sons may again share the sacrifice and rule the three worlds; he is called the remover of the pain of those who take refuge and the one who keeps the world in order. The Sun, gracious, told her he would be born from her womb with a thousandth part of himself and quickly destroy her sons' enemies, and then vanished. Aditi, all her wishes fulfilled, ended her penance. Then, from his thousand rays, the ray of the Sun called Sushumna took birth in the womb of the mother of the gods. With a focused mind she kept hard vows such as krichchhra and chandrayana and carried the divine embryo in purity. Kashyapa, somewhat angry, said to her: why do you kill the embryo (garbhanda) by fasting all the time? She angrily replied: look at this embryo; it is not killed (marita); it will be the death of the enemies. Saying this, the mother of the gods, stung by her husband's words, brought out the embryo, blazing with light. Seeing it shine like the rising sun, Kashyapa bowed and praised it with the first Rig verses. As he praised, the child came out of the egg, coloured like a lotus leaf, his light filling all directions. Then a voice from the sky, deep as a rain cloud, said to Kashyapa: since you called this egg 'killed' (marita), your son will be named Martanda; he will perform the office of the Sun in the world and will kill the asuras, the enemies who took the shares of the sacrifice. Hearing this voice, the gods rejoiced greatly, and the danavas lost their strength. Indra (Shatakratu) joyfully called the daityas to battle with the gods, and the danavas came. There was a terrible war between the gods and the asuras, with weapons and missiles lighting up all the worlds. In that battle the great asuras, looked at by the lord Martanda, were burned by his light and turned to ashes. All the gods, overjoyed, praised Martanda and Aditi; they regained their offices and their shares of the sacrifice as before, and Martanda took up his own office. Like a kadamba flower, with rays going up and down, the Sun took a body like a round ball of fire, not too brilliant.

103.json.summary: Markandeya tells Kraushtuki that Vishvakarma the Prajapati, bowing and seeking the Sun's favour, gave him his daughter Sanjna in marriage, and from her Vivasvat had Vaivasvata Manu, as told before. (An unnumbered verse follows in which Kraushtuki asks to hear again the story of Martanda, which destroys the sins of those who hear it in the Kali age.) Markandeya says the Sun had three children by her: two sons and the daughter Yamuna. The eldest was Vaivasvata Manu, the Shraddhadeva and a Prajapati; then the twins Yama and Yami were born. Martanda's very great brightness scorched the three worlds. Seeing the Sun's ball-shaped form and unable to bear his brightness, Sanjna looked at her shadow (Chhaya) and told her: she would go to her father's house; Chhaya should stay here unchanged at her order, care for the two boys and the lovely girl, and not tell the Lord. Chhaya said she would never tell until seized by the hair or cursed, and told her to go where she wished. Sanjna went to her father's house and stayed for some time; told again and again by her father to go back to her husband, she became a mare and went to the Northern Kurus, where the virtuous woman did penance without food. Chhaya, obedient to Sanjna, took her form and went to the Sun, who, thinking she was Sanjna, had by her two sons and a daughter. The first son was like the elder Manu and so became Savarni; the second became the planet Shanaishchara (Saturn); the daughter, Tapati, was chosen as wife by King Samvarana. Chhaya-Sanjna did not show the elder children the same love as her own; Manu bore this, but Yama did not. Pained by her repeated slights, from anger, from childishness and by the force of what was to be, Yama threatened her with his foot, and she angrily cursed him: since he threatened his father's honoured wife with his foot, that foot would surely fall. Deeply troubled, the righteous Yama, with Manu, told his father everything: their mother did not love them equally, but put the elder ones aside and wanted to favour the younger; he had raised his foot at her but had not brought it down on her body, from childishness or confusion, and his father should forgive this; since his mother cursed her son in anger, he did not think she was really his mother, for a mother is not cruel even to bad sons; he asked his father to find a way, by his grace, that his foot would not fall through this curse. The Sun said there must be a reason why anger entered him, who knew dharma and spoke the truth; there is a remedy for every curse, but never a way to undo a curse from a mother; her word cannot be made false, but out of love he would do him a favour: worms would take flesh from his foot and go to the ground, so her word would come true and he would be saved. The Sun then asked Chhaya why she loved one child more than others who were equal; surely she was not their mother but some other Sanjna who had come, for how could a mother curse her son even if he was bad? She avoided the question and did not tell him, so he looked within by meditation and saw the truth. When he was about to curse her, Chhaya-Sanjna, shaking with fear, told him what had happened. Angry, the Sun went to his father-in-law, who honoured him and calmed him as he was about to burn everything in his rage. Vishvakarma said that the Sun's form, filled with too much brightness, was very hard to bear; unable to bear it, Sanjna was doing penance in the forest; he would see his virtuous wife today, doing great penance in the forest for the sake of his form; recalling Brahma's words, Vishvakarma offered, if the Sun agreed, to make his form pleasing. Since the Sun's form had earlier been perfectly round, the Sun agreed. With his permission, Vishvakarma, in Shaka-dvipa, put the Sun on his lathe (bhrami) to trim his brightness. As the Sun, the centre of all worlds, was turned, the earth with its seas, mountains and forests rose into the sky, and the whole sky with the moon, planets and stars went down, shaken; the oceans spilled their waters, great mountains split with their peaks broken, the stars held by Dhruva (the pole star) fell by thousands as the bonds of their rays snapped, and great clouds, hurled by the wind of the fast turning, burst with terrible roars; the earth, sky and underworld were thrown into great confusion by the Sun's turning. While the three worlds spun, the divine sages and gods with Brahma praised the Sun: he is the first god of the gods, and in creation, preservation and the end he stands in three forms; they wished him well, the maker of dharma, rain and cold, and asked him to bring peace to the worlds. Indra came and praised him as he was being trimmed: 'Victory, O god who pervades the world, lord of all worlds.' The seven sages led by Vasishtha and Atri praised him with many hymns, saying 'Svasti, svasti'; the Valakhilyas joyfully praised him with the foremost Vedic Rig verses: he is the liberation of those seeking liberation, the highest object of the meditators, the refuge of all beings; may there be peace (sham) for all creatures, for two-footed and four-footed beings. The vidyadharas, yakshas, rakshasas and snakes, with joined palms and bowed heads, asked that his brightness become bearable for beings. Haha, Huhu, Narada and Tumburu, skilled in music and the three scales (shadja, madhyama and gandhara), with their modes and melodies, began to sing to him; the apsaras Vishvachi, Ghritachi, Urvashi, Tilottama, Menaka, Sahajanya and Rambha danced with many gestures; flutes, vinas, cymbals, drums of many kinds, divine kettledrums and conches sounded by hundreds and thousands, and all became a great noise. With joined palms, bowed in devotion, all the gods bowed to the thousand-rayed Sun as he was being trimmed, and amid that tumult of the assembled gods Vishvakarma slowly cut down his brightness. Whoever hears this account of the trimming of the body of the Sun, the cause of the seasons of cold, rain and heat, praised by Shiva, Brahma and Vishnu, goes at the end of life to the world of the Sun.

104.json.summary: Markandeya tells Kraushtuki that while the sun was being trimmed down on the lathe, Vishvakarma the Prajapati, his hair standing on end, sang this hymn of praise to Vivasvat. He bows to the sun who is kind to those who bow to him, the great soul with seven swift horses, the bright one who wakes the lotuses and tears away the veil of darkness; to the one whose deeds purify, who grants many wishes and does good to all worlds; to the unborn cause of the three worlds, the soul of beings, lord of rays, most compassionate, the home of the eye's light; to the inner soul without whom there is no knowledge, the support of the world, self-born, the eye of all worlds, of boundless brightness. For a moment he is the jewel on the crest of the eastern mountain, honoured by the gods, and with a body of a thousand rays he shines and drives away darkness. He rides his well-made, beautiful chariot with tireless horses for the good of the world, and with his nectar-like essence he satisfies gods and ancestors. Vishvakarma says that, having bowed to him, he now 'writes' (shapes) the sun's body, and prays to the lord, kind to those who bow, purifier of the three worlds, whose horses are green like a parrot and whose foot-dust is most holy, to protect him. He ends by bowing for ever to the sun, the source of all the world, the one lamp of all the worlds.

105.json.summary: Markandeya continues. While praising the sun, Vishvakarma left in his disc only one sixteenth of his brightness; the fifteen parts he trimmed off made the sun's body most lovely. From the trimmed brightness Vishvakarma made Vishnu's discus, Shiva's trident, Kubera's palanquin, the staff of Yama, lord of the dead, the spear of Skanda, the army chief of the gods, and the weapons of the other gods, to destroy enemies. With his brightness reduced, the sun took a body beautiful in every limb. In meditation he saw his wife Samjna in the form of a mare, doing penance and self-control, unapproachable by all beings, in the land of the Northern Kurus. He went there in the form of a horse. Fearing he was a strange male, she faced him to guard her back; their noses met, and the sun's seed passed through his nostrils into the mare. From the horse's mouth were born the two Ashvins, Nasatya and Dasra, the best of physicians, sons of the sun in horse form; and at the end of the seed was born Revanta, riding a horse, with sword, bow, armour, arrows and quiver. Then the sun showed his own pure form; seeing it calm, Samjna was glad, took her own form and he led her home. Her eldest son became Vaivasvata Manu; the second, Yama, was freed from the curse by his father's grace and became Dharmaraja, since he loved dharma; the father ended the curse by saying worms would take flesh from his feet and fall to the earth. Because Yama looks on friend and foe alike, the sun made him ruler of the south and lord of the ancestors and a guardian of the world. He made Yamuna a river flowing from Mount Kalinda, the Ashvins physicians of the gods, and Revanta lord of the guhyakas, telling him that he will be worshipped by all, that people who remember him in forests, great fires and danger from enemies and robbers will be saved, and that, pleased, he will give safety, wisdom, happiness, kingship, health, fame and rise. Chhaya's son Savarni will be the eighth Manu and still does hard penance on Meru's ridge; his brother Shani became a planet by the sun's order; the sun's youngest daughter became the holy river Tapati. Markandeya says he will now tell in detail of Vaivasvata Manu, whose creation is the present one. Whoever hears or reads this birth of the gods, the sun's sons, and the sun's glory is freed from trouble and gains great fame; hearing it removes the sins of a day and night.

106.json.summary: Kraushtuki asks to hear more of the sun's glory, and Markandeya tells what the sun once did when worshipped by people. Rajyavardhana, son of Dama, ruled the earth justly; his kingdom grew in people and wealth, with no plague, illness, danger from snakes or drought; he made great sacrifices, gave gifts and enjoyed pleasures without harming dharma, and seven thousand years passed like one day. His wife was Manini, daughter of Viduratha, a southern king. Once, while oiling his head, she wept silently before the assembled kings. Asked again and again, she at last showed him a grey hair among his locks. The king laughed and told her, before the kings and citizens, not to grieve: change comes to all beings; he had studied the Vedas, made thousands of sacrifices, given gifts, had sons, enjoyed rare pleasures with her, ruled well, fought bravely and played with friends; he has done what he had to do, and the cure for this grey hair is to go to the forest, as is fitting in old age and as their ancestors did. The kings and citizens said that it was they who should weep: if he went to the forest they would all go with him and all rites on earth would fail; his seven thousand years of ruling gave merit that forest penance could not match a sixteenth part of. The king said his time for the forest had come; the grey hair was the messenger of cruel Death, who would not wait; he would crown his son and do penance before Yama's soldiers came. When he asked the astrologers for a day for the crowning, they were so upset they said their knowledge had left them. Brahmins and people from other cities and the whole kingdom came and begged him to stay, but he answered that Death would not spare him. So the ministers, kings, elders and Brahmins agreed to win long life for him by worshipping the sun. Some worshipped the sun at home with water offerings and gifts, some kept silence, some recited the Rig, Yajur and Sama verses, some fasted lying on river banks, some kept the fire rite and recited sun hymns day and night, some stood gazing at the sun. Then the gandharva Sudaman told them to go to the forest called Guruvishala, visited by siddhas, on the great mountain at Kamarupa, a place of success, and worship there. They went and found a holy temple of the sun; people of all classes, eating in measured ways, worshipped with incense, flowers, ointments, japa, homa and gifts of food, and praised the sun: they take refuge in the sun, brighter than gods, demons, yakshas, planets and stars, called Aditya, Bhaskara, Bhanu, Savitri, Divakara, Pushan, Aryaman; terrible as the fire at the end of the ages, lord of yogis, endless, red, yellow, white and dark, present in the sages' fire rites, the imperishable highest secret and door to liberation, drawn by the metres as horses, always circling Meru; he is Brahma, Shiva, Vishnu and Prajapati, wind, sky, water, earth, mountains, seas, planets, plants; his body is threefold, of Brahma, Shiva and Vishnu; one form is the dazzling imperishable disc, the other the gentle form of the moon, and from these two, fire and Soma, the world is made. After three months the sun was pleased, came down from his disc, showed himself to them in clear form, and they bowed, praising him as the thousand-rayed cause of all, the protector, to be meditated on by yogis.

107.json.summary: Markandeya continues. The pleased sun told the people to choose a boon. Bowing in awe, they asked that the king live ten thousand years, free from illness, victorious, with a full treasury and lasting youth. The sun said 'So be it' and vanished, and they went and told the king. Queen Manini was overjoyed and wished him long life, but the king sat long in thought and said nothing. When she asked why he was not glad, he said this was no good fortune but the coming of a thousand sorrows: he would live ten thousand years alone, while she, his sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, dear relatives, devoted servants and friends would die; those who had grown thin doing penance for him would die while he lived on enjoying pleasures, and he cursed that. Manini agreed that she and the citizens had not seen this fault out of love, and asked what to do, since the sun's word cannot fail. The king said he could not enjoy pleasures without repaying the citizens and servants; he would go to the mountain and, fasting and self-controlled, do penance to please the sun for their sake, as they had done for him. If the sun gave the same long life to all his people, servants, wife, sons, grandsons and friends, he would rule and enjoy; if not, he would fast there until his life ended. Manini agreed and went with him to that temple; both worshipped the sun, fasting and thin, bearing cold, wind and heat. After a little more than a year the sun was pleased and gave the boon he wished for all his servants, citizens and sons. The king returned, ruled justly, made sacrifices, gave gifts and enjoyed life with Manini for ten thousand years with his family and servants, keeping his youth. Seeing this, Pramati of Bhrigu's line sang a verse in wonder: how great is the power of devotion to the sun, that King Rajyavardhana increased the life of his own people and himself. Markandeya says that reading this glory of the sun frees a man from sins of seven nights; one who keeps it in mind is born healthy, rich and very wise in a great family of wise people, and hearing it gives the same fruit as great sacrifices with full fees. The prayers given here, each recited at the three times of day, remove sin; where this glory is read in a sun temple the sun never leaves. One who hears it for three days with self-control gains merit equal to giving a fine milk cow with gold-tipped horns.

108.json.summary: Markandeya says such is the power of the sun, without beginning or end, the supreme self of yogis, the knower of the field for the Sankhya followers and lord of sacrifice for those who sacrifice. His son was Manu, lord of the seventh Manu period, who had no doubts about anything. Manu's sons were Ikshvaku, Nabhaga, Rishta, Narishyanta, Nabhaga, Prishadhra and Dhrishta, each ruling a separate kingdom, all famous and masters of weapons. Wanting a still better son, Manu made an offering to Mitra and Varuna, but through a mistake of the hotri priest a daughter named Ila was born. Manu praised Mitra and Varuna and asked that, if they were pleased, this daughter born from the rite should become a son with great virtues; they agreed, and Ila at once became the famous Sudyumna. Later, while hunting in a forest, through the anger of the Lord (Ishvara), Sudyumna became a woman again, and as a woman bore the mighty emperor Pururavas to Budha, son of Soma. After the son was born, Sudyumna performed the great horse sacrifice, became a man again and was king. As a man he had three strong sons who sacrificed: Utkala, Vinaya and Gaya, who ruled the earth with dharma. Pururavas, born when the king was a woman, did not get a share, since he was Budha's son; but on Vasishtha's word he was given the fine city of Pratishthana, and he became king there.

109.json.summary: Markandeya tells the story of Prishadhra, a son of Manu. He went hunting in a lonely forest, found no game, and wandered about burning from the sun, hungry and thirsty. There he saw the lovely sacrificial cow (homa-dhenu) of a Brahmin who kept the fire rite, half hidden among creepers; thinking it was a wild ox (gavaya), he shot it, and it fell with its heart pierced. The Brahmin's son Babhravya, a young celibate student given to penance, who had been sent to look after the cow, saw his father's cow killed and grew furious, sweat running and eyes rolling. The king told him to calm down, asking why he showed anger like a shudra, though born in a fine Brahmin family; neither a kshatriya nor a vaishya gets so angry. Rebuked like this, the boy cursed him: 'You will become a shudra, and what you learned from your teacher will be lost, since you killed my teacher's sacrificial cow.' The angry king took water in his hand to curse him back, and the boy grew angry again, but his father hurried up and stopped him. He told his son that anger is an enemy; calm is the good of Brahmins in this world and the next; anger destroys penance, shortens life, makes knowledge slip away and loses wealth; the angry have no dharma, wealth or happiness. If the king killed the cow knowingly, it is still right to show mercy; if he did it without knowing, he is not fit to be cursed, as his mind was not wicked; if the wise punish acts done in ignorance, the ignorant are better than the wise. The cow fell by her own karma. Prishadhra bowed and begged the boy's pardon, saying he had killed the cow by mistake, taking it for a wild ox. The boy said he had never spoken a lie since birth, nor had his anger ever been in vain, so he could not undo the curse; but the second curse he was about to give had been held back. His father took him back to the hermitage, and Prishadhra became a shudra.

110.json.summary: Markandeya says the sons of Karusha were the brave kshatriyas called Karushas, seven hundred heroes, and from them thousands more. Nabhaga, son of Dishta, in his first youth saw a very beautiful vaishya girl and fell in love at once, sighing with desire. He went to her father and asked for her. The vaishya, afraid of the prince's father, said with joined hands that the princes are rulers and his family pay them tax, so how could the prince want a marriage with people not his equal? The prince argued that human bodies are alike, shaped by desire and the like, and that what is unfit becomes fit in time, as food taken at the right time nourishes; if the girl were not given, his body would perish. The vaishya said they both depended on others; if the king allowed it, he would give her. The prince said elders are asked about all things, but not about such matters as love. The vaishya said he himself would ask, and told the king all. The king called the sages, Richika and others, and asked what should be done. The sages said that if the prince loved the vaishya girl it could be lawful, but in proper order: first he must marry the daughter of a crowned king, and after that she could be his wife; otherwise his high birth would be lost. Ignoring them, the prince went out, seized the girl with a raised sword and said he had taken her by the rakshasa form of marriage; let whoever could, free her. The vaishya ran to the king for help, and the angry king ordered his army to kill Nabhaga as a spoiler of dharma. The prince, skilled in weapons, struck down much of the army; the king himself came to fight and was overpowered by his son. Then a wandering sage came down from the sky and told the king to stop: the son had acted against dharma, but it was also not right for the king to fight a vaishya. A Brahmin, kshatriya or vaishya who first marries a wife of his own class may afterwards marry women of lower classes without losing his class; but one who marries a lower-class woman without first marrying one of his own class falls into her class. So the foolish son has become a vaishya and has no right to fight a kshatriya. The last line is unclear in the text.

111.json.summary: Markandeya continues. The king stopped fighting, and his son married the vaishya girl. Having become a vaishya, Nabhaga asked his father what work he should do. The king told him to ask the ascetics in charge of law, Babhravya and others, and they told him that herding cattle, farming and trade were his duty; he did so. His son Bhalandana was born, and his mother sent him off, saying 'Become a protector of the cow' (gopala, which also means protector of the earth). Bowing to her, he went to the royal sage Nipa in the Himalaya, touched his feet and said his mother had told him to become a gopala, but the earth he should protect had been taken by powerful kinsmen; he asked how to win it back. Nipa taught Bhalandana all the weapon lore. He then went to his father's cousins, Vasurata and others, and asked for half the kingdom, the share of his fathers; they said he was a vaishya's son and could not rule. In the battle that followed he beat them all in a fair fight and took the earth. He offered the whole kingdom to his father, who refused before his wife: he had given up rule to obey his own father; having displeased his father by marrying a vaishya girl, he would lose the worlds of merit if he now ruled against his father's command; nor would it be fitting for a proud man to enjoy a kingdom won by his son's arm like a weak man. Bhalandana should rule himself or give it back to the kinsmen; obeying a father is better than ruling the earth. Then his wife Suprabha laughed and told him to take the kingdom: neither he nor she is a vaishya; she too was born of kshatriyas. She tells the story: there was a famous king Sudeva, whose friend was Nala, son of Dhumrashva. In the month of Madhava (spring) they went to a mango grove with their wives, drank and feasted, and by a lotus pond they saw the beautiful wife of Pramati, son of Chyavana, a princess. The drunken Nala seized her while the king watched, as she cried for help. Pramati came running and told Sudeva to punish Nala, since he was the ruler there. Out of regard for Nala, Sudeva said he was a vaishya and Pramati should go to some kshatriya for protection. Angry, Pramati said: so be it; a kshatriya is one who protects from harm, and kshatriyas bear arms so that no cry of distress is heard; you will not be a kshatriya but a vaishya, the lowest of your family.

112.json.summary: Suprabha's story continues. Having cursed Sudeva, Pramati of Bhrigu's line, burning with anger, told Nala that since, drunk with pride, he had seized his wife by force in his hermitage, he would turn to ashes; at once Nala was burned to a heap of ashes by a fire from his own body. Seeing this, Sudeva, sober now, bowed and begged forgiveness for what he had said while drunk, and asked that the curse be taken back. Pramati, his anger gone once Nala was burned, said his words could not fail, but he would grant a favour: Sudeva would surely become a vaishya, but in that very birth he would soon become a kshatriya again; when a kshatriya born of his line takes a girl by force, then Sudeva, the vaishya, will be taken back as a kshatriya. Suprabha says this Sudeva became her father, a vaishya. Then she tells of herself. The royal sage Surata lived as an ascetic on Mount Gandhamadana, eating little and free from attachment. Seeing a myna bird (sharika) fall to the ground from a hawk's beak, he fainted with pity, and when he came to, she was born from his body. He took her lovingly and named her Kripavati, 'full of pity', since she was born when he was overcome by pity. She grew up in his hermitage and roamed the forests with friends. A sage, the brother of Agastya, also called Agastya, while gathering forest food, was angered by her friends and cursed her: 'Since you called me a vaishya, you will become a vaishya.' She pleaded that she had done nothing; why curse her for others' fault?
