The sage said the innocent become stained by keeping company with the wicked, as a pot of the five cow products is spoiled by a drop of liquor; but since she had bowed and pleased him, he granted that when born in a vaishya family she would remember her past birth when she urged her son to win a kingdom, and then she would regain kshatriya birth with her husband and enjoy divine pleasures. So, she tells Nabhaga, she was cursed like this, and her father was cursed by Pramati; he is not a vaishya, nor is her father; since she is not at fault, how can he, who is not at fault, be made impure?

113.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Hearing her, the righteous King Nabhaga still told his wife and son that he would not take back the kingdom he gave up on his father's order; holding to the vaishya way of life, he would pay tax to his son, who should rule or give it up as he wished. So Prince Bhalandana ruled with dharma and married; his power was unchecked on earth, all kings obeyed him, he made sacrifices and was sole lord of the earth. His son was Vatsapri, who surpassed his father in virtues. Vatsapri's wife was Saunanda (Sunanda), the faithful daughter of Viduratha, whom he won by killing Kujrimbha, lord of the daityas and enemy of Indra. Kraushtuki asks how. Markandeya tells: King Viduratha had two sons, Suniti and Sumati. Hunting in a forest, he saw a huge pit like a mouth of the earth and wondered if it was an opening to the underworld. A Brahmin ascetic named Suvrata told him that a mighty demon living in Rasatala is called Kujrimbha because he makes the earth gape; he steals every jewel-like thing on earth and in heaven. He has stolen the club (mushala) Sunanda, made long ago by Tvashtri, with which he kills enemies, splits the earth from below and makes doorways for all the asuras; he ruins sacrifices and strengthens the daityas. If the king kills him he will be supreme lord of the earth. The club loses its power when touched by a woman, and regains it the next day; the demon does not know this. The pit is near the king's city. The king told his ministers all this in council, and his daughter Mudavati, standing nearby, heard it. A few days later Kujrimbha carried her off from the garden with her friends. The angry king sent his two sons through the pit by the Nirvindhya river to kill the abductor, but after a hard battle the demon, strong in magic, killed their soldiers and bound both princes. In despair the king proclaimed that whoever killed the demon and freed his children would marry his daughter. [The verse naming who came forward is incomplete in the text; the story shows it was Vatsapri, son of the king's friend Bhalandana.] The young man, strong and skilled in weapons, bowed and offered to free them; the king embraced him and sent him off. Armed with sword, bow and finger guard, Vatsapri went down the pit and twanged his bowstring so that the whole underworld rang. Kujrimbha came with his army and they fought for three days; then the angry demon ran for his club, which was kept in the inner palace, worshipped with scents, garlands and incense. Mudavati, knowing its secret, had bowed and touched it, and while the demon was taking it up she touched it again and again, pretending to honour it. So its blows were useless, and the demon fought with other weapons; the prince overcame them, made him chariotless, and as the demon rushed at him with shield and sword, struck him in the chest with the fire weapon. The demon died; the great serpents of the underworld rejoiced, flowers rained, gandharvas sang. The prince freed the king's two sons and Mudavati. Shesha (Ananta), king of the nagas, took the club, and pleased with Mudavati, who knew the power of a woman's touch on it, named her Sunanda. Vatsapri brought her and her brothers to the king, who, overjoyed, said he was honoured for three reasons: he had gained such a son-in-law, the enemy was dead, and his children were back unharmed. He asked the prince to marry her that day; the prince said he would do whatever his father allowed. The wedding was held, Vatsapri enjoyed life with her, and when Bhalandana grew old and went to the forest, Vatsapri became king, made sacrifices and ruled the people like his children; in his time there was no mixing of classes and no fear of robbers, snakes, wicked men or disasters.

114.json.summary: Markandeya continues the dynasty. Vatsapri and Sunanda had twelve sons: Pramshu, Pravira, Shura, Suchakra, Vikrama, Krama, Bali, Balaka, Chanda, Prachanda, Suvikrama and Sunaya, all great in battle. The eldest, Pramshu, became king and the others served him. At his sacrifices so much wealth was given away by the twice-born and left behind by lower classes that the earth truly earned its name Vasundhara ('holder of wealth'); with his treasury he performed countless sacrifices. His son was Prajati, at whose sacrifice Indra, fully satisfied with his shares, killed ninety-nine mighty danavas, Bala and Jambha and other enemies of the gods. Prajati had five sons headed by Khanitra, who became king, famous for his valour: calm, truthful, brave, kind to all beings, devoted to his duty, serving elders, learned, eloquent, modest, skilled in weapons but not boastful. Day and night he prayed: may all beings be happy and loving even in lonely places, may all be well and free from fear, illness and worry; may all beings feel friendship, may Brahmins be well and love each other, may all classes prosper and all works succeed; people, treat all beings as you would yourself or your son, since harm done to others returns to the doer; may good come to those who love me, and may even those who hate me see good. He gave his four brothers separate kingdoms: Shauri in the east, Udavasu in the south, Sunaya in the west and Maharatha in the north, each with family priests of a different line: Suhotra of Atri's family for Shauri, Kushavarta of Gautama's line for Udavasu, Pramati of Kashyapa's line for Sunaya, and a Vasishtha for Maharatha. Khanitra was overlord of all and cared for them and all his people like sons. Once Vishvavedin, Shauri's minister, told Shauri in private that the one who owns the whole earth passes it to his sons and grandsons, while the younger brothers' lines shrink over time until their descendants live by farming; a brother's love does not extend to brothers' sons. Why keep a minister if a king is content with little? With his ministers as tools he should take his ancestral kingdom, and they would bring him fruit in the next world too. Shauri said the eldest brother rules the earth and the younger ones have small lands; there are five brothers and one earth. Vishvavedin said then he should take the whole earth himself and rule as lord of all, and the other ministers would help. Shauri objected that the eldest loved them like sons; the minister said he could honour the eldest with royal gifts once he ruled, for those who want a kingdom, what is younger or older? Shauri agreed. Vishvavedin won over the other brothers, employed their priests and his own in rites of peace and the like and then in hostile black magic (abhichara) against Khanitra, secretly split his supporters with soft words and gifts, and built up his own army. From the four priests' daily fierce rites four terrible kritya spirits arose, huge-mouthed, horrible, with raised tridents. They went to Khanitra, but his great merit, since he had done no wrong, turned them back; they fell on the wicked priests of the kings and on Vishvavedin, and the priests and the evil minister were burned up by them.

115.json.summary: Markandeya continues. All the world was amazed that the priests, living in separate cities, died at the same moment. Khanitra heard that his brothers' priests and his brother's minister Vishvavedin had been burned, and, not knowing why, asked Vasishtha when he came to his house. Vasishtha told him everything: what Shauri's minister said, what Shauri answered, how the minister split the brothers, what the priests did, and that they perished because they harmed a sinless king who was kind even to enemies. Crying 'I am ruined', the king blamed himself bitterly before Vasishtha: shame on him, unlucky and without merit, since four Brahmins died because of him; had he not been born, his brothers' priests would not have died; shame on his kingship and his birth in a great royal family, for he has become the cause of Brahmins' death; they were doing their masters' work and were not wicked, but he is wicked as the cause; there is no greater sinner on earth. Deeply troubled, he crowned his son Kshupa and went to the forest with his three wives to do penance. Knowing the rules of the forest-dweller's life, he did penance for three hundred and fifty years, and when his body was worn out he closed all the senses' openings and gave up his life. He went to holy, everlasting worlds that grant every wish, which kings reach by the horse sacrifice and other rites. His three wives gave up their lives with him and reached the same world. Markandeya says this story of Khanitra destroys sin for those who hear and read it, and he will now tell of Kshupa.

116.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Kshupa, son of Khanitra, ruled like his father, pleasing the people with dharma; he was generous, made sacrifices, and was fair to friend and foe in lawsuits and conduct. Once, at court, the bards told him that long ago there was a king Kshupa, son of Brahma, and that his conduct was like that earlier king's. The king asked to hear the earlier Kshupa's deeds so that he could copy them if he was able. The bards said that king freed cows and Brahmins from tax and performed sacrifices on earth with a sixth share of the crops. The king said no one like him could equal such great kings, but one should strive to follow the noble; he vowed to copy King Kshupa, to perform three sacrifices at every harvest across the four-cornered earth, and to give back to Brahmins and cows the tax they once paid to the king. He did so: at each harvest he made three sacrifices, and gave Brahmins and cows wealth equal to the tax they used to pay. His wife Pramatha bore him a blameless, brave son, Vira, whose might made all kings submit. Vira's beloved wife was Nandini of Vidarbha, and she bore Vivimsha. While mighty Vivimsha ruled, the earth was full of people without gaps; the rain came on time, the earth was full of crops and juicy fruit, food gave strength without causing madness, and wealth did not make people proud. Enemies feared his power, and the people and his friends lived well and happy. After many sacrifices and good rule he died in battle and went to Indra's world.

117.json.summary: Markandeya says Vivimsha's son was the mighty Khaninetra, at whose sacrifices the gandharvas sang in wonder that no one on earth would ever sacrifice like him. After ten thousand sacrifices he gave the whole earth with its seas to Brahmins, then got wealth by penance and pleased them again; having received such wealth from him, Brahmins would not take gifts from any other king. He performed 67 thousand, 67 hundred and 67 sacrifices with rich fees. Being without a son, he went hunting, alone on horseback without an army, armed with bow, arrows and sword, to get meat for a rite to the ancestors to win a son. A deer came out of a thicket and told him to kill it and do what he wished. The king asked why it offered itself to death when other deer flee. The deer said it had no son, its life was useless, and it saw no reason to keep living. Then another deer came and said, in front of the first, that the king should kill him instead: he wants a son, so how could he win one with the flesh of a sonless deer? One should use material that suits the rite, as one cannot judge sweet scents with foul ones. The king asked this deer why he wanted to die. The second deer said he had many sons and daughters and lived in a forest fire of worry: deer are timid and easily killed, afraid of men, lions, tigers, wolves and even dogs and jackals; because of his attachment he even wishes the earth were empty of men and lions, and that cows, goats, sheep and horses that eat grass were dead so his children would have food. When his children go out he worries whether they are caught in a trap, net or snare, or by a lion; he longs for safety each night, each day, always. Yet he does not kill himself, because suicides go to the sunless worlds, while animals used in sacrifice rise high: Agni, Varuna and the sun were once sacrificial animals and reached a high state. So the king should be kind, lead him to that high state, and himself gain the son he wants. The first deer said the king should not kill this one, who is blessed with many children; he himself, childless, should be killed. The second said the first was blessed, having fear for one body only; at first he too had only his own body's pain, then his wife's doubled it, and with each child born came as many more sorrows; his offspring bring sorrow here and trouble in the next world, since caring for them makes him think thoughts that lead to hell. The king said he did not know whether one with children or one without was blessed; his mind swung back and forth. Children do bring sorrow in this world and the next, yet he has heard that the sonless keep their debts; so he would try to get a son without killing any creature, by fierce penance, as kings did before.

118.json.summary: Markandeya continues. King Khaninetra went to the sin-destroying Gomati river and, controlling speech, body and mind and doing hard penance, praised Indra for a son. Pleased by his hymn, penance and devotion, Indra offered a boon. The king asked for a son who would be the best of all warriors, of unbroken power, righteous, wise in dharma and able. Indra agreed; the king returned to his city, and while he ruled and sacrificed, a son was born by Indra's grace. The father named him Balashva and had him taught all the weapon lore. When his father died, Balashva became king, brought all kings on earth under his rule and made them pay tax and tribute. But the proud kings, his kinsmen, rose up in their own lands, stopped paying, and seized his territory, and he was left holding only his own city. Many strong kings, with troops and wealth, joined together and besieged him there. With little treasure and few soldiers he was in despair; seeing no refuge, he put his two hands before his mouth and sighed in grief. Then from between his hands, struck by his breath, hundreds of warriors, chariots, elephants and horses came out, and in a moment the whole city was filled with a mighty army. Surrounded by it, he broke out of the city, defeated the kings and made them pay tax again as before. Because this enemy-burning army was born from his shaken hands (kara + dhama, blowing), Balashva was called Karandhama. He was righteous, great-souled and friendly to all beings, famous in the three worlds; the text says that when he was in great distress, dharma itself came to the king and gave him the army that destroyed his enemies.

119.json.summary: Markandeya says Vira, the lovely, virtuous daughter of Viryachandra, chose Karandhama at her self-choice ceremony (svayamvara), and he had by her a son famed as Avikshit. When the son was born the king asked the astrologers whether he was born under a good star and moment and whether good planets looked on him and no evil ones. They said he was born at a good moment, star and rising sign; he would be very mighty and a great king. Jupiter, guru of the gods, looked on him, and Venus from the seventh house, the Moon from the fourth, and Mercury, Soma's son, from close by; the Sun, Mars and Saturn did not look on him; he would be blessed with every good fortune. Delighted, the king said that since they kept saying 'avaikshata' (looked on), the boy's name would be Avikshit. Avikshit mastered the Vedas and their branches and learned all weapon lore from Kanva's son. He was like the Ashvins in beauty, Brihaspati in mind, the moon in charm, the sun in brilliance, the ocean in steadiness and the earth in patience; no one matched him in valour. At their self-choice ceremonies he was chosen by Vara, daughter of Hemadharma, Gauri daughter of Sudeva, Subhadra daughter of Bali, Lilavati daughter of Vira, Nibha daughter of Virabhadra, Manyavati daughter of Bhima and Kumudvati daughter of Dambha; those who did not choose him he carried off by force, pushing aside all kings and their families, trusting his own strength. Once Vaishalini, the fine-toothed daughter of Vishala, king of Vaishali, held her self-choice ceremony; she did not choose him, but, proud of his strength, he seized her by force as before. The kings, who had been humiliated by him many times, said to one another in disgust: shame on the birth of so many kings of one class who put up with this insult from one man; a kshatriya is one who protects from harm (kshata) those being struck by the proud, and others bear the name for nothing; what kind of kshatriyas are they who cannot protect even themselves from this wicked man? Let the praise sung by bards and minstrels be made true by killing the enemy; who does not fear death, and who becomes immortal without war? Those who live by weapons must not give up manliness. Hearing this, the kings, full of anger, rose up with their weapons; some mounted chariots, some elephants and horses, others went at him on foot.

120.json.summary: Markandeya continues. The kings and princes, so often humiliated by Avikshit, fought him in a terrible battle, one against many, with swords, spears, maces and arrows. Skilled in weapons, he pierced them with hundreds of arrows: he cut off one man's arm, another's neck, pierced one in the heart and another in the chest, cut off an elephant's trunk and a horse's head, cut chariot poles, horses and charioteers, split enemy arrows in flight, and cut swords and bows. One prince fled when his armour was stripped, a foot soldier left the field. When the whole host of kings was thrown into confusion, seven hundred heroes, proud of birth, age, courage and shame, stood their ground, resolved to die. He fought them fairly, without much anger, and was about to strip them of their gear and armour, when they, enraged, gave up fair fighting and all attacked him at once: some pierced him with arrows, one cut his bow, another his banner, others killed his horses and broke his chariot, struck him with maces and shot him in the back. When his bow was cut he took sword and shield, and these too were struck down; then he took a mace, which another cut with a razor-headed arrow. Surrounded and pierced with hundreds and thousands of arrows by kings who had turned from fair war, he fell to the ground overpowered, and the princes bound him. Having captured him unfairly, they entered the city of Vaidisha with King Vishala, full of joy, bringing the bound prince. The girl was placed in front of them, and her father and the family priest told her again and again to choose whichever king she liked as husband. When the proud girl chose no one, the king asked his astrologer for a better day for the wedding, since today's battle had caused an obstacle. The astrologer, thinking it over and knowing the truth, said sadly that other good days with fine rising signs would soon come, and the king should hold the wedding then; enough of this day, on which a great obstacle has arisen.

121.json.summary: Markandeya continues. King Karandhama, his wife Vira and other kings heard that Avikshit had been captured unfairly. The king thought long with his vassals. Some said all the kings who together had bound one man unfairly should be killed; others said to ready the army at once and bind the wicked Vishala and those with him; others said the prince himself had first broken dharma by seizing an unwilling girl by force and shaming all the kings at every self-choice ceremony, so they had joined to overpower him. Hearing this, Vira, daughter, wife and mother of heroes, was glad and said before her husband and the kings that her son had done well: he seized the girl by force after beating all the kings and was bound while fighting alone for her, unfairly; this is no disgrace. True manliness is when a man in his anger ignores caution like a lion about to kill; he took many princesses before proud kings; a kshatriya does not beg, which is fit for lowly people, but takes by force before the strong. The kings' own ancestors won greatness by killing enemies and seizing land, wives and wealth. So they should quickly mount chariots, ready elephants and horses, and not fear fighting many kings; a hero shines over all as the sun over darkness. Roused by her, Karandhama raised his army, and fought for three days against Vishala and the kings. When the kings were almost defeated, Vishala came to Karandhama with a guest offering and honoured him; the son was freed and Karandhama stayed the night happily. Vishala brought the girl to marry Avikshit before his father, but Avikshit refused her and any woman: he had been defeated in battle while she watched; let her choose someone whose fame and might were unbroken; beaten by enemies, he was no better than a timid woman; men are free, women depend on others, and a man who depends on others is no man; how could he show his face to her again? The king told his daughter to choose another husband, or let them give her to one she liked. The girl said he was beaten by many, not fairly, while he fought fairly; standing alone against many, like a lion against elephants, he showed great courage, often defeated them all, and they won only by foul means, so there is no shame. She did not love him only for his looks; his courage, valour and steadiness had won her heart; let her father ask for him, as no one else would be her husband. Vishala praised her words and begged the prince to purify his family by accepting her, but Avikshit said he would take no woman, since in himself he felt like a woman. Karandhama told his son to take her as she loved him firmly; Avikshit said he had never broken his father's order, so let his father command. Seeing the prince firmly decided, Vishala told his daughter to turn her mind elsewhere, as there were many princes; she said she had chosen her husband, and if he did not want her, she would have no other in this life but penance. Karandhama stayed three days with Vishala and returned home, and Avikshit, consoled with old stories by his father and other kings, went back too. The girl, sent off by her family, went to the forest and did penance without food, fully detached. After three months of fasting she was thin, weak and near death and resolved to give up her body. The gods sent a divine messenger who told her not to give up her precious body: she would be the mother of an emperor (chakravartin) who would rule the seven-continent earth with unbroken command, kill before the gods the enemies Tarujit and the cruel Ayahshanku, set people on dharma, protect the four classes in their duties, kill robbers, mlecchas and other wicked people, and perform six thousand sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice with full fees. She said she believed he came from heaven, but how could she have a son without a husband? She had vowed before her father to have no husband but Avikshit, who did not want her even when asked by both fathers and by herself. The messenger said she should not argue, her son would be born; she must not kill herself against dharma, but stay in this forest and nourish her body, and by the power of her penance all would go well. He left, and she began to look after her body day by day.

122.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Avikshit's mother Vira called her son on a holy day and said she had her husband's permission to keep the hard fast called kimichhaka ('what do you wish?'), in which the one fasting must grant whatever is asked. This depends on his father and also on him and her; she would give half the wealth of the great treasury, with his father's leave, but some requests might need effort from him, by strength and valour, and could not be fulfilled otherwise; if he made a promise, she would undertake it, and she asked his view. Avikshit said the wealth belongs to his father and he has no ownership of it, but whatever can be done with his own body he would do; she should keep the vow without worry, since his father, master of the wealth, had allowed it. The queen kept the fast with self-control and worshipped Kubera, king of the yakshas, all the treasures (nidhis), their guardians and Lakshmi, with great devotion. Meanwhile, in private, Karandhama's ministers, skilled in statecraft, told him: you have grown old while ruling; your only son Avikshit has given up taking a wife; when he dies without a son, your earth will surely pass to your enemies, your line will end and the offerings of rice-balls and water to the ancestors will stop; so make your son think of helping the ancestors. Just then the king heard the family priest of Vira calling out to those who had come to ask: who wants anything, however hard, from Karandhama's queen, who is keeping the kimichhaka fast? Prince Avikshit also told all the petitioners at the palace gate: whatever can be done by my body, let anyone ask it, for my mother keeps the kimichhaka fast; I promise to give what you wish. Hearing this from his son's own mouth, the king jumped up and said, 'I am a petitioner; give to me.' Avikshit asked what he should give or do, easy or hard. The king said that if he kept his promise, he should show him the face of a grandson sitting in his lap. Avikshit said he was the only son and lived in celibacy; with no son, how could he show a grandson's face? The king said his celibacy was a sin; he should give it up and show him a grandson. Avikshit asked for something else, since he had given up women out of disgust. The king said that being defeated by many enemies is common, and to turn away from life over it is foolish; he should give up celibacy and, for his mother's wish, show him his grandson's face. When the king would ask nothing else, the son said he was trapped by having granted the wish; though it was very hard for one beaten and thrown down before a woman to become a husband again, he was bound by the noose of truth and would take a wife without shame, as his father said, and his father's order would be done.

123.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Once Avikshit was hunting in a forest, shooting deer, boars, tigers and other tusked beasts, when he suddenly heard a woman crying again and again in fear, 'Save me!' Calling 'Do not fear', he spurred his horse toward the sound. The proud girl was crying in the lonely forest, seized by Dridhakesha, a son of Danu: 'I am the wife of Avikshit, son of the wise king Karandhama, and this wretch is carrying me off; I am the wife of the one before whom no kings, gandharvas or guhyakas can stand, whose anger is like Death and valour like Indra's.' Hearing this, the prince wondered how his wife could be in the forest; was it a trick of wicked forest rakshasas? He would go and find out. He found a lovely girl in all her ornaments, held by the danava with a club, crying pitifully. He told her not to fear, and told the demon he was dead: who could cause grief while Karandhama ruled the earth? Seeing him with his bow, she again cried that she was the daughter-in-law of King Karandhama and wife of Avikshit, being carried off as if she had no protector. Avikshit wondered how she could be his wife and his father's daughter-in-law, but decided to free her first and find out later, since kshatriyas bear arms to protect those in distress. He told the demon to let her go and leave alive. The demon dropped her, raised his club and ran at him; the prince covered him with arrows. The demon threw his club studded with hundreds of spikes; the prince cut it with arrows. The demon pulled up a tree and threw it, and the prince cut it to bits with broad arrows; a rock thrown at him fell harmlessly. Everything the demon threw, the prince cut down with ease. With all his weapons gone, the demon rushed at him with raised fist, and the prince cut off his head with a reed-leaf arrow. The gods cried 'Well done' and offered a boon; to please his father, he chose a mighty son. The gods said he would have a mighty emperor as son by this very girl he had freed. The prince said he was bound by his promise to his father to want a son, but since being defeated by kings he had given up marriage; he had rejected Vishala's daughter, and she had given up all men except him for his sake; how could he cruelly leave her and take another woman? The gods said this girl is the very one he always praises, Vishala's daughter, who took up penance for him; by her he would have a heroic son, an emperor who would rule the seven continents and make thousands of sacrifices. Then the gods left. The prince asked her what this was all about. She told him that when he rejected her she left her family and came to this forest in despair, and when she was about to give up her worn-out body by penance, a divine messenger stopped her, saying she would have a mighty emperor son who would please the gods and kill the asuras; so, by the gods' order, she did not give up her body, hoping to be united with him. The day before yesterday, when she went to bathe in a pool of the Ganga, an old naga dragged her down to the underworld, where thousands of nagas, their wives and children praised and worshipped her and humbly begged her favour: her son should be held back when about to kill them, as the nagas (the air-eaters) would commit an offence against him. When she agreed, they adorned her with divine ornaments of the underworld, flowers, perfumes and fine clothes, and the naga brought her back to this world, as radiant and beautiful as before. Seeing her so beautiful and adorned, the wicked Dridhakesha seized her to carry her off, and she was freed by the strength of the prince's arm. She begs him to be gracious and not refuse her, for there is no other prince on earth like him.

124.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Hearing her and remembering what his father had asked during the kimichhaka vow, Avikshit, now loving the girl who had given up pleasures for him, said: 'When I, beaten by enemies, rejected you, you were won by me after I conquered enemies; what shall I do now?' She asked him to take her hand in this lovely forest, as union of two who desire each other is good. He agreed, saying fate alone had brought them together. Just then a gandharva prince came with fine apsaras and other gandharvas and said: this proud girl Bhamini is his daughter; she was born as Vishala's daughter because of Agastya's curse. As a child at play she angered Agastya, who cursed her to become a human; when they begged him, saying she was a thoughtless child, the great sage said that, thinking her a child, he had given only a small curse, but it could not be undone. So she was born in Vishala's house. He had come for her sake; the prince should take her, and her son would be an emperor. Avikshit took her hand with the proper rites, and Tumburu performed the fire offering; divine gandharvas sang, apsaras danced, clouds rained flowers and divine drums sounded at the wedding of the prince with her, who would be the cause of protection for the whole earth. They all went to the world of the gandharvas, where Avikshit and Bhamini lived happily, enjoying themselves in city gardens, on hills, on river banks bright with swans and cranes and in fine palaces, while sages, gandharvas and kinnaras brought them food, ointments, clothes, garlands and drinks. In the gandharva world she bore him a son. At his birth there was a great festival: some sang, some played drums, flutes and vinas, hosts of apsaras danced and clouds rained flowers. Remembered with affection, the sage Tumburu came and performed the birth rites (jatakarma). All the gods, the pure divine sages, the naga kings Shesha, Vasuki and Takshaka from the underworld, the leaders of gods and asuras, yakshas, guhyakas and all the winds came, filling the great gandharva city. Tumburu performed the birth rites and spoke a blessing with praise: may he be a mighty emperor, lord of the whole earth for a long time; may Indra, the world guardians and the sages bless him; and he prayed to the four winds (marut) for him: 'Marut-tava', may the pure east wind be for his good, the south wind keep him free from harm, the west wind give him great valour and the north wind great strength. At the end a bodiless voice said that since the teacher had said 'Maruttava' again and again, the boy would be famous on earth as Marutta; all kings would obey him, he would stand at the head of all rulers, conquer and enjoy the seven-continent earth unchecked, and be the foremost of kings who sacrifice, above all in courage and valour. Hearing this voice from heaven, the Brahmins, gandharvas and his parents rejoiced.

125.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Avikshit, with his dear son and his wife, came with the gandharvas to his father's city; he and his shy wife bowed at the king's feet. Taking the baby, he said to Karandhama, who sat on the seat of justice among kings, 'Look at the face of your grandson in your lap, as I promised you at my mother's kimichhaka vow,' put the child in his lap and told him everything. Eyes wet with joy, the king embraced his grandson, again and again calling himself fortunate, honoured the gandharvas with guest offerings, and forgot all else. There was great joy in every house in the city, since an heir had been born to their lord; women danced to songs and music, and the king gave Brahmins jewels, wealth, cows, clothes and ornaments. The boy grew like the moon in the bright half of the month, loved by his elders and the people. He learned the Vedas from teachers, then all the sciences, then archery; he mastered sword and bow and other weapons, and received the divine missiles from Bhargava of Bhrigu's line, humble and devoted to his teacher; there was none greater than him in all knowledge. Vishala also heard all about his daughter and rejoiced at his grandson's merit. King Karandhama, his wish fulfilled, made many sacrifices, gave gifts, finished his duties, ruled the earth justly with the classes in their places and beat his enemies; wishing to go to the forest, he told Avikshit he was old and asked him to take the kingdom, since his only remaining task was to crown him. Avikshit, humbly, wanting to go to the forest for penance himself, refused: shame still did not leave his mind; he had been freed from bondage by his father, not by his own strength; one who cannot protect himself cannot protect the earth; a man rescued by another is like a woman, and how could one like a woman be king? A man who is a husband and protector is brave, and such a one is king. The father said father and son are not separate; being freed by one's father is not being freed by another. The son said he could not change his heart; he felt deep shame at being freed by his father; let no one in their family be a man who enjoys wealth gained by his father, is saved from trouble by his father and is known by his father's name; may he go the way of those who earn their own wealth, fame and escape from danger. When he kept saying this, the king made his grandson Marutta king, and Marutta, with his father's consent, received the kingdom from his grandfather and ruled well, delighting his friends. Karandhama went to the forest with Vira for penance, controlling speech, body and mind; after a thousand years of hard penance he left his body and reached Indra's world. Vira, wishing to reach her husband's world, did penance for another hundred years, with matted hair and covered in dirt, living on fruits and roots at the hermitage of the Bhargavas among the wives of Brahmins and serving the Brahmins.

126.json.summary: Kraushtuki asks to hear the deeds of Marutta, son of Avikshit, a famous emperor, brave, handsome, wise and righteous. Markandeya says Marutta ruled justly, like a father with his own sons, and made many sacrifices with full fees as his priests directed; his power was unchecked in all seven continents and he could travel freely to heaven, the underworld and the waters. With the wealth he gained he worshipped Indra and the gods with great sacrifices, and the other classes, diligent in their own work, used the wealth they got from him for sacrifices, wells, gardens and other good works. He rivalled the gods and surpassed not only all kings but even Indra of a hundred sacrifices. His priest was Samvarta, son of Angiras and brother of Brihaspati, a store of penance, who by his penance threw down a peak of the golden mountain Munjavat for the king, and with it made the whole sacrificial ground and shining palaces all of gold. Sages still sing verses about him as if reciting scripture: no sacrificer on earth equalled Marutta, whose whole assembly hall and palaces were golden; Indra was drunk with Soma and the Brahmins with fees; Indra and the best gods served food to the Brahmins; all were satisfied; the Brahmins left gold behind in houses full of jewels; the three classes took that gold and some also gave gifts, and the people, their wishes fulfilled, made sacrifices of their own in many lands. While Marutta was ruling, an ascetic came and gave him a message from his father's mother (Vira), who had seen a group of ascetics poisoned by serpents mad with pride. She says: your grandfather went to heaven after ruling well, your father went to the forest, and she is doing penance at the hermitage of Aurva; but she sees a failure in his rule that did not happen under his ancestors; he must be careless, attached to pleasures, or without self-control, blind for lack of spies, not knowing good from bad. Snakes from the underworld have bitten seven sons of sages and fouled the ponds, spoiled the offerings with sweat, urine and dung; the sages could burn the snakes to ashes, but this is not their task; it is his. The pleasures of princes last only until the water of the crowning falls on their heads. A king must always ask: who are my friends and enemies, how strong are my enemies, who am I, who are my ministers and allied kings, how big are my treasury and army, who is loyal or disloyal or won over by others, who in the city and country is good or bad, who should be punished, protected or ignored; he must control them by soft words and division, considering place and time; he must send spies, unknown to each other, even among his ministers; he must spend day and night on his work, not on pleasures. Kings take a body not for enjoyment but for the great toil of protecting the earth and their duty; great toil here brings lasting joy in heaven. Since he, blind without spies, did not know the trouble the sages suffered from the snakes during his rule, he should punish the wicked and protect the good, and so gain a sixth of their merit; if he does not protect, he will surely take on all the sin done by the wicked. She says she has told him all as his grandmother, and he should do as he sees fit.

127.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Hearing the ascetic's message, King Marutta was ashamed, cried 'Shame on me, blind without spies', sighed and took up his bow. He hurried to Aurva's hermitage, bowed his head to Vira, his father's mother, and to the ascetics, who blessed him, and seeing seven ascetics lying dead on the ground, bitten by snakes, he blamed himself again and again before them. He declared that the whole world, with gods, asuras and men, should see what he would do to the wicked snakes who hate Brahmins, and in anger took up the samvartaka missile to destroy all the nagas who move in the underworld and on earth. At once the world of the nagas blazed on all sides, burned by the great weapon's fire, and in the panic the snakes cried 'Ah father! Ah mother! Ah child!' Some with burning tails, others with burning hoods, carrying their children and wives and leaving behind ornaments and clothes, left the underworld and went for refuge to Bhamini, Marutta's mother, who had earlier given them her promise of safety. Bowing, in fear and choked voices, they reminded her of what they had begged in the underworld: now the time has come; let her stop her son and spare their lives, since the whole naga world is burning in the weapon's fire and they have no refuge but her. Remembering her promise, the good Bhamini anxiously told her husband Avikshit what the snakes had asked of her concerning her son; they have come in fear, burning, and she had promised them safety; since she and her husband follow dharma together, those who took refuge with her have taken refuge with him, and she too seeks his refuge; let him stop Marutta, who will surely calm down at his word and her request. Avikshit said Marutta had become angry at a great offence, and he thought his anger would be hard to turn back. The nagas said they had come to him for refuge; a kshatriya bears arms to protect the distressed. Moved by the snakes' plea and his wife's request, Avikshit said he would go at once and tell her son that those who seek refuge must not be abandoned; if Marutta would not withdraw the weapon at his word, he would stop his son's weapon with his own weapons. Then Avikshit, best of kshatriyas, took his bow and hurried with his wife to the hermitage of the Bhargavas.

128.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Avikshit found his son with bow drawn and the fierce weapon pouring fire that filled the directions, lit up the earth and reached into the underworld. Seeing the king frowning, he told him again and again, clearly, not to be angry and to withdraw the weapon. Marutta looked at him, bowed respectfully to his parents and said the snakes had greatly wronged him: despising his power while he ruled, they came to the hermitage and bit seven sons of sages, fouled the sages' offerings and all the ponds; his father should say nothing on this and not stop him from punishing these Brahmin-killers. Avikshit said that if the Brahmins killed by them have died, the snakes will go to hell anyway; let him do as his father asks and stop. Marutta said he would not forgive these wicked offenders; if he did not try to restrain sinners, he himself would go to hell, so his father should not stop him. Avikshit said the snakes had come to him for refuge, out of respect for him; enough anger. Marutta said he could not break his own duty to obey him: a king who punishes those who deserve it and protects the good reaches holy worlds, and goes to hell by neglecting it. Though his father and mother kept trying to stop him, he would not withdraw the weapon. Then Avikshit said: since you harm the frightened snakes who sought my refuge, I will act against you; I too have weapons; you are not the only one on earth who knows them; how much is your manliness, wicked one, before me? Red-eyed with anger, he strung his bow and fixed on it the mighty kala missile (the weapon of Time), surrounded by flames, and the whole earth with its seas and mountains shook. Seeing it, Marutta called out that his weapon was raised to punish the wicked, not to kill his father; why would his father loose the kala weapon at a son who follows his duty and always obeys him? Avikshit said he had resolved to protect those who sought refuge, and Marutta, who blocked this, would not escape alive: either Marutta kills him and then the snakes, or he kills Marutta and saves the snakes; shame on a man who does not help one in distress who comes for refuge, even an enemy. Marutta said a king must kill even a friend, kinsman, father or teacher who obstructs the protection of his people; so he would strike his father, who should not be angry, for he must keep his own duty and bears him no anger. Seeing them set on killing each other, the Bhargava sages and others jumped between them and told Marutta not to shoot at his father, and Avikshit not to kill his famous son. Marutta said the king must kill the wicked and protect the good, and the snakes are wicked; where is his fault? Avikshit said he must protect those who seek refuge, and a son who kills them is at fault. The sages said the trembling snakes now offer to bring back to life the Brahmins they bit; so let both noble kings, who have kept their vows and know dharma, stop fighting. Vira then told her grandson that her word had set him to kill the snakes, and that task was done if the Brahmins live again; and the snakes, revived, may go free, since they took refuge with his parents. Bhamini said the nagas had begged her long ago, so she had sent her husband; now all has turned out well for both her husband and her son, Vira's grandson. The snakes brought the Brahmins back to life with divine herbs and by drawing out the poison. Marutta bowed at his parents' feet, and Avikshit embraced him lovingly and blessed him: may he humble his enemies, rule the earth long, enjoy his sons and grandsons and have no foes. With the Brahmins' and Vira's leave, father and son mounted a chariot and returned to their city with Bhamini. Vira, after great penance, reached her husband's world. Marutta ruled the earth justly, conquered the six inner enemies and enjoyed pleasures. His wives were Prabhavati of Vidarbha, Sauviri daughter of Suvira, Sukeshi daughter of Ketuvirya of Magadha, Kekayi daughter of Sindhuvirya king of Madra, Sairandhri daughter of Kekaya, Vapushmati daughter of the king of Sindhu, and a lovely daughter of the king of Chedi. He had eighteen sons, the eldest and chief being Narishyanta. His power was unchecked in the seven continents; there was never and will never be a king like him. Hearing the deeds and noble birth of Marutta frees one from all sins.

129.json.summary: Kraushtuki asks to hear about Marutta's descendants, the mighty kings fit to rule. Markandeya says Narishyanta was the eldest and best of Marutta's eighteen sons. Marutta ruled the whole earth for 85,000 years (the text says seventy, ten and five thousand), made great sacrifices, crowned Narishyanta and went to the forest, where after great penance he rose to heaven, his fame filling earth and sky. Wise Narishyanta reflected on the deeds of his father and other kings: his great ancestors in this line sacrificed, ruled justly, gave wealth and never fled from battle; who could follow them? He wished to do their righteous deeds, but what was left for him to do? A king who rules by dharma does no more than his duty, and one who rules badly goes to hell; with wealth a king must make sacrifices and give to those in need, nothing wonderful in that. Noble birth, shame, anger at enemies and protecting people make a king keep his duty and not flee from battle; all this his ancestors and his father Marutta did perfectly, and who can match them? Should he seek out wars to equal their courage? Or, since those kings made sacrifices themselves but did not cause others to make them, he would do that. So he made a single sacrifice such as no one else had made, glorious with gifts of wealth: first he gave Brahmins enough wealth to live on, then a hundred times more for their own sacrifices, and to every person on earth he gave cows, clothes, ornaments, granaries and the like. When he then began his own sacrifice again, he could not find Brahmins: every priest he chose said he too was consecrated for his own sacrifice; the king should choose another; with the endless wealth he had given them, how could he still give them anything? Finding no priests, he tried to give gifts outside the altar, but the Brahmins, their houses full of wealth, would not take them. Downcast, he said it was very good that no Brahmin on earth was poor, but bad that his treasury was useless, since he could not sacrifice: no one acts as priest, everyone is a sacrificer himself, and no Brahmin accepts gifts. Then he bowed with devotion again and again to some Brahmins and made them his priests, and they performed the great rite. It was a great wonder: during his sacrifice everyone on earth was a sacrificer; there were no Brahmins free to sit as assembly members; some Brahmins were sacrificers and some were their priests. With the wealth he had given, people all over the earth sacrificed at the same time: 18 crore sacrifices in the east, 7 crore in the west, 14 crore in the south and 50 crore in the north, all Brahmin sacrifices performed at once when Narishyanta sacrificed. Such was the righteous King Narishyanta, son of Marutta, famed for strength and manliness.

130.json.summary: Markandeya says Narishyanta's son was Dama, tamer (dama) of wicked enemies, strong as Indra and kind as a sage, born of Indrasena of Babhru's line after staying nine years in his mother's womb. Because he made his mother practise self-control (dama) while in the womb, and because he would be self-controlled, the family priest, who knew past, present and future, named him Dama. He learned all archery from Vrishaparvan, the whole set of missiles from the daitya Dundubhi who lived in a penance grove, the Vedas and all their branches from Shakti, and yoga from the royal sage Arshtishena. At a self-choice ceremony arranged by her father, Sumana, daughter of the strong Charuvarman, king of Dasharna, chose him before all who had come. But Mahananda, son of the king of Madra, and Vapushman, son of Sankrandana king of Vidarbha, a great archer, both desired her, and seeing Dama chosen, these and a third prince, maddened by love, plotted to seize her by force and take her home, where she could choose one of them; if she wanted none, she would belong to whoever killed Dama. The three princes seized her at Dama's side. Some kings of their party cheered, others protested, some stayed neutral. Dama, calm, asked the kings whether it was dharma or not that these men took by force a girl given at a lawful self-choice: if it is not, she should not become another's wife; if it is, he must give his life defending her. Charuvarman silenced the assembly and asked the kings to say how neither his dharma nor Dama's would be lost. Some kings said the gandharva form of marriage, by mutual love, is best for kshatriyas, not for vaishyas, shudras or Brahmins, and it was completed when the princess chose Dama, so she is Dama's by dharma; anyone acting otherwise acts from lust. Others, of the princes' party, said the gandharva form is not the rule for kshatriyas; the rakshasa form is, for those who live by arms: whoever carries her off by force after killing his rivals wins her, and of the two forms this is the more important, so Mahananda and the others acted rightly. The first kings replied that the rakshasa form is indeed approved for kshatriyas, but it applies when a girl, still under her father's authority, is taken by force after defeating her family; here, before all the kings, she chose Dama, so the gandharva marriage is complete; a married girl is no longer a maiden, and marriage creates the bond; those who would take her from Dama by force may do it if they are strong, but it is not right. Hearing this, Dama, eyes red with anger, strung his bow and said: if his wife is carried off by the strong before his eyes, what good is his family or his arms? Shame on his weapons, courage, arrows and bow, and on his birth in great Marutta's family, if these fools take his wife while he lives; let them fight hard to win her by defeating him. He covered them with arrows as darkness covers trees; they hurled arrows, spears, swords and clubs, which he cut with ease. Mahananda, sword in hand, came at him; Dama rained arrows like Indra, Mahananda cut them with his sword, climbed onto Dama's chariot and fought him; Dama shot an arrow like the fire of doom into his heart; Mahananda pulled it out and hurled his shining sword, which Dama broke with a spear, and with a reed-leaf arrow cut off Mahananda's head. Most kings turned away, but Vapushman, lord of Kundina, prince of the southern king, proud of his strength, fought on; Dama cut his sword, his charioteer's head and his banner, cut the spiked mace in his hand, and before he could take another weapon, shot him to the ground, where he lay trembling and gave up fighting. Seeing him so, Dama let him go and left with Sumana. The king of Dasharna happily held their wedding with due rites. After a short stay, Dama went home with his wife, and the king sent them off with elephants, horses, chariots, cattle, donkeys, camels, many male and female servants, clothes, ornaments, bows, fine furniture, seats and other goods.

131.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Dama and Sumana bowed at the feet of his father and mother and were blessed, and there was a great festival in Narishyanta's city at his return with a wife; Narishyanta rejoiced to hear from his son of his new relative, the king of Dasharna, and the defeated kings. Dama enjoyed life with Sumana in fine gardens, forests and on hills near the palace, and in time she conceived. King Narishyanta, having enjoyed life and grown old, crowned Dama and went to the forest with his wife Indrasena, living by the rules of the forest-dweller. The wicked southern prince Vapushman, son of Sankrandana, went into that forest to hunt deer with a few followers. He saw Narishyanta, an ascetic covered in dirt, and his wife Indrasena, very weak from penance, and asked whether he was a Brahmin, a kshatriya living in the forest, or a vaishya in the forest stage. The king, keeping a vow of silence, did not answer, but Indrasena told him everything truly. Learning that this was Narishyanta, father of his enemy, Vapushman cried 'I have got you', seized him by his matted hair in anger and dragged him while Indrasena (here once called Chandrasena) wept, saying: he would kill the father of Dama, who beat him in battle, took Sumana from him and drove away all the princes who had come for her; let Dama save him if he could. Then, as Indrasena cried, he cut off Narishyanta's head. The sages and other forest dwellers cried 'Shame!', and he went back to his city. After he left, Indrasena sighed and sent a shudra ascetic to her son Dama with a message: you know what happened to my husband; still I, deeply grieved, tell you to see this insult to the king. My husband made you king, protector of the four stages of life; is it right that you do not protect ascetics? My husband was an ascetic devoted to penance; as I lament, you are like one with no protector. Dragged by the hair without any fault, he was killed by Vapushman, and the king has become famous for this. In this state, do what keeps dharma from being lost; I cannot stay, since I am an ascetic. Your aged father, an ascetic with no fault, was killed; think what must be done to his killer; consult your brave ministers who know all the sciences and act; we ascetics have no right to act here. She gives examples: when Viduratha's father was killed by a Yavana, Viduratha destroyed his family; when the asura king Jambha's father was bitten by snakes, Jambha killed all the snakes of the underworld; when Parashara heard that his father Shakti had been killed by a rakshasa, he burned the whole race of rakshasas in fire. A kshatriya cannot bear an insult even to another of his line, much less his father's murder. It was not your father who was killed, not on him the weapon fell; I think it was you who were killed and on you the weapon fell. Who fears the weapons of one who has given up protecting forest dwellers? Whether the king's son fears or not, deal with Vapushman, his servants, kin and relatives as this insult deserves. Having sent this message, the brave Indrasena embraced her husband's body and entered the fire.

132.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Sent by Indrasena, the shudra ascetic went and told Dama of his father's death just as it happened. Hearing of his father's murder, Dama blazed with anger like a fire fed with ghee, ground one hand against the other and said: while I, his son, live, my father was killed like one without a protector by a most cruel man, in contempt of my family. Should I just grieve, or forgive out of cowardice? We are charged with putting down the wicked and protecting the good, yet my enemies live after killing my father; what use is crying 'Ah father'? I will do what must be done instead of lamenting. He vowed: if he did not satisfy his father with the blood from Vapushman's body, offering water rites to his father with his blood, feeding Brahmins properly with his flesh and giving the rice-ball offering, he would enter the fire. If asuras, gods, yakshas, gandharvas, vidyadharas or siddhas help Vapushman, he would burn them to ashes with his missiles. After killing in battle that cowardly, unrighteous, base southern king he would rule the whole earth, or else enter the fire. Today he would kill that wicked killer of an old ascetic living in the forest, together with all his kin, friends, foot soldiers, elephants, horses and army; taking bow and sword, mounted on his chariot, he would make such a slaughter of the enemy that all the gods could watch; whoever helps Vapushman, he would destroy that one's whole family with the army of his own arms. Even if Indra with his thunderbolt, Yama with his fierce staff raised in anger, Kubera, Varuna and the sun try to protect him, he would still kill him with sharp arrows. Since his father, self-controlled and blameless, living in the forest on fallen fruit and friendly to all beings, was killed while his son was able to protect him, let the vultures today be filled with the killer's flesh and blood.

133.json.summary: Markandeya continues. Having vowed this, Dama, eyes rolling with anger, gripped his beard, cried 'Ah, I am ruined', thought of his father, blamed fate, and called all his ministers and the family priest. He told them what the shudra ascetic had said: his old father, an ascetic in the forest stage, keeping a vow of silence and unarmed, was identified to Vapushman by his mother Indrasena, who honestly told him who they were; the wicked man drew his sword, held his matted hair in his left hand and killed the lord of the world as if he had no protector; his mother, sending him a message and crying shame on her unlucky, luckless son, entered the fire embracing Narishyanta and went to heaven. He would now do what his mother said: let the army of elephants, horses, chariots and foot soldiers be readied; how could he wish to live without avenging his father, killing the murderer and doing his mother's word? The ministers, crying out in grief, did so, and set out with servants, troops and vehicles, putting King Dama in front, after taking the blessing of the priest who knew the three times. Hissing like a king of snakes, Dama marched quickly south against Vapushman, killing border guards and vassals on the way. Vapushman, full of anger, learned that Dama had come with his followers, ministers and gear; with a steady mind he ordered out his troops, went outside the city and sent a messenger: 'Come quickly, Narishyanta is waiting for you; come to me with your wife, you poor excuse for a kshatriya; my sharp, thirsty arrows will pierce your body in battle and drink your blood.' Hearing this, Dama hurried on, remembering his vow and hissing like a snake. A fierce battle followed, chariot against chariot, elephant against elephant, horse against horse, while the gods, siddhas, gandharvas and rakshasas watched and the earth shook. No elephant, chariot fighter or horseman could stand his arrows. Vapushman's army chief fought Dama and, struck in the heart, went to Yama; when he fell, the army fled. Dama called to Vapushman: 'Where are you going, wicked one, after killing my father, an unarmed ascetic? You are a kshatriya; turn back.' He turned and fought Dama with his younger brother, his sons, relatives and kin, filling the directions with arrows and covering Dama and his chariot. Dama, with the anger born of his father's murder, cut their arrows and pierced them, killing seven sons with one arrow each, and sending relatives, kinsmen and friends to Yama. Vapushman, his sons and kin dead, fought on with snake-like arrows, which Dama cut; both bows were broken, and the two mighty men came down with swords and fought. Dama, thinking for a moment of his father killed in the forest, dragged Vapushman by the hair, threw him down, put his foot on his neck and, raising his arm, said: 'Let all the gods, men, snakes and birds see the heart of this low kshatriya Vapushman torn open.' He tore open his heart, and when he wanted to drink the blood the gods stopped him. He then offered the water rite to his father with that blood, and, freed of his debt to his father, returned home. He made the rice-ball offering with Vapushman's flesh and, the text says, fed Brahmins born of rakshasa families with it. Markandeya says such were the kings born in the solar line, and there were others too, wise, brave, sacrificers, knowers of dharma, masters of the Vedanta, too many to count here; hearing their deeds frees a person from sins.

134.json.summary: The birds tell Jaimini that after telling all this, the great sage Markandeya sent Kraushtuki away and performed his midday rites. They have told Jaimini what they heard from him: this Purana, without beginning, was told long ago by Brahma, the self-born, to Markandeya; it is holy, purifying, gives long life and success in dharma, pleasure and wealth, and frees those who read or hear it from all sins at once. They have answered the four questions asked at the start, and covered the dialogue of father and son, Brahma's creation, the periods of the Manus and the deeds of kings; whoever hears or recites all this in assemblies shakes off all sins and merges in Brahma at the end. Of the eighteen Puranas told by Brahma, the Markandeya is the seventh: Brahma, Padma, Vishnu, Shiva, Bhagavata, Naradiya, Markandeya, then Agni (eighth), Bhavishya (ninth), Brahmavaivarta (tenth), Linga (eleventh), Varaha (twelfth), Skanda (thirteenth), Vamana (fourteenth), Kurma (fifteenth), then Matsya, Garuda and Brahmanda. One who recites the names of the eighteen Puranas at the three times of day gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. A Purana has five marks: creation, re-creation, lineages, Manu periods and the deeds of dynasties; this one, with its four questions, is the best. Hearing it destroys the sins of countless ages, even killing a Brahmin, like grass blown by wind; hearing it gives the merit of gifts at Pushkara, and finishing it gives more than all the Vedas. One who has it recited should honour the reciter like Brahma with scents, flowers, clothes and feeding Brahmins, and kings should give villages and vehicles as they can; after hearing the whole Purana one should worship Vyasa and give the teacher a cow with gold, clothes and ornaments. One who hears even one verse without honouring the reciter gets no merit and is called a thief of scripture; gods and ancestors are not pleased with him, he gets no fruit from shraddha or bathing at holy places and is blamed among good people; one who scorns it while it is read is born dumb and foolish for seven births. One who hears and honours it is freed from all sins, purifies his family, goes to Vishnu's eternal world and is never born a man again, and gains the highest yoga. It must not be given to an unbeliever, a vrishala, one who reviles the Veda, teachers, Brahmins or parents, one who has broken vows or limits, or one angry with his kin, even at the cost of one's life; one who reads or teaches it to such people from greed, delusion or fear surely goes to hell. Markandeya's closing words say this whole story gives heaven and release; whoever hears or reads it gets what he wishes, is free from mental and bodily suffering and from sins like killing a Brahmin or taking another's wife or wealth; good people become his friends, he has no enemies or robbers, no famine, and always has prosperity, memory, peace, fortune, health and contentment; he is honoured in heaven by Indra and the gods and rises there on a fine aerial chariot. The text gives the size of the Purana as 6,800 verses plus a further number (the wording, 'eighty-nine' and 'eleven', is unclear). Jaimini then tells the birds that they have cleared the doubts the Mahabharata raised in him, as no one else could; he blesses them with long life, wisdom, steady understanding of Sankhya and yoga, and freedom from the sorrow caused by their father's curse; then he goes back to his hermitage, thinking about the birds' noble words. The closing line of the file is cut off.
